Code that used acc.balance directly would all break. This freedom to change the inside is one of the biggest practical benefits.

Read-only and write-only properties: A field with only a getter is read-only from outside, like an account number. A field with only a setter is write-only, like a PIN that can be changed but never read back. Combining private fields with a chosen set of methods lets you design exactly what is allowed.

Encapsulation versus abstraction: These two are often confused. Encapsulation is about how: putting data and code together and controlling access with modifiers, so the inside cannot be misused. Abstraction is about what: exposing a simple idea and hiding complexity, so users think only about essentials. An ATM's buttons are abstraction (you just think "withdraw"); the locked cash box behind them is encapsulation. In code, private fields are an encapsulation tool, while interfaces and abstract classes are abstraction tools (lessons 13 and 14).

Immutable classes: An immutable object cannot change after it is created. Java's String is immutable. To make your own immutable class: make the class final so nobody can subclass it and add changing methods; make all fields private and final; set them only in the constructor; provide getters but no setters; and if a field refers to a mutable object, such as an array, copy it in the constructor and return copies from getters. final class Point { private final int x, y; Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } int getX() { return x; } int getY() { return y; } }.

Why immutability helps: An immutable object can be shared freely between parts of a program, or between threads (lesson 21), with no fear that someone will change it behind your back. It is always in a valid state, because the constructor checked it once. To "change" it, you create a new object: p.moveRight() returns new Point(x + 1, y). Values like dates, money amounts and coordinates are often made immutable.

The leaking reference trap: Suppose class Team { private String[] players; public String[] getPlayers() { return players; } }. The field is private, but the getter returns the actual array reference. Outside code can do team.getPlayers()[0] = "Hacker"; and change the team. Encapsulation has leaked. The fix is to return a copy: return players.clone();, or an unmodifiable list in modern code. The same applies when a constructor receives a mutable object: store a copy, not the caller's reference.

Benefits of encapsulation, summarized: Data integrity, because rules are enforced in one place. Flexibility, because the internal representation can change. Easier debugging, because if a field goes wrong only the class's own methods could have done it. Clear interfaces, because the public methods document what the class offers. Security, because sensitive data like PINs is not exposed.

Private helper methods: Fields are not the only things to hide. Methods that are just internal steps should be private too. In an Account class, a method private boolean isValidAmount(double a) { return a > 0 && a <= 50000; } can be used by deposit, withdraw and transfer, but outsiders have no reason to call it. Keeping helpers private means you can rename, split or delete them later without breaking anyone, because nobody outside could depend on them.

A tiny design exercise: Design a Thermometer class for a fridge. The temperature must stay between -20 and 10 degrees. Field: private double temp. Constructor: takes a starting temperature and rejects values outside the range. Getter: getTemp(). No plain setter; instead, methods colder() and warmer() change temp by 1 degree, but refuse to go past the limits. Notice how thinking about the rules first decides which methods exist. This is exactly the kind of short design answer that earns full marks.

Encapsulation in other languages: C++ uses the same words, private, protected and public, but writes them as sections: class Account { private: double balance; public: void deposit(double a); };, and members of a C++ class are private by default (lesson 22). Python has no enforced private; it uses a naming convention, a leading underscore like _balance, to say "please do not touch". The idea is the same everywhere, but Java and C++ let the compiler enforce it.

Real life example 1, a bKash wallet: class Wallet { private String pin; private double balance; public boolean sendMoney(Wallet to, double amt, String enteredPin) { if (!pin.equals(enteredPin) || amt <= 0 || amt > balance) return false; balance -= amt; to.receive(amt); return true; } private void receive(double amt) { balance += amt; } }. Note that receive is private: only Wallet objects themselves can call it, so outsiders cannot create money. In Java, private means private to the class, so one Wallet object can call another Wallet object's private method.

Real life example 2, a student result portal: class Result { private int[] marks; public Result(int[] marks) { for (int m : marks) if (m < 0 || m > 100) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad mark"); this.marks = marks.clone(); } public double average() { int sum = 0; for (int m : marks) sum += m; return (double) sum / marks.length; } }. Marks are checked once, copied so nobody can change them from outside, and there is no setter. Teachers can see the average; nobody can quietly bump a mark from 38 to 80.

Common mistakes: Making fields public "to keep it simple". Writing a setter for everything. Returning internal arrays or lists directly. Confusing default (no modifier) with public. Thinking protected means "only subclasses" (it also includes the same package). Thinking private hides data from other objects of the same class (it does not; privacy is per class).

What exams ask: "Define encapsulation with an example", "What are access modifiers? Show their visibility in a table", "Why should fields be private?", "Write a BankAccount class with proper encapsulation", "Differentiate between encapsulation and abstraction", and "How do you make a class immutable?".

Recap: Encapsulation bundles data and methods and hides the data behind access modifiers. private, default, protected and public give increasing visibility. Getters and setters, used thoughtfully, guard and validate data, and let the internal representation change freely. Immutable classes take this further: final fields, no setters, defensive copies. Next, we look at the most used class in Java, String, and the wrapper classes, both of which are built on these ideas.
key_points: Encapsulation = bundling data with its methods + hiding the data from direct outside access.
Access levels from strict to open: private, default (package), protected, public.
protected allows the same package and subclasses in other packages.
Getters and setters let the class validate, convert and protect its data.
Only expose what is needed: not every field needs a setter (or a getter).
Encapsulation lets the internal representation change without breaking other classes.
Immutable class: final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies.
Returning an internal array or list directly leaks encapsulation.
lessons.tip: For every field ask two questions: should outsiders read it, and should outsiders change it? Your answers decide which getters and setters exist.
lessons.task: Write a BankAccount class with a private balance, a getter, and deposit/withdraw methods that reject negative or too-large amounts. In main, try acc.balance = 100 and read the compiler error.

quiz.q: Which access modifier makes a member visible only inside its own class?
quiz.explain: private is the most restrictive level.

quiz.q: A member with no access modifier is visible to:
quiz.explain: No modifier means default (package-private) access.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a setter with validation?
options: To stop invalid values being stored
quiz.explain: The class checks rules in one place before changing its data.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a step in making a class immutable?
options: Return internal arrays directly from getters
quiz.explain: Returning internal mutable objects lets outsiders change the state; return copies instead.

quiz.q: protected members are accessible from:
options: Same package and subclasses in other packages
quiz.explain: protected = package access plus subclass access.

lessons.title: Strings and Wrapper Classes
lessons.content:
Every app you use is full of text: your name on Facebook, the message you send on WhatsApp, the address you type into Foodpanda, the OTP code from your bank. In Java, text is handled by the String class. It is probably the most used class in the whole language, and it is a wonderful example of the OOP ideas from the last lessons, especially immutability. In this lesson we study String, its faster cousin StringBuilder, and the wrapper classes that turn simple numbers into objects.

String is a class, not a primitive: String name = "Nusrat"; looks like a primitive assignment, but name is a reference to a String object. Java gives String special treatment: you can create one with a literal in double quotes instead of new, and you can join strings with +. Under the hood, a String holds a sequence of characters, and it offers dozens of methods.

Common String methods: For String s = "Bangladesh";: s.length() is 10. s.charAt(0) is 'B'. s.indexOf("desh") is 6, the position where "desh" starts, and indexOf returns -1 if not found. s.substring(0, 6) is "Bangla", from index 0 up to but not including 6. s.toUpperCase() is "BANGLADESH". s.contains("lad") is true. s.startsWith("Ban") and s.endsWith("sh") are true. s.replace('a', 'o') gives "Bonglodesh". "  hi  ".trim() gives "hi". "a,b,c".split(",") gives an array of three strings.

Strings are immutable: Once a String object is created, its characters can never change. Every method that seems to change a string actually returns a new String. s.toUpperCase() does not change s; it returns a new string. If you write s.toUpperCase(); on its own line and then print s, you still see "Bangladesh". You must write s = s.toUpperCase(); to make s point to the new object. This is the number one String bug in student code.

Why Java made String immutable: Strings are used as keys in maps, as file names, as passwords, as network addresses and as class names. If they could change after being checked, that would be a security and correctness risk: a file name checked as safe could be changed before the file opens. Immutable strings can also be shared safely between threads, and their hash code can be cached, which makes them fast as HashMap keys (lesson 19). It also makes the string pool possible.

The string pool: Because strings cannot change, Java can safely share identical literals. All string literals live in a special area called the string pool. When you write String a = "Dhaka"; String b = "Dhaka";, Java creates only one "Dhaka" object in the pool, and both a and b point to it. But String c = new String("Dhaka"); forces a brand new object on the heap, outside the pool, even though the text is the same.

== versus equals for strings: Now you can see why == is dangerous. == compares references. In the example above, a == b is true (same pooled object), but a == c is false (different objects), even though all three say "Dhaka". Strings typed by the user or read from a file are usually new objects, so == will often be false for equal text. Always use a.equals(c), which compares the characters and returns true. For case-insensitive comparison, use equalsIgnoreCase. For alphabetical order, use compareTo, which returns a negative number, zero or a positive number.

Concatenation and its cost: "Roll: " + 42 + " CGPA: " + 3.8 builds a new string. Because strings are immutable, a loop like String s = ""; for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) s = s + i; creates a new String object in every round and copies all previous characters each time. The work grows roughly with the square of the length, so it gets very slow for big loops.

StringBuilder: When you need to build up text step by step, use StringBuilder, a mutable sequence of characters. StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) sb.append(i); String result = sb.toString();. append changes the same object instead of creating new ones, so this is far faster. StringBuilder also has insert, delete, reverse and setCharAt. new StringBuilder("level").reverse().toString() gives "level", a quick palindrome test. Notice append returns this, which allows chaining like sb.append("Hi").append(' ').append(5).

StringBuffer: StringBuffer is an older class with the same methods as StringBuilder, but its methods are synchronized, which makes it safe for multiple threads at a small speed cost. In normal single-threaded code, prefer StringBuilder. Exams often ask for a three-way comparison: String is immutable; StringBuilder is mutable and not thread-safe but fast; StringBuffer is mutable and thread-safe but slower.

Converting to and from strings: String.valueOf(42) gives "42". Integer.toString(42) also works, as does "" + 42. In the other direction, Integer.parseInt("42") gives the int 42 and Double.parseDouble("3.75") gives 3.75. If the text is not a valid number, such as Integer.parseInt("4o2"), Java throws a NumberFormatException, a common runtime error when reading user input.

Characters and Unicode: Java's char is a 16-bit Unicode unit, and Strings are Unicode too, so they can hold Bangla text like "আমার সোনার বাংলা". The Character class has helpers: Character.isDigit('7') is true, Character.isLetter('a') is true, Character.toUpperCase('q') is 'Q'. A simple loop with charAt and these helpers lets you count vowels, digits or spaces in a sentence.

Wrapper classes, the idea: Java's primitives (int, double, char, boolean and the rest) are not objects. They have no methods and cannot be null. But many parts of Java, especially the collections in lesson 19, only work with objects. So Java provides a wrapper class for each primitive: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character and Boolean. A wrapper object simply holds one primitive value inside, like a gift box around a single sweet.

What wrappers give you: Useful constants and methods, such as Integer.MAX_VALUE (2147483647), Integer.MIN_VALUE, Integer.parseInt, Integer.toBinaryString(10) which gives "1010", and Double.compare. The possibility of null, which can mean "no value yet", for example a Double score that has not been entered. And the ability to be stored in collections like ArrayList<Integer>, because you cannot write ArrayList<int>.

Autoboxing and unboxing: Converting a primitive into its wrapper is called boxing; converting back is called unboxing. Since Java 5 the compiler does it automatically. Integer x = 25; is autoboxing (the compiler writes Integer.valueOf(25) for you). int y = x; is auto-unboxing (it calls x.intValue()). In a list, list.add(7) boxes the 7, and int first = list.get(0) unboxes it. It feels like magic, but there are traps.

Trap 1, null unboxing: Integer marks = null; int m = marks; compiles but throws a NullPointerException at runtime, because there is no int inside a null box. This often happens when reading a missing value from a map: int count = map.get("Sylhet"); crashes if the key is not present.

Trap 2, == on wrappers: Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100; a == b is true, but Integer c = 1000; Integer d = 1000; c == d is usually false. Why? Integer.valueOf caches objects for small values, from -128 to 127, so a and b share one cached object, while c and d are separate objects. == compares references again. Always compare wrapper values with equals, or unbox to int first.

Trap 3, performance: Boxing creates objects. A loop that adds a million numbers into a Long sum, Long sum = 0L; for (...) sum += i;, boxes and unboxes a million times and runs much slower than with a primitive long sum. Use primitives for heavy arithmetic and wrappers when you need objects.

A worked string example, counting words: Suppose you want to count words in "  Amar   sonar Bangla  ". First trim the ends, giving "Amar   sonar Bangla". Then split on one or more spaces with split("\\s+"), a regular expression meaning "one or more whitespace characters". The result is an array of three strings, so the word count is 3. In Java source the backslash itself must be escaped, which is why you type two backslashes before the s. If you split on a single space " " instead, the extra spaces create empty strings in the array and your count is wrong. Small details like this are why reading the documentation of String methods pays off.

String formatting: For neat output, String.format works like printf but returns a string instead of printing it: String line = String.format("%-10s %5.2f", "Rahim", 3.756); gives the name padded to 10 characters and the CGPA rounded to 3.76 in a 5-character column. This is handy for receipts, tables and reports. Modern Java also has text blocks, written between triple double quotes, for multi-line strings such as an SMS template.

Comparing strings alphabetically: compareTo compares character by character using Unicode values. "apple".compareTo("banana") is negative because 'a' comes before 'b'. "Zebra".compareTo("apple") is also negative, because all capital letters come before small letters in Unicode, which surprises people when sorting names. Use compareToIgnoreCase when case should not matter. Sorting a list of names, covered in lesson 19, relies on exactly this method.

Empty, blank and null strings: Three different situations often get mixed up. A null String reference points to no object at all, so calling any method on it throws a NullPointerException. An empty string "" is a real object with length 0, and s.isEmpty() returns true. A blank string such as "   " has length 3 but contains only spaces; s.isBlank(), available since Java 11, returns true for it. When checking form input, a safe pattern is if (s == null || s.isBlank()), which tests null first so the second call never runs on a null reference.

Real life example 1, validating a Bangladeshi mobile number: String n = input.trim(); if (n.startsWith("+88")) n = n.substring(3);. Then check n.length() == 11, n.startsWith("01"), and that every char is a digit with Character.isDigit. Notice that every step returns a new string and we reassign n. Finally, the operator code n.substring(0, 3), such as "017", can be compared with equals against a list of known codes.

Real life example 2, building an SMS receipt: A shop sends a receipt after each sale. StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); sb.append("Thank you, ").append(name).append("! Items: ").append(count).append(", Total: Tk ").append(total); String sms = sb.toString();. Prices typed by the cashier arrive as text, so Double.parseDouble turns them into numbers, and a try-catch (lesson 17) handles a NumberFormatException if the cashier types "12o".

Common mistakes: Using == to compare strings. Calling s.toUpperCase() and expecting s to change. Building long strings with + in a loop. Forgetting that substring's end index is exclusive. Unboxing a null wrapper. Comparing Integer objects with ==. Calling parseInt on text with spaces; trim it first.

What exams ask: "Why is String immutable in Java?", "Differentiate between String, StringBuilder and StringBuffer", "What is the string pool?", "Explain == versus equals() with an example", "What are wrapper classes and why are they needed?", "Explain autoboxing and unboxing", and output questions like the Integer 127 versus 128 comparison.

Recap: String is an immutable class with a pool for literals; compare content with equals, and build text in loops with StringBuilder. StringBuffer is the synchronized version. Wrapper classes box primitives into objects so they can live in collections and be null, with autoboxing doing it for you, but watch out for null unboxing and == on wrappers. Next we go from single objects to groups: how objects relate to and contain each other.
key_points: String is an immutable class; methods like toUpperCase return new strings.
Identical literals share one object in the string pool; new String() makes a separate object.
Compare strings with equals (or equalsIgnoreCase, compareTo), never ==.
Use StringBuilder to build text in loops; StringBuffer is the synchronized version.
Integer.parseInt and Double.parseDouble convert text to numbers and may throw NumberFormatException.
Wrapper classes (Integer, Double, Character...) box primitives into objects.
Autoboxing/unboxing is automatic, but unboxing null throws NullPointerException.
Integer caches -128..127, so == on wrappers is unreliable; use equals.
lessons.tip: Whenever you call a String method, ask: where does the new string go? If you do not assign it, it is lost.
lessons.task: Write a program that reads a sentence, counts its vowels and digits using charAt and Character methods, and prints the sentence reversed using StringBuilder.

quiz.q: String s = "dhaka"; s.toUpperCase(); System.out.println(s); prints:
quiz.explain: Strings are immutable; the result was not assigned back to s.

quiz.q: Which compares the content of two strings correctly?
quiz.explain: equals compares characters; == compares references.

quiz.q: Which is mutable and best for building text in a single-threaded loop?
quiz.explain: StringBuilder is mutable and not synchronized, so it is fast.

quiz.q: Integer m = null; int x = m; What happens?
quiz.explain: Unboxing null has no int to extract.

quiz.q: Why do we need wrapper classes?
options: Collections like ArrayList store objects, not primitives
quiz.explain: Generic collections need objects, so ints are boxed as Integer.

lessons.title: Object Relationships: Association, Aggregation, Composition
lessons.content:
No object lives alone. A student belongs to a department, takes several courses and has a library card. A car has an engine and four wheels. A teacher teaches many students, and a student is taught by many teachers. In a real program, the interesting part is not a single object but how objects connect. This lesson is about those connections: association, aggregation, composition and dependency, plus the "has-a" and "is-a" relationships, and how to hold many objects in arrays.

Why relationships matter: If you put everything into one class, you get a giant blob that is hard to change. If you split into classes but they cannot talk to each other, nothing useful happens. Good OOP design is about choosing the right classes and the right links between them. The words in this lesson are used in UML diagrams, in design discussions and in exam questions, so learn them precisely.

How a link looks in code: An object is linked to another object when it holds a reference to it, usually in a field. class Student { private String name; private Department dept; }. The field dept refers to a Department object that exists somewhere on the heap. Through it, a student can ask dept.getName(). The link is just a reference, exactly like the ones in lesson 3.

Association, the general idea: Association is the most general relationship: two classes are associated if objects of one know about, or use, objects of the other for some lasting period. Teacher and Student are associated; a teacher teaches students. Doctor and Patient are associated. Association says nothing about ownership or lifetime; it just says "these two are connected".

Direction of association: An association can be one-way (unidirectional) or two-way (bidirectional). If only Student holds a reference to Department, you can go from a student to its department but not back; that is unidirectional. If Department also holds a list of its students, you can navigate both ways; that is bidirectional. Bidirectional links are more convenient but harder to keep consistent: when a student changes department, both sides must be updated.

Multiplicity: Associations also have numbers, called multiplicity or cardinality. One-to-one: a person has one NID card, and each NID belongs to one person. One-to-many: a department has many students, each student belongs to one department. Many-to-many: a student takes many courses, a course has many students. In UML you write these as 1, 0..1, * or 1..* at the ends of the line. In code, "many" usually becomes an array or a list.

Implementing one-to-many: class Department { private String name; private Student[] students = new Student[100]; private int count = 0; public void addStudent(Student s) { if (count < students.length) students[count++] = s; } }. Each Department object holds up to 100 references. In lesson 19 we will replace the fixed array with an ArrayList that grows by itself.

Implementing many-to-many: Many-to-many often needs a class of its own in the middle. Student and Course are many-to-many, but there is extra data about each pairing: the grade and the semester. So we create Enrollment { Student student; Course course; String semester; String grade; }. Each enrollment links one student and one course. This "association class" idea is also how databases handle many-to-many relationships.

Aggregation, a weak has-a: Aggregation is a special kind of association that means "whole and part", but where the part can exist independently of the whole. A Department has Teachers, but if the department is closed, the teachers still exist; they can move to another department. A cricket Team has Players; if the team is dissolved, the players are still players. In UML aggregation is drawn with a hollow diamond at the whole's end.

Aggregation in code: Usually the part is created outside and passed in. Player p = new Player("Shakib"); Team t = new Team("Bangladesh"); t.addPlayer(p);. The team stores the reference, but it did not create the player and does not control the player's life. The same player object could also be referenced by a ClubTeam object at the same time.

Composition, a strong has-a: Composition is a stronger form of whole and part: the part cannot exist without the whole, and the whole is responsible for creating and destroying it. A House has Rooms; if the house is demolished, its rooms are gone too, and a room belongs to exactly one house. A Human has a Heart. An Order has OrderLines. In UML composition is drawn with a filled black diamond.

Composition in code: The whole usually creates its parts itself, often in its constructor, and never gives out references that would let them live elsewhere. class Car { private final Engine engine; Car(int cc) { engine = new Engine(cc); } public void start() { engine.ignite(); } }. Nobody outside creates or holds this Engine, so when the Car object becomes unreachable, its engine becomes unreachable too, and both are garbage collected.

Aggregation versus composition, the test: Ask two questions. Can the part exist on its own, meaningfully, without this whole? Can the part be shared by several wholes? If yes, it is aggregation. If the part lives and dies with the whole and belongs to only one whole, it is composition. Library has Books: aggregation, since books can move to another library. Book has Pages: composition, since a page of this book does not exist separately.

Dependency, the weakest link: A dependency means one class uses another briefly, without holding a reference as a field. For example, a method void print(Printer p) uses a Printer only during the call, or a method creates a temporary Formatter inside. If the Printer class changes, this class might need to change, which is why it is called a dependency. In UML it is a dashed arrow. Dependencies are normal, but fewer dependencies make code easier to change.

Has-a versus is-a: Inheritance (lesson 10) models "is-a": a Car is a Vehicle. Association, aggregation and composition model "has-a": a Car has an Engine. Beginners sometimes make Car inherit from Engine to reuse engine methods, which is wrong, because a car is not an engine. The well-known design advice "favour composition over inheritance" says: when in doubt, put an object inside rather than inheriting from it. Composition is more flexible because you can swap the part at runtime, for example replacing a PetrolEngine with an ElectricEngine.

Delegation: When a whole receives a request and passes it on to a part, that is called delegation. car.start() calls engine.ignite(); the car delegates the job. Delegation is how composition gives the whole new abilities without inheritance. Users of Car do not even need to know there is an Engine object inside, which is encapsulation and abstraction working together.

Arrays of objects in depth: Since many relationships are "one-to-many", arrays of objects are everywhere. Student[] batch = new Student[3]; creates three null references. You must fill them: for (int i = 0; i < batch.length; i++) batch[i] = new Student("S" + i, i + 1);. To process them: for (Student s : batch) total += s.getCgpa();. To find the topper, loop and keep a reference to the best one so far: Student best = batch[0]; for (Student s : batch) if (s.getCgpa() > best.getCgpa()) best = s;.

Sorting an array of objects, a preview: Arrays.sort works on numbers directly, but for objects Java must know what order you mean: by roll, by name, or by CGPA? That is solved with Comparable or Comparator in lesson 19. For now you can write a simple bubble sort that compares s[j].getCgpa() with s[j + 1].getCgpa() and swaps the references, not the data inside the objects.

Keeping a bidirectional link consistent, worked example: Suppose Student has a field dept and Department has a list of students. A safe way is to let one method do both updates: in Department, public void addStudent(Student s) { students[count++] = s; s.setDepartmentInternal(this); }. Now when the CSE department adds Rahim, Rahim's dept also points to CSE. When Rahim moves to EEE, the move method should remove him from CSE's list and add him to EEE's, again in one place. If two different parts of the code each update one side, sooner or later they disagree, and the program shows Rahim in two departments at once.

Composition and copying: Because a composed part belongs to its whole, copying the whole should copy the part too. If you write a copy constructor Car(Car other) { engine = other.engine; }, the two cars share one Engine object, which breaks composition: starting one car's engine changes the other's state. The correct copy is engine = new Engine(other.engine);, a fresh engine with the same settings. This is the shallow versus deep copy question, which lesson 15 studies with clone().

Choosing relationships, a quick checklist: First, is it is-a? If a sentence like "every Manager is an Employee" is always true, consider inheritance. Second, is it a lasting has-a? Then use a field. Third, does the part belong only to this whole and die with it? Then composition; otherwise aggregation or plain association. Fourth, is the use only inside one method? Then it is just a dependency, and you should not store it in a field at all. Going through these four questions on every link keeps designs clean.

Real life example 1, a university system: University has Departments (composition: a department belongs to one university and is created by it). Department has Teachers (aggregation: teachers can move). Teacher is associated with Courses (one teacher teaches many courses; a course may have several teachers, so many-to-many). Student and Course are linked through Enrollment, which holds the semester and grade. Drawing this on paper with diamonds and multiplicities is the exact skill exam questions test.

Real life example 2, a Foodpanda style order: An Order is composed of OrderItems: an item line like "2 x Kacchi Biryani, Tk 640" has no meaning outside its order, so the Order creates and owns them. The Order is associated with one Customer and one Restaurant, which exist independently (aggregation or plain association). The Rider is associated with the order only during delivery. A method calculateTotal() in Order loops over its items and delegates to each item's getSubtotal().

Common mistakes: Using inheritance where has-a is meant (Car extends Engine). Calling every has-a relationship "composition" without checking lifetime. Forgetting to create the objects inside an array of objects. Making bidirectional links and updating only one side. Exposing the internal array of parts through a getter, which breaks composition's control over its parts.

What exams ask: "Differentiate between association, aggregation and composition with examples", "What is the difference between is-a and has-a relationships?", "Why is composition often preferred over inheritance?", "Draw a UML diagram showing these relationships", and "Write a program using an array of objects to find the student with the highest CGPA".

Recap: Objects connect through references. Association is a general link with a direction and multiplicity. Aggregation is a weak whole-part link where parts live independently; composition is a strong one where parts live and die with the whole. Dependency is a temporary use. Has-a is modelled with these links, is-a with inheritance, and composition with delegation is often the more flexible choice. Next, we finally study inheritance itself.
key_points: Objects link to each other by holding references, usually in fields.
Association is a general link with a direction (uni/bi) and multiplicity (1-1, 1-many, many-many).
Aggregation: weak whole-part; the part can exist independently (hollow diamond).
Composition: strong whole-part; the part lives and dies with the whole (filled diamond).
Dependency: a temporary use, e.g. a method parameter (dashed arrow).
is-a is inheritance; has-a is association/aggregation/composition.
Favour composition over inheritance; the whole delegates work to its parts.
new Student[n] creates null references; each object must be created separately.
lessons.tip: For every pair of classes ask: can the part live without the whole, and can it be shared? Those two answers tell you aggregation or composition.
lessons.task: Draw (on paper) classes for your university: University, Department, Teacher, Student, Course, Enrollment. Mark each link as association, aggregation or composition and write multiplicities.

quiz.q: A Team has Players who can join other teams after the team is dissolved. This is:
quiz.explain: The parts exist independently of the whole, so it is aggregation.

quiz.q: A House has Rooms that cannot exist without that house. This is:
quiz.explain: Rooms live and die with their house: composition.

quiz.q: Which is a correct is-a relationship?
quiz.explain: Inheritance models is-a; a car really is a kind of vehicle.

quiz.q: What does Student[] batch = new Student[5]; create?
quiz.explain: The array holds references that must each be assigned a new Student.

quiz.q: Student and Course have many-to-many links with a grade per pair. A good design is:
options: An Enrollment class linking one student, one course and the grade
quiz.explain: An association class holds the data that belongs to each pairing.

lessons.title: Inheritance
lessons.content:
In many Bangladeshi families, children inherit things from their parents: the family name, the house, maybe even the shape of their nose. But every child also has their own talents. One becomes a doctor, another a cricketer. They did not start from nothing; they started from what the parents had, and added their own. Inheritance in OOP works the same way: a new class starts with everything an existing class has, and then adds or changes what it needs. It is the third pillar of OOP.

What inheritance is: Inheritance is a mechanism where one class acquires the fields and methods of another class. The existing class is called the superclass, parent class or base class. The new class is called the subclass, child class or derived class. In Java you write it with the keyword extends: class CSEStudent extends Student { ... }. A CSEStudent object automatically has everything a Student has, such as name, roll and introduce(), plus whatever CSEStudent adds.

The is-a test: Inheritance should model an is-a relationship. A CSEStudent is a Student. A Car is a Vehicle. A SavingsAccount is an Account. If you cannot honestly say "every X is a Y", inheritance is probably the wrong tool; lesson 9 showed that has-a relationships should use composition instead. The is-a test is the first thing to check before writing extends.

A first example: class Animal { String name; void eat() { System.out.println(name + " is eating"); } } class Dog extends Animal { void bark() { System.out.println(name + " says woof"); } }. In main: Dog d = new Dog(); d.name = "Tommy"; d.eat(); d.bark();. Output: "Tommy is eating" then "Tommy says woof". Dog never declared name or eat(), but it has them, because it inherited them from Animal.

Why inheritance is useful: Reuse, because common code is written once in the parent. Extension, because a child adds new features without touching the tested parent code. Organisation, because classes form a natural family tree that matches how we think. And polymorphism, which needs inheritance (or interfaces) to work, as lesson 12 shows. Imagine ten kinds of bank accounts: without inheritance, the balance, deposit and owner code would be copied ten times.

What is inherited and what is not: A subclass inherits all public and protected members of its parent, and package-private members if it is in the same package. Private fields are part of every child object in memory, but the child's code cannot touch them directly by name; it must use the parent's public or protected methods, such as getters. Constructors are never inherited. Static members belong to the class, and although a child can access them through its own name, they are not copied per object.

Private fields and inheritance in practice: class Account { private double balance; protected void addToBalance(double amt) { balance += amt; } public double getBalance() { return balance; } } class SavingsAccount extends Account { void addInterest(double rate) { addToBalance(getBalance() * rate); } }. SavingsAccount cannot write balance += ... because balance is private to Account, but it can use the protected and public methods. This keeps the parent's rules in control even when children are written by other programmers.

The super keyword: Inside a subclass, super refers to the parent part of the current object. It has two uses. super(...) calls a parent constructor. super.method() calls the parent's version of a method, which becomes important when the child overrides it (lesson 11). You can also write super.field to reach a parent field that is hidden by a child field with the same name, although hiding fields like that is confusing and should be avoided.

Constructors and super(...): Since constructors are not inherited, a child must make sure the parent part is initialized. It does this by calling a parent constructor with super(...), which must be the first statement in the child constructor. class Student { String name; Student(String name) { this.name = name; } } class CSEStudent extends Student { String favLang; CSEStudent(String name, String favLang) { super(name); this.favLang = favLang; } }. The parent sets name, the child sets favLang.

The hidden super(): If a child constructor does not call super(...) or this(...) itself, Java inserts super(); automatically as the first line, calling the parent's no-argument constructor. If the parent has no no-arg constructor, for example because it only has Student(String name), the child fails to compile with an error like "constructor Student in class Student cannot be applied to given types". This is one of the most common inheritance errors in labs. The fix is to call super(name) explicitly.

Constructor execution order: When you create a child object, constructors run from the top of the family tree down. For class A, class B extends A, class C extends B, new C() runs A's constructor first, then B's, then C's. It makes sense: a child is built on top of its parent, like floors of a building, so the ground floor must be finished first. If each constructor prints a message, the output is A, B, C.

Types of inheritance: Single inheritance: one parent, one child, such as Dog extends Animal. Multilevel inheritance: a chain, such as Puppy extends Dog extends Animal. Hierarchical inheritance: one parent, many children, such as Dog, Cat and Cow all extending Animal. Multiple inheritance: one child with several parents. Hybrid inheritance: a mix of the above. Java classes support single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance directly.

Why Java has no multiple inheritance of classes: In Java a class can extend only one class. class C extends A, B is a compile error. The reason is the diamond problem. Suppose A and B both have a method show() with different code, and C extends both. Which show() should c.show() run? Worse, if A and B both extend a common class D, does C contain one copy of D's fields or two? C++ allows multiple inheritance and needs extra rules (virtual inheritance) to handle this, as lesson 22 shows. Java's designers chose simplicity: one parent class, but a class can implement many interfaces (lesson 14), which gives most of the benefits safely.

The Object class at the top: Every Java class that does not extend anything explicitly extends Object automatically. So class Student is really class Student extends Object. That means every class is part of one big tree with Object at the root, and every object has methods like toString(), equals() and hashCode(), which lesson 15 covers. In a multilevel chain, Object is the top ancestor, so its constructor runs first of all.

protected, revisited: protected was designed for inheritance. A protected member is visible to subclasses even when they are in another package, while staying hidden from unrelated classes in other packages. It is useful for helper methods that children need but the public should not call, like addToBalance above. Use it carefully: every protected member is a promise to all future subclasses, so changing it later can break them.

Inheritance and memory: A child object is a single object on the heap that contains the parent's fields and the child's fields together. new CSEStudent("Rafi", "Java") makes one object with name (from Student), favLang (from CSEStudent) and everything from Object. There are not two separate objects, a parent and a child; super just names the parent part of the same object.

A worked trace: class Person { Person() { System.out.println("Person"); } } class Teacher extends Person { Teacher() { System.out.println("Teacher"); } Teacher(String s) { this(); System.out.println("Teacher " + s); } }. What does new Teacher("Math") print? Teacher(String) calls this(), which goes to Teacher(); that constructor has no explicit super, so Java inserts super(), which prints "Person". Then Teacher() prints "Teacher". Back in Teacher(String), it prints "Teacher Math". Output: Person, Teacher, Teacher Math.

Drawing the hierarchy: In UML, inheritance is drawn as a solid line with a hollow triangle arrowhead pointing from the child to the parent, so the arrow reads "is a kind of". For a bank: SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount each have a triangle arrow up to Account, and Account has an arrow up to Object (usually left out). Exam answers that show the types of inheritance should include one small diagram for each type: a single arrow, a vertical chain, a fan of children under one parent, and for multiple inheritance a child with two arrows, marked "not allowed for Java classes".

Generalization and specialization: Two words describe how designers find inheritance. Generalization is going upward: you notice that Bike, Car and CNG share regNo, seats and baseFare, so you pull those into a general class Vehicle. Specialization is going downward: you start with Account and create SavingsAccount for a special case with interest. Both lead to the same kind of tree. In a design exam, explaining which common fields you moved up, and why, shows real understanding.

When not to use inheritance: Do not inherit just to reuse a couple of methods; use composition. Do not create deep chains of six or seven levels; they become hard to follow and fragile, because a change high up affects everything below. Do not inherit from a class that was not designed for it; such a parent may change in ways that break your child. A good rule of thumb is to keep hierarchies shallow and meaningful.

Real life example 1, bank accounts: class Account { private String number; private double balance; ... deposit, withdraw, getBalance } class SavingsAccount extends Account { private double interestRate; void addMonthlyInterest() { ... } } class CurrentAccount extends Account { private double overdraftLimit; }. Both children reuse deposit and getBalance from Account, and each adds what is special about it. Later, lesson 11 lets CurrentAccount change how withdraw works so it can go below zero up to the overdraft limit.

Real life example 2, a ride sharing app: class Vehicle { String regNo; int seats; double baseFare; } class Bike extends Vehicle { boolean helmetProvided; } class Car extends Vehicle { boolean hasAC; } class CNG extends Vehicle { }. Every vehicle has a registration number and seats; Bike and Car add their own details. The app can keep all vehicles in one Vehicle[] array, which works because every Bike is a Vehicle; lesson 12 explains why that is so powerful.

Common mistakes: Using inheritance for has-a relationships. Forgetting super(...) when the parent has no no-arg constructor. Placing super(...) after another statement. Trying to access a parent's private field directly from the child. Writing class C extends A, B. Thinking constructors are inherited. Thinking a child object contains a separate parent object.

What exams ask: "What is inheritance? What are its advantages?", "Explain the types of inheritance with diagrams", "Why does Java not support multiple inheritance through classes?", "What is the use of the super keyword?", "In what order are constructors called in multilevel inheritance?" and output tracing questions with constructors printing messages.

Recap: Inheritance lets a subclass extend a superclass with extends, reusing its accessible members and adding new ones, and should model is-a. Private members exist in the child but are reached only through methods; constructors are not inherited, and super(...) must be the first line to initialize the parent part, with a hidden super() inserted when you write none. Constructors run from parent to child. Java allows single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance of classes but not multiple, because of the diamond problem, and every class descends from Object. Next, children learn to change their parents' behaviour: method overriding.
key_points: A subclass extends a superclass and inherits its accessible fields and methods.
Use inheritance only for true is-a relationships.
Private fields exist in the child object but are reached only through parent methods.
Constructors are not inherited; super(...) must be the first statement of a child constructor.
If you write no super(...), Java inserts super() and needs a parent no-arg constructor.
Constructors run from the top ancestor (Object) down to the child.
Java supports single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance of classes, not multiple (diamond problem).
Every class implicitly extends Object.
lessons.tip: Before typing extends, say the sentence 'every X is a Y' out loud. If it sounds wrong, use composition.
lessons.task: Write classes Person, Teacher extends Person and HeadTeacher extends Teacher, each constructor printing its name. Create a HeadTeacher and check that the output order is Person, Teacher, HeadTeacher.

quiz.q: Which keyword makes one class inherit from another in Java?
quiz.explain: class B extends A makes B a subclass of A.

quiz.q: Which is NOT inherited by a subclass?
quiz.explain: Constructors are never inherited; children call them with super(...).

quiz.q: For C extends B extends A, which constructor body finishes first for new C()?
quiz.explain: Constructors run from the top of the hierarchy down.

quiz.q: Why does Java not allow class C extends A, B?
options: To avoid the diamond problem ambiguity
Because classes cannot have two methods
quiz.explain: Two parents could provide conflicting members; Java uses interfaces instead.

quiz.q: Parent has only Parent(int x). Child() { } has no explicit super call. What happens?
options: Compile error: no Parent() to call
quiz.explain: Java inserts super(), but Parent has no no-arg constructor.

lessons.title: Method Overriding
lessons.content:
Think about how different people greet you on Eid. Your grandmother hugs you and gives salami. Your little cousin shouts "Eid Mubarak!" and runs off. Your teacher shakes hands politely. They are all doing the same action, greeting, but each in their own way. In OOP, when a child class provides its own version of a method it inherited from its parent, we call it method overriding. It is what lets a family of classes share one method name while each member behaves in its own style.

What overriding is: Method overriding happens when a subclass defines a method with the same name, the same parameter list and a compatible return type as a method in its superclass. The child's version replaces the parent's version for objects of the child class. class Animal { void makeSound() { System.out.println("Some sound"); } } class Cat extends Animal { void makeSound() { System.out.println("Meow"); } }. Now new Cat().makeSound() prints "Meow", not "Some sound".

Why we override: Inheritance gives a child the parent's behaviour, but often that behaviour is too general. Every Account can withdraw, but a CurrentAccount may withdraw below zero up to an overdraft limit, while a basic account cannot. Every Shape has an area, but the formula for a circle is different from a rectangle. Overriding lets each child keep the same method name, so the rest of the program does not need to know which kind it has, while doing the right thing.

The rules of overriding, part 1, the signature: The method name and the parameter types must be exactly the same, in the same order. If the parameters differ, you have not overridden; you have overloaded, creating a second method. This is a classic silent bug: class Cat { void makeSound(String mood) { ... } } does not override makeSound(), so calling makeSound() on a Cat still runs Animal's version.

Rules part 2, the return type: For primitive return types, the child must return exactly the same type. For reference types, the child may return the same type or a subtype; this is called a covariant return type. If Animal has Animal reproduce(), then Cat can override it as Cat reproduce(), because a Cat is an Animal. This lets callers who know they have a Cat get a Cat back without casting.

Rules part 3, access cannot be reduced: The overriding method cannot be more private than the method it overrides. If the parent's method is public, the child's must be public. If the parent's is protected, the child's can be protected or public. The reason is simple: code that can call the method on a parent reference must still be able to call it, whatever child object is really there. Making it more visible is allowed.

Rules part 4, exceptions: If the parent method declares checked exceptions with throws (lesson 17), the overriding method may throw the same exceptions, fewer, narrower ones, or none at all, but it cannot add new or broader checked exceptions. Again, callers who prepared for the parent's exceptions must not be surprised by new ones.

Rules part 5, what cannot be overridden: final methods cannot be overridden; that is the whole point of final on a method. static methods are not overridden; if a child declares a static method with the same signature, it hides the parent's one instead (more on that below). private methods are not visible to the child, so a child method with the same name is just a new, unrelated method. Constructors are not inherited, so they cannot be overridden either.

The @Override annotation: Java lets you write @Override on the line before an overriding method. @Override public void makeSound() { ... }. It does not change how the program runs, but the compiler checks that the method really overrides something. If you misspell the name as makeSond or change a parameter, the compiler reports an error immediately instead of letting the silent overloading bug slip through. Always use @Override; good teachers and code reviewers expect it.

Calling the parent's version with super: Often the child wants to extend the parent's behaviour rather than replace it entirely. Inside the overriding method, super.methodName(...) calls the parent's version. class Employee { double salary() { return basic; } } class Manager extends Employee { @Override double salary() { return super.salary() + allowance; } }. The manager's salary is the normal salary plus an allowance, and the basic calculation is written only once.

A worked example with super: class Account { protected double balance; public boolean withdraw(double amt) { if (amt <= 0 || amt > balance) return false; balance -= amt; return true; } } class CurrentAccount extends Account { private double overdraft = 10000; @Override public boolean withdraw(double amt) { if (amt <= 0 || amt > balance + overdraft) return false; balance -= amt; return true; } }. With balance 2000, a CurrentAccount can withdraw 8000, ending at -6000, while a plain Account refuses. Same method name, different rule.

Which version runs: When you call a method on an object, Java runs the most specific version for that object's actual class, searching from the object's class upward. For a Manager object, salary() runs Manager's version. If Manager did not override toString(), the call goes up to Employee, and if Employee did not either, to Object. This runtime choice is called dynamic method dispatch, and it is the engine behind polymorphism in lesson 12.

Overriding toString, a first taste: Every class inherits toString() from Object, which returns something like Student@1b6d3586. Override it to describe your object: @Override public String toString() { return name + " (" + roll + ")"; }. Now System.out.println(s) prints "Rahim (101)", because println calls toString() on the object. Lesson 15 covers toString, equals and hashCode in depth.

Overloading versus overriding: This comparison appears in nearly every OOP exam. Overloading: same method name, different parameter lists, usually in the same class (or added in a child); resolved by the compiler at compile time; return type can differ; it is compile-time polymorphism. Overriding: same name and same parameters in a parent and child; resolved at runtime based on the actual object; return type the same or covariant; access cannot be reduced; it is runtime polymorphism. A table with these rows earns full marks.

Static methods and hiding: If Parent has static void info() and Child has static void info(), the child's method hides the parent's. Which one runs depends on the declared type of the reference (or the class name used), not on the actual object, because static methods do not belong to objects. Parent p = new Child(); p.info(); runs Parent's info(). This is why we say static methods are not overridden, and why calling static methods through object references is confusing.

Fields are not overridden either: If both Parent and Child declare a field called name, the child's field hides the parent's. Which one you see depends on the reference type: Parent p = new Child(); p.name gives the parent's field. Only methods are dispatched at runtime; fields are chosen at compile time. This difference is a favourite trick question, and the practical lesson is simple: never reuse field names in a hierarchy.

A tricky trace with fields and methods together: class P { String name = "P"; String who() { return "P"; } } class C extends P { String name = "C"; @Override String who() { return "C"; } }. Now P x = new C(); System.out.println(x.name + " " + x.who());. The field is chosen by the declared type P, so x.name is "P". The method is chosen by the actual object, a C, so x.who() is "C". The output is "P C". If you can explain this one line clearly, you understand the difference between hiding and overriding better than most of the class.

Overriding equals the wrong way: A very common real bug is writing public boolean equals(Student other) in a Student class. Because the parameter type is Student and Object's method takes Object, this is an overload, not an override. Collections like ArrayList.contains call equals(Object), so they never use your method, and searching for a student silently fails. Writing @Override on it would have produced a compiler error at once. Lesson 15 shows the correct equals(Object o).

final methods and final classes: Marking a method final prevents overriding: public final boolean checkPin(String p) in a Wallet class ensures no subclass can weaken the PIN check. Marking a class final prevents inheritance entirely: final class String means nobody can create a subclass of String. Use final for security-critical methods and for classes, such as immutable value classes, whose behaviour must never change.

Overriding and constructors, a trap: Avoid calling an overridable method from a constructor. When a parent constructor calls an overridden method, the child's version runs, but the child's fields have not been initialized yet, because the child's constructor body has not run. For example, a child override that prints a child field during the parent constructor will print null or 0. Experienced programmers call only private or final methods from constructors.

Real life example 1, delivery charges: class Delivery { double charge(double km) { return 30 + 10 * km; } } class ExpressDelivery extends Delivery { @Override double charge(double km) { return super.charge(km) * 1.5; } } class FreeDelivery extends Delivery { @Override double charge(double km) { return 0; } }. For 4 km, normal delivery costs 30 + 40 = 70 taka, express costs 105 taka, and free delivery during a campaign costs 0. The checkout screen calls charge(km) and gets the right price for each type.

Real life example 2, employee payroll: class Employee { double pay() { return basic; } } class HourlyWorker extends Employee { @Override double pay() { return hours * rate; } } class SalesPerson extends Employee { @Override double pay() { return super.pay() + 0.05 * sales; } }. At month end, the payroll program asks each employee for pay(), and each object answers by its own rule. When a new type such as Intern is added, only a new class is written; the payroll loop does not change.

Common mistakes: Changing the parameter list and thinking you overrode (use @Override). Reducing access, for example making a public method protected in the child. Trying to override a final or private method. Expecting static methods or fields to behave polymorphically. Forgetting super.method() when you meant to extend, not replace, the parent's behaviour. Calling overridable methods from constructors.

What exams ask: "What is method overriding? State its rules", "Differentiate between method overloading and overriding", "What is the use of @Override?", "Can we override static, private or final methods?", "What is a covariant return type?" and output prediction questions mixing overridden methods, hidden static methods and hidden fields.

Recap: Overriding lets a child replace or extend an inherited method with the same signature; the return type may be covariant, access may not shrink, and checked exceptions may not grow. Use @Override to let the compiler check your work and super.method() to reuse the parent's code. final, static and private methods are not overridden, and fields are hidden, not overridden. At runtime Java picks the version for the actual object, which is the key idea of the next lesson: polymorphism.
key_points: Overriding: a subclass redefines an inherited method with the same name and parameters.
Return type must match, or be a subtype for reference types (covariant return).
Access cannot be reduced, and checked exceptions cannot be broadened.
final, static and private methods are not overridden; static methods are hidden.
Fields are hidden, not overridden; they are chosen by reference type at compile time.
@Override makes the compiler verify that you really override.
super.method() calls the parent's version so the child can extend it.
Overloading is compile-time (different parameters); overriding is runtime (same signature).
lessons.tip: Put @Override on every overriding method, every time. It turns a silent bug into a compiler error.
lessons.task: Write Delivery, ExpressDelivery and FreeDelivery classes with an overridden charge(km). Print the charge for 5 km for each, and use super.charge in ExpressDelivery.

quiz.q: Which is required for overriding?
options: Same name and same parameter types
quiz.explain: Overriding needs the same signature; different parameters means overloading.

quiz.q: Parent has public void show(). Which child version compiles as an override?
quiz.explain: Access cannot be reduced below public.

quiz.q: What does @Override do?
options: Asks the compiler to check that the method overrides one
quiz.explain: It is a compile-time check against typos and wrong signatures.

quiz.q: Can a final method be overridden?
quiz.explain: final methods cannot be overridden.

quiz.q: Parent p = new Child(); Both declare static void info(). What does p.info() run?
quiz.explain: Static methods are hidden and chosen by the reference type, not the object.

lessons.title: Polymorphism
lessons.content:
Your TV remote has one power button. Press it while pointing at a Walton TV, and the Walton turns on. Point the same kind of remote at a Sony, and the Sony turns on in its own way. The button does not care which brand is in front of it; it just sends "power". Each TV knows how to respond. That is polymorphism: one interface, many behaviours. It is the fourth pillar of OOP and the one that makes object oriented code truly flexible.

What polymorphism means: The word comes from Greek: poly means many, morph means form. In OOP, polymorphism means one name can stand for many forms. A single variable of a parent type can refer to objects of many child types, and a single method call can do different things depending on which object receives it. You write code once against a general type, and it works for every specific type, including ones invented later.

Two kinds of polymorphism: Compile-time polymorphism, also called static polymorphism or early binding, is decided by the compiler. Method overloading (lesson 4) is the main example in Java: add(int, int) and add(double, double) share one name, and the compiler picks one based on the argument types. Runtime polymorphism, also called dynamic polymorphism or late binding, is decided while the program runs. Method overriding (lesson 11) combined with parent references is the example. When people say "polymorphism" without a qualifier, they usually mean the runtime kind.

The key rule, a parent reference can hold a child object: Because every Dog is an Animal, Java lets you write Animal a = new Dog();. The variable's declared type, also called its static or compile-time type, is Animal. The object's actual type, also called its runtime type, is Dog. This is legal for any subclass, at any depth: Animal a = new Puppy(); works if Puppy extends Dog extends Animal. It also works with interfaces: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();.

Upcasting: Converting a child reference to a parent type is called upcasting. It is always safe, so Java does it automatically: Dog d = new Dog(); Animal a = d; needs no cast. Nothing happens to the object; only the view through the variable changes. Through a, you can call only the methods that Animal declares, because the compiler only knows that a is some Animal.

What the compiler checks and what the JVM decides: This is the heart of the lesson. With Animal a = new Dog();, the compiler checks a.makeSound() against the Animal class: does Animal have makeSound()? Yes, so it compiles. a.bark() does not compile, because Animal has no bark(), even though the real object can bark. At runtime, the JVM looks at the actual object, finds it is a Dog, and runs Dog's makeSound(). So: the reference type decides what you are allowed to call; the object type decides which version runs.

Dynamic method dispatch: The runtime mechanism that picks the overridden method based on the actual object is called dynamic method dispatch. Each object knows its real class, and when an overridden method is called, the JVM looks up the version for that class, walking up the hierarchy if needed. Conceptually it is like asking the object itself "how do you do this?" rather than asking the variable's label.

A worked example: class Shape { double area() { return 0; } } class Circle extends Shape { double r; Circle(double r) { this.r = r; } @Override double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; } } class Rect extends Shape { double w, h; Rect(double w, double h) { this.w = w; this.h = h; } @Override double area() { return w * h; } }. Now Shape[] shapes = { new Circle(1), new Rect(4, 3), new Circle(2) }; double total = 0; for (Shape s : shapes) total += s.area();. The loop calls area() on each element; the first returns about 3.14, the second 12, the third about 12.57. Total is about 27.71. The loop never mentions Circle or Rect.

Why this is powerful, the open-closed idea: Suppose next week you add class Triangle extends Shape with its own area(). The loop above does not change at all; it already handles triangles. Code written against the parent type is open for extension (new kinds of shapes) but closed for modification (no need to edit the loop). This is called the open-closed principle (lesson 25), and polymorphism is how OOP achieves it. Without polymorphism you would write if (s is a circle) ... else if (s is a rectangle) ..., and every new shape would require editing every such chain.

Polymorphic parameters: Methods can accept a parent type and work with any child. void printArea(Shape s) { System.out.println(s.area()); } can be called with a Circle, a Rect or a future Triangle. Similarly, a method can return a parent type: Shape makeShape(String kind) can return different subclasses depending on kind. This is the basis of the Factory pattern in lesson 25.

Downcasting: Sometimes you have a parent reference but need a child-only method. Animal a = new Dog(); Dog d = (Dog) a; d.bark();. Converting a parent reference to a child type is called downcasting, and it needs an explicit cast because it might be wrong. If the object is not really a Dog, for example Animal a = new Cat(); Dog d = (Dog) a;, the code compiles but throws a ClassCastException at runtime.

instanceof, checking before casting: Use instanceof to check the actual type safely: if (a instanceof Dog) { Dog d = (Dog) a; d.bark(); }. a instanceof Dog is true if a's object is a Dog or any subclass of Dog, and false if a is null. Newer Java versions (16 and later) allow pattern matching that combines the check and the cast: if (a instanceof Dog d) { d.bark(); }.

instanceof is a smell when overused: If your code is full of if (x instanceof A) ... else if (x instanceof B) ..., you are probably doing by hand what polymorphism should do for you. Usually the better design is to add an overridden method to the parent, so each child handles its own case. instanceof is fine for occasional checks, such as in equals methods (lesson 15), but it should not replace dispatch.

What is not polymorphic: Remember from lesson 11: fields are chosen by reference type, not object type. Static methods are chosen by reference type. Private and final methods are not overridden, so they are bound at compile time. Only overridden instance methods are dispatched dynamically. This is why the advice is: access data through methods, not through fields, if you want polymorphic behaviour.

Static binding versus dynamic binding: Binding means connecting a method call to the method body that will run. Static (early) binding happens at compile time; it applies to overloaded methods, static, private and final methods, and fields. Dynamic (late) binding happens at runtime; it applies to overridden instance methods. Exams often ask you to define both and say which calls use which.

Overloading and overriding together: A subtle case: overload resolution uses the declared types at compile time, then overriding picks the version at runtime. If class Printer has print(Animal a) and print(Dog d), then Animal a = new Dog(); printer.print(a); calls print(Animal), because the compiler only sees Animal. Inside that method, a.makeSound() still dispatches to Dog's version. Students often expect print(Dog) to be chosen; it is not.

Polymorphism with interfaces, a preview: Interfaces (lesson 14) give polymorphism without a shared parent class. interface Payable { double amountDue(); } can be implemented by Invoice and Employee, which are unrelated classes. A Payable[] array can hold both, and a loop can call amountDue() on each. In fact, most real-world Java code relies more on interface polymorphism than on class inheritance.

A full output-prediction example: class A { int x = 1; void show() { System.out.println("A " + x); } static void s() { System.out.println("static A"); } } class B extends A { int x = 2; @Override void show() { System.out.println("B " + x); } static void s() { System.out.println("static B"); } }. Then A obj = new B(); obj.show(); System.out.println(obj.x); obj.s();. Line by line: show() is overridden, so B's version runs, and inside B the name x means B's field, so it prints "B 2". obj.x uses the reference type A, so it prints 1. obj.s() is static and chosen by the reference type, so it prints "static A". Output: "B 2", "1", "static A". This one example tests every rule of the lesson.

How dispatch works inside the JVM, simply: You do not need the details for most exams, but a picture helps. For each class, the JVM keeps a table of its methods, often called a method table or vtable. A child's table starts as a copy of its parent's, and every overridden method's entry is replaced with the child's version. When the program calls show() on an object, the JVM goes to that object's class, looks up show in the table, and jumps to whatever is there. That is why the decision depends on the object, not on the variable. C++ uses a similar table for virtual functions, as lesson 22 explains.

Real life example 1, mobile payments: abstract idea Payment with method pay(double amount). Classes BkashPayment, NagadPayment, CardPayment and CashOnDelivery each override pay with their own steps: OTP for bKash, PIN for Nagad, card network for cards, nothing online for cash. The checkout code holds Payment p = chosenMethod(); and calls p.pay(total). When the shop adds Rocket next month, it writes one new class; the checkout code stays the same.

Real life example 2, a game with enemies: class Enemy { void attack(Player p) { ... } } class Zombie extends Enemy, class Archer extends Enemy, class Dragon extends Enemy, each overriding attack. The game keeps List<Enemy> enemies and every frame does for (Enemy e : enemies) e.attack(player);. Zombies bite, archers shoot arrows from a distance, dragons breathe fire. One loop, many behaviours, and the game designer can add new enemy types freely.

Common mistakes: Thinking the reference type decides which overridden method runs (the object does). Trying to call a child-only method through a parent reference without casting. Downcasting without instanceof and getting ClassCastException. Expecting fields or static methods to be polymorphic. Using long instanceof chains instead of overriding. Thinking upcasting changes or copies the object.

What exams ask: "What is polymorphism? Explain compile-time and runtime polymorphism with examples", "What is dynamic method dispatch?", "Differentiate between static and dynamic binding", "What is upcasting and downcasting?", "What is the use of instanceof?" and output questions like: Animal a = new Dog(); a.makeSound(); with overridden methods, hidden fields and static methods mixed together.

Recap: Polymorphism means one interface, many forms. Overloading gives compile-time polymorphism; overriding plus parent references gives runtime polymorphism through dynamic method dispatch. The reference type controls what you may call; the object type controls which overridden version runs. Upcasting is automatic and safe; downcasting needs a cast and ideally an instanceof check. Polymorphism lets code written for a parent type work with any present or future child. Next, abstract classes let us declare methods that every child must override.
key_points: Polymorphism: one interface, many forms.
Compile-time polymorphism = overloading (static/early binding).
Runtime polymorphism = overriding + parent references (dynamic method dispatch, late binding).
A parent reference can hold a child object: Animal a = new Dog(); (upcasting, automatic).
The reference type decides what you may call; the object type decides which overridden version runs.
Downcasting needs an explicit cast and can throw ClassCastException; check with instanceof.
Fields, static, private and final methods are bound at compile time, not dynamically.
Polymorphism lets code for a parent type work with future child types (open-closed principle).
lessons.tip: For every polymorphism question, write two labels on paper: 'reference type' and 'object type'. Then ask which one each line depends on.
lessons.task: Create Shape, Circle, Rect and Triangle with overridden area(). Put them in one Shape[] array and print the total area with a single loop. Then add a new shape and confirm the loop needs no change.

quiz.q: Animal a = new Dog(); a.makeSound(); Dog overrides makeSound. Which version runs?
quiz.explain: Dynamic dispatch uses the actual object type.

quiz.q: Animal a = new Dog(); a.bark(); where only Dog has bark(). Result?
quiz.explain: The compiler checks calls against the reference type Animal, which has no bark().

quiz.q: Which is an example of compile-time polymorphism?
quiz.explain: Overloads are chosen by the compiler from argument types.

quiz.q: Animal a = new Cat(); Dog d = (Dog) a; What happens?
quiz.explain: The cast compiles but the object is not a Dog.

quiz.q: Which calls are resolved by dynamic binding?
quiz.explain: Only overridden instance methods are dispatched at runtime.

lessons.title: Abstract Classes
lessons.content:
If someone asks you to "draw a shape", you will probably ask back: which shape? A circle? A triangle? "Shape" is an idea, not something you can actually draw by itself. Every real shape is some particular kind. Similarly, "Animal" is a category; every real animal you meet is a cat, a cow or a crow. In OOP, a class that represents such a general idea, which should never be turned into an object by itself, is called an abstract class. This lesson explains abstract classes and abstract methods, the first tool for the abstraction pillar.

The problem abstract classes solve: In lesson 12 we wrote class Shape { double area() { return 0; } }. That return 0 is a lie. A plain Shape has no real area, and someone could write new Shape() and get a meaningless object. Worse, a programmer writing a new subclass Triangle could forget to override area(), and Java would silently use the fake 0. We want two guarantees: nobody can create a plain Shape, and every concrete shape must provide its own area().

Abstract methods: An abstract method is a method declared without a body; it only states the signature and ends with a semicolon. abstract double area();. It says: "every concrete subclass must provide this method", but it does not say how. Because the method has no body, it cannot be called on the class that declares it; it only makes sense in a child that fills it in.

Abstract classes: Any class with at least one abstract method must itself be declared abstract: abstract class Shape { abstract double area(); }. You cannot create an object of an abstract class: new Shape() is a compile error, "Shape is abstract; cannot be instantiated". A class can also be declared abstract even if it has no abstract methods, simply to prevent instantiation; this is less common but legal.

Concrete subclasses must implement: class Circle extends Shape { private double r; Circle(double r) { this.r = r; } @Override double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; } }. Circle provides a body for area(), so it is concrete and can be instantiated: new Circle(2). If Circle forgot to implement area(), the compiler would complain: "Circle is not abstract and does not override abstract method area() in Shape". That compile error is the guarantee we wanted.

Abstract subclasses: A subclass does not have to implement every abstract method if it is itself declared abstract. abstract class Polygon extends Shape { abstract int sides(); } leaves area() unimplemented and adds another abstract method. Then class Square extends Polygon must implement both area() and sides() to be concrete. Abstract classes can form several levels, each adding a bit more detail.

What an abstract class can contain: Unlike a pure interface in older Java, an abstract class is a full class. It can have fields, including private ones. It can have constructors. It can have concrete methods with bodies, static methods and final methods. It can have abstract methods. So an abstract class is a partially built class: it provides some code and leaves some holes for children to fill.

Constructors in abstract classes: Even though you cannot create an abstract class's object directly, it can and often should have constructors. They run when a concrete child is created, through super(...), to initialize the fields the abstract class owns. abstract class Shape { private String colour; Shape(String colour) { this.colour = colour; } String getColour() { return colour; } abstract double area(); } class Circle extends Shape { private double r; Circle(String c, double r) { super(c); this.r = r; } ... }.

Abstract references and polymorphism: You cannot write new Shape(), but you can write Shape s = new Circle("red", 2);. Abstract types are perfect as reference types, parameter types and array element types. Shape[] shapes = { new Circle("red", 1), new Square("blue", 3) }; for (Shape s : shapes) total += s.area();. Because every concrete Shape must implement area(), this loop is guaranteed to work; there is no fake 0 anywhere.

The template method idea: A powerful use of abstract classes is to write the overall algorithm once in the parent, as a concrete (often final) method, and leave certain steps abstract for children. abstract class Exam { final void conduct() { distributePaper(); startTimer(); collectAnswers(); grade(); } abstract void distributePaper(); abstract void grade(); void startTimer() { ... } void collectAnswers() { ... } }. A WrittenExam and a MCQExam fill in distributePaper and grade differently, but the order of steps is fixed and cannot be broken. This is the Template Method design pattern.
