A worked template example: abstract class Beverage { final void prepare() { boilWater(); brew(); pourInCup(); addExtras(); } void boilWater() { System.out.println("Boiling water"); } void pourInCup() { System.out.println("Pouring"); } abstract void brew(); abstract void addExtras(); } class Tea extends Beverage { void brew() { System.out.println("Steeping tea leaves"); } void addExtras() { System.out.println("Adding milk and sugar"); } } class Coffee extends Beverage { void brew() { System.out.println("Dripping coffee"); } void addExtras() { System.out.println("Adding nothing"); } }. Calling new Tea().prepare() prints boiling, steeping, pouring, milk and sugar, in exactly that order.

Tracing constructor order with an abstract parent: abstract class Vehicle { Vehicle() { System.out.println("Vehicle ready, wheels = " + wheels()); } abstract int wheels(); } class Rickshaw extends Vehicle { private int w = 3; Rickshaw() { System.out.println("Rickshaw ready"); } int wheels() { return w; } }. What does new Rickshaw() print? The Vehicle constructor runs first and calls wheels(), which dispatches to Rickshaw's version. But Rickshaw's field w has not been initialized yet, so it is still 0. The output is "Vehicle ready, wheels = 0" and then "Rickshaw ready". This is the constructor trap from lesson 11, and it appears even more often with abstract classes, because their constructors are tempted to call the abstract methods.

Choosing what goes in the abstract parent: A practical method is to list what all children share and what differs. For an e-commerce product system: every product has a name, price and stock, and can be added to a cart, so those go into abstract class Product as fields and concrete methods. But shipping cost differs: a book ships by weight, a digital course has no shipping, a fridge needs special delivery. So abstract double shippingCost(); goes into Product, and each child implements it. Shared things up, differing things down as abstract methods.

Partial implementation as a helper for children: Sometimes an abstract class implements the boring parts of a larger contract so children only write the interesting part. Java's own library does this: AbstractList implements most of the List operations, and a subclass only needs to provide get(int) and size() to get a working read-only list. This idea, "implement the hard parts once in an abstract base class", saves enormous amounts of repeated code in big projects.

Abstract classes and testing: Because the shared logic lives in one place, you test it once. If payslip() in Employee formats correctly for one subclass, it formats correctly for all of them, since they all use the same code. The tests for each child then only need to check its own monthlyPay() rule. This is one more practical benefit of pushing shared code up into an abstract parent.

Rules and restrictions: An abstract method cannot be private, because children could not see it to implement it. It cannot be final, because final forbids overriding, which is the only way to implement it. It cannot be static, because static methods are not overridden. A class cannot be both abstract and final, since abstract demands subclasses and final forbids them. Abstract methods can be public, protected or package-private.

Abstraction, the pillar, more precisely: Abstraction means focusing on what an object does and hiding how it does it. An abstract class expresses "what" through its abstract method signatures: every Shape can tell its area, every Payment can pay. Users of Shape think only in terms of area(), not formulas. This makes large systems manageable, because each part can be understood at the level of its abstract contract.

Abstract class versus concrete class: A concrete class has bodies for all its methods and can be instantiated. An abstract class may have unimplemented methods and cannot be instantiated. When designing, ask: does it make sense to have a plain object of this type? A plain Account with no account type might make sense in some banks; a plain Shape never does. If it never makes sense, make the class abstract.

Abstract class versus interface, a preview: Both define contracts that other classes fulfil, and both cannot be instantiated. The main differences: a class can extend only one abstract class but implement many interfaces; an abstract class can have instance fields with state and constructors, while an interface cannot hold instance state. Use an abstract class when closely related classes share code and state; use an interface for a capability that unrelated classes can have. Lesson 14 covers this comparison in full.

Real life example 1, a payroll system: abstract class Employee { private String name; private String id; Employee(String name, String id) { ... } abstract double monthlyPay(); String payslip() { return name + " (" + id + "): Tk " + monthlyPay(); } }. class SalariedEmployee extends Employee { double monthlyPay() { return salary; } } class HourlyEmployee extends Employee { double monthlyPay() { return hours * rate; } } class CommissionEmployee extends Employee { double monthlyPay() { return base + 0.07 * sales; } }. payslip() is written once and calls the abstract monthlyPay(), which every kind of employee must implement. Nobody can hire a plain "Employee" with no pay rule.

Real life example 2, notification sending: abstract class Notifier { final void send(String user, String msg) { if (msg.isBlank()) return; String formatted = format(msg); deliver(user, formatted); log(user); } abstract String format(String msg); abstract void deliver(String user, String msg); void log(String user) { System.out.println("Sent to " + user); } }. SmsNotifier formats messages to 160 characters and sends them through an SMS gateway; EmailNotifier adds a subject line and sends email; PushNotifier sends to the phone app. The checking and logging are shared and fixed; only formatting and delivery differ.

Common mistakes: Trying to instantiate an abstract class. Giving an abstract method a body, or forgetting the semicolon. Forgetting to declare a class abstract when it has abstract methods. Forgetting to implement an abstract method in a concrete subclass. Thinking an abstract class cannot have constructors or concrete methods. Combining abstract with private, final or static.

What exams ask: "What is an abstract class? Can we create its object?", "What is an abstract method?", "Can an abstract class have a constructor? Why?", "Can an abstract class have non-abstract methods?", "Write an abstract class Shape with subclasses Circle and Rectangle and compute areas polymorphically", and "Differentiate between abstract class and interface".

Recap: An abstract method has a signature but no body; a class with one must be abstract, and abstract classes cannot be instantiated. They can still have fields, constructors and concrete methods, so they are partially built classes. Concrete subclasses must implement every inherited abstract method, which the compiler enforces. Abstract types make excellent references for polymorphism, and the template method pattern fixes an algorithm's steps while letting children fill in details. Next, interfaces take abstraction one step further.
key_points: An abstract method has a signature but no body: abstract double area();
A class with any abstract method must be declared abstract.
Abstract classes cannot be instantiated, but can be used as reference types.
Abstract classes can have fields, constructors, concrete, static and final methods.
A concrete subclass must implement every inherited abstract method (compiler-enforced).
Abstract methods cannot be private, final or static; a class cannot be abstract and final.
Template method: a final method fixes the steps; abstract steps are filled by children.
Use an abstract class when related classes share state and code.
lessons.tip: When a parent method has no honest default body (like area of a general Shape), that is your signal to make it abstract.
lessons.task: Write abstract class Employee with abstract monthlyPay() and a concrete payslip(). Add two concrete subclasses, store them in an Employee[] and print every payslip in one loop.

quiz.q: What happens with new Shape() if Shape is abstract?
quiz.explain: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated.

quiz.q: Which can an abstract class NOT do?
quiz.explain: Everything else is allowed; only direct instantiation is forbidden.

quiz.q: A concrete class extends an abstract class but does not implement one abstract method. Result?
quiz.explain: The compiler forces concrete classes to implement all abstract methods.

quiz.q: Which combination is illegal?
options: abstract and final on the same class
abstract class with a static method
quiz.explain: abstract requires subclasses; final forbids them.

quiz.q: In the template method pattern, which method is usually final?
options: The method that fixes the order of steps
quiz.explain: The skeleton method is final so children can only change the steps, not the order.

lessons.title: Interfaces
lessons.content:
Look at the charging port of your phone. Most new phones use USB Type-C. A Samsung, a Xiaomi and a Walton phone are made by completely different companies, but they all accept the same charger, because they all follow the same agreement about the shape of the port and how power flows. The charger does not care about the brand; it only cares that the phone "implements" the USB-C rules. In Java, such an agreement is called an interface. It is the most important abstraction tool in modern Java code.

What an interface is: An interface is a reference type that declares a set of methods a class promises to provide, without (traditionally) saying how. interface Chargeable { void charge(int watts); int batteryLevel(); }. A class signs the contract with the keyword implements: class Phone implements Chargeable { public void charge(int watts) { ... } public int batteryLevel() { ... } }. If the class leaves out any method, it must be declared abstract, or the compiler complains.

Interface methods are public and abstract by default: Inside an interface, a method written without a body, such as void charge(int watts);, is automatically public and abstract. You do not need to write those keywords. As a consequence, the implementing class must declare the method public; writing just void charge(int watts) { ... } in the class reduces access to package-private and fails to compile. This is a very common lab error.

Interface fields are constants: Any field declared in an interface is automatically public, static and final. interface Limits { int MAX_TRANSFER = 25000; } means Limits.MAX_TRANSFER is a constant shared by everyone. Interfaces cannot have instance fields, so they hold no per-object state. That is a key difference from abstract classes.

No constructors, no objects: An interface has no constructors and you cannot write new Chargeable(). But, just like an abstract class, an interface can be used as a type for variables, parameters, return values and arrays: Chargeable c = new Phone(); Chargeable[] gadgets = { new Phone(), new PowerBank(), new Laptop() };. Through c you can call only the methods Chargeable declares, and the actual object's implementation runs, which is the same dynamic dispatch as lesson 12.

Implementing many interfaces: A class can extend only one class, but it can implement any number of interfaces: class Smartphone extends Device implements Chargeable, Camera, GPS { ... }. This is how Java gives the main benefit of multiple inheritance, being many kinds of thing at once, without the diamond problem of fields. The extends clause must come before implements.

Why no diamond problem with fields: The diamond problem in lesson 10 was about two parents providing conflicting state and code. Interfaces have no instance state at all, so there is never a question of which copy of a field to use. For traditional abstract methods there is no conflict either: if two interfaces both declare void reset();, the class provides one reset() and satisfies both.

Interfaces can extend interfaces: interface Camera { void takePhoto(); } interface VideoCamera extends Camera { void recordVideo(); }. A class implementing VideoCamera must provide both methods. An interface can even extend several interfaces: interface SmartDevice extends Chargeable, Connectable { }. Note the keywords: a class implements interfaces, and an interface extends other interfaces.

Default methods (Java 8): Before Java 8, adding a new method to a widely used interface would break every class that implemented it. So Java 8 added default methods, which have a body: interface Chargeable { void charge(int watts); int batteryLevel(); default boolean isLow() { return batteryLevel() < 20; } }. Every implementing class gets isLow() for free and can override it if it wants. Default methods let interfaces evolve without breaking existing code.

Default method conflicts: Default methods bring back a small version of the diamond problem. If interface A and interface B both have default void hello(), and class C implements A, B, the compiler forces C to override hello() to resolve the conflict. Inside, C can choose one: public void hello() { A.super.hello(); }. A class's own method, or one inherited from a superclass, always wins over an interface default.

Static and private methods in interfaces: Java 8 also allows static methods in interfaces, called with the interface name: interface MobileNumber { static boolean isValid(String n) { return n.matches("01[3-9][0-9]{8}"); } } then MobileNumber.isValid("01712345678"). Java 9 added private methods inside interfaces, which help default methods share code without exposing helpers to implementers.

Marker and functional interfaces: Some interfaces have no methods at all; they just mark a class with a capability. Serializable (lesson 20) and Cloneable (lesson 15) are such marker interfaces. A functional interface has exactly one abstract method, such as Runnable (void run()) or Comparator<T> (int compare(T a, T b)). You can mark one with @FunctionalInterface so the compiler checks there is only one abstract method.

Lambdas, a short introduction: For a functional interface, Java 8 lets you provide the implementation as a lambda expression instead of writing a whole class. interface Discount { double apply(double price); } then Discount eid = p -> p * 0.8; and Discount none = p -> p;. eid.apply(1000) gives 800.0. The lambda p -> p * 0.8 is a short way to write an object whose single method takes p and returns p * 0.8. Lambdas make event handling (lesson 24) and sorting (lesson 19) much shorter.

Common built-in interfaces you will meet: Comparable<T> with compareTo, which gives objects a natural order. Comparator<T> with compare, for custom orders. Runnable with run, for threads. Iterable<T> with iterator, which makes the enhanced for loop work. AutoCloseable with close, which makes try-with-resources work. List, Set and Map, the collection interfaces. Learning to read and implement interfaces is learning to use the Java library.

Programming to an interface: Experienced Java programmers write List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); rather than ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();. The variable's type is the interface, and only the creation line names the concrete class. If later a LinkedList suits better, only one line changes. Methods should likewise accept interface types: void notifyAll(List<User> users) works with any List. This habit, "program to an interface, not an implementation", keeps code flexible.

Abstract class versus interface, full comparison: An abstract class can have instance fields and constructors; an interface cannot have instance fields or constructors, only constants. A class can extend one abstract class but implement many interfaces. Abstract class methods can have any access level; interface abstract methods are public. An abstract class models an is-a family that shares code and state; an interface models a capability (can-do), often named with -able: Comparable, Runnable, Chargeable. Since Java 8 both can have methods with bodies, but only abstract classes can hold per-object state.

When to choose which: If the classes are close relatives sharing fields and code, such as SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount sharing balance, use an abstract class. If unrelated classes need a common ability, such as both Invoice and Employee being Payable, or both Phone and Laptop being Chargeable, use an interface. Often you use both: an interface for the contract and an abstract class that implements the common parts of it, like List and AbstractList in Java's library.

A complete small example: interface Shape { double area(); default String describe() { return getClass().getSimpleName() + " with area " + String.format("%.2f", area()); } } class Circle implements Shape { private final double r; Circle(double r) { this.r = r; } public double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; } } class Square implements Shape { private final double s; Square(double s) { this.s = s; } public double area() { return s * s; } }. Then for (Shape sh : new Shape[]{ new Circle(1), new Square(2) }) System.out.println(sh.describe()); prints "Circle with area 3.14" and "Square with area 4.00". The default method calls the abstract area(), and dynamic dispatch picks the right one. This is the same idea as the template method, but in an interface.

Anonymous classes, the older way: Before lambdas, a quick one-off implementation of an interface was written as an anonymous class: Discount eid = new Discount() { public double apply(double p) { return p * 0.8; } };. This creates an object of a class that has no name and implements Discount. You will still see anonymous classes in older code and in Swing examples (lesson 24), and they are needed when the interface has more than one abstract method, since lambdas only work for functional interfaces.

Interfaces and loose coupling: Coupling means how much one class depends on the details of another. If CheckoutService has a field of type BkashGateway, it is tightly coupled to bKash. If the field type is PaymentGateway, it is loosely coupled: it only knows the contract. Loose coupling makes code easier to test, because during testing you can pass a FakeGateway that always succeeds without touching real money, and easier to change, because a new gateway does not affect CheckoutService at all.

Real life example 1, payment gateways in a Bangladeshi e-commerce site: interface PaymentGateway { boolean pay(String orderId, double amount); boolean refund(String orderId); default String currency() { return "BDT"; } }. Classes BkashGateway, NagadGateway, SslCommerzGateway and CashOnDelivery implement it. The checkout service has a field PaymentGateway gateway and calls gateway.pay(id, total). Adding a new gateway means writing one class that implements the interface; checkout code is untouched, and every gateway gets currency() for free.

Real life example 2, a smart home: interface Switchable { void on(); void off(); } interface Dimmable { void setLevel(int percent); }. A Fan implements Switchable and Dimmable (speed levels). A Light implements both too. A WaterPump implements only Switchable. The home app keeps a Switchable[] devices list and turns everything off at night with one loop: for (Switchable d : devices) d.off();. Fans and pumps have nothing else in common, yet the loop handles both.

Common mistakes: Forgetting public on implemented methods. Trying to instantiate an interface. Writing a class that implements an interface without all methods and without abstract. Using extends for a class implementing an interface (it is implements). Expecting interface fields to be per-object variables (they are constants). Ignoring the compile error from two conflicting default methods.

What exams ask: "What is an interface? How is it different from an abstract class?", "How does Java achieve multiple inheritance?" (through interfaces), "What are default and static methods in interfaces?", "What is a functional interface? Give an example with a lambda", "Can an interface have a constructor?" and "Write an interface Shape with area() and implement it in Circle and Rectangle".

Recap: An interface is a contract of methods a class implements. Its abstract methods are public, its fields are public static final constants, and it has no constructors or instance state. A class can implement many interfaces, which gives Java multiple inheritance of type without the diamond problem of state. Default, static and private methods let interfaces carry some code. Functional interfaces have one abstract method and can be implemented with lambdas. Program to interfaces to keep code flexible. Next we look at the class at the top of every hierarchy: Object.
key_points: An interface is a contract of methods; a class signs it with implements.
Interface abstract methods are implicitly public abstract; implementations must be public.
Interface fields are implicitly public static final constants; no instance state, no constructors.
A class can implement many interfaces, giving multiple inheritance of type safely.
Default methods (Java 8) have bodies; conflicting defaults must be overridden (A.super.m()).
Interfaces can also have static methods (Java 8) and private methods (Java 9).
A functional interface has exactly one abstract method and can be implemented by a lambda.
Program to an interface: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
lessons.tip: Name interfaces after abilities (Payable, Chargeable, Switchable). If you can say 'X can do Y', Y is probably an interface.
lessons.task: Write interface Switchable { void on(); void off(); } and implement it in Fan, Light and WaterPump. Store them in a Switchable[] and switch everything off with one loop.

quiz.q: Which keyword does a class use to adopt an interface?
quiz.explain: Classes implement interfaces; interfaces extend other interfaces.

quiz.q: A field int MAX = 10; inside an interface is:
quiz.explain: Interface fields are always constants.

quiz.q: Why does void charge(int w) { } in an implementing class fail to compile?
quiz.explain: Interface methods are public, and overriding cannot reduce access.

quiz.q: How does Java let a class be several kinds of thing at once?
quiz.explain: A class may implement any number of interfaces.

quiz.q: Which is a functional interface?
options: An interface with exactly one abstract method
An interface with only default methods
quiz.explain: One abstract method lets it be implemented by a lambda.

lessons.title: The Object Class: toString, equals, hashCode, clone
lessons.content:
In a big family tree, if you keep going up through parents and grandparents, eventually you reach one great ancestor that everyone in the family shares. In Java, every class has such an ancestor: the class java.lang.Object. Whether you write class Student or class Rickshaw, if you do not extend anything, Java quietly makes it extend Object. That means every single object in Java inherits a small set of methods from Object. In this lesson we study the most important ones, toString, equals, hashCode, getClass and clone, and learn how and why to override them.

Object, the root of the hierarchy: Object is the only class in Java with no parent. Every other class has exactly one direct parent, and following parents upward always ends at Object. As a result, a variable of type Object can refer to any object at all: Object o = new Student(); Object p = "Hello"; Object q = new int[3];. Before generics (lesson 18), collections stored everything as Object, which is why you may see casts like (String) list.get(0) in old code.

The main methods of Object: toString() returns a text description of the object. equals(Object o) says whether another object is "equal" to this one. hashCode() returns an int used by hash-based collections. getClass() returns the runtime class of the object. clone() makes a copy, if the class allows it. There are also wait(), notify() and notifyAll() for threads (lesson 21), and finalize(), which is deprecated. You will override the first three in almost every class that holds data.

toString, the default: Object's toString returns the class name, an @ sign and the hash code in hexadecimal, such as Student@1b6d3586. This is useless to a human. Since println, string concatenation and debuggers all call toString automatically, a good toString makes your objects readable everywhere. "Student: " + s calls s.toString() behind the scenes.

Overriding toString: @Override public String toString() { return "Student[name=" + name + ", roll=" + roll + ", cgpa=" + cgpa + "]"; }. Now System.out.println(s) prints Student[name=Rahim, roll=101, cgpa=3.75]. Include the fields that identify and describe the object, but never secrets like passwords or PINs, because toString output often ends up in logs that many people can read.

equals, the default: Object's equals is the same as ==: it returns true only if both references point to the same object. For many classes that is wrong. Two Student objects created separately with the same roll number in the same department usually represent the same real student, so they should be equal. Java's String, Integer and other library classes already override equals to compare content, which is why "abc".equals(new String("abc")) is true.

The equals contract: If you override equals, Java requires it to behave sensibly, following five rules. Reflexive: x.equals(x) is true. Symmetric: if x.equals(y) then y.equals(x). Transitive: if x.equals(y) and y.equals(z), then x.equals(z). Consistent: repeated calls give the same answer as long as the objects do not change. And x.equals(null) is false, never an exception. Collections and many library methods rely on these rules.

Writing a correct equals, step by step: @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { if (this == o) return true; if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false; Student other = (Student) o; return roll == other.roll && Objects.equals(dept, other.dept); }. Step 1: the same object is equal to itself, fast. Step 2: null or a different class is not equal. Step 3: cast safely. Step 4: compare the significant fields, using == for primitives and Objects.equals for references, which handles nulls.

The parameter must be Object: As lesson 11 warned, writing public boolean equals(Student other) creates an overload, not an override. Collections call equals(Object), so they will ignore your method. list.contains(new Student(101, "CSE")) will return false even when an equal student is in the list. Always declare the parameter as Object and add @Override, which would catch the mistake.

getClass versus instanceof in equals: Using getClass() != o.getClass() means a Student is never equal to a CSEStudent subclass object, even with the same roll. Using if (!(o instanceof Student)) return false; allows subclasses to be equal to parents, but can break symmetry if a subclass also overrides equals with extra fields. A common rule: use getClass when subclasses may add fields that matter to equality; use instanceof when the class is final or subclasses never change what equality means.

hashCode, what it is for: hashCode returns an int that hash-based collections like HashMap and HashSet use to decide which bucket an object goes into, so they can find it quickly without comparing it with every element. Think of a library that stores books on shelves by the first letter of the title: to find "Himu", you go straight to shelf H instead of searching the whole library. The hash code is the shelf number.

The hashCode contract: First, if two objects are equal according to equals, they must have the same hashCode. Second, the same object must return the same hashCode while its relevant fields do not change. Third, unequal objects may have the same hashCode (this is a collision), although fewer collisions mean better speed. Note the direction: equal objects must share hash codes, but sharing a hash code does not mean equal.

Why overriding equals without hashCode breaks things: Suppose you override equals to compare roll numbers but keep Object's hashCode, which is based on identity. Two equal Student objects will then usually have different hash codes. Put one in a HashSet and ask set.contains(theOther): the set looks in the bucket for theOther's hash code, finds nothing there, and says false, even though an equal student is inside. The rule is simple: always override equals and hashCode together, using the same fields.

Writing hashCode: The easy, correct way is Objects.hash with the same fields used in equals: @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(roll, dept); }. Internally it combines the fields' hash codes, roughly as 31 times the running result plus each field's hash. Most IDEs, such as IntelliJ IDEA and Eclipse, can generate matching equals and hashCode for you; just check that the fields are right.

Mutable fields and hashing, a warning: If an object is stored in a HashSet and you then change a field used in hashCode, the object is now in the wrong bucket. The set can no longer find it, and contains returns false. Prefer immutable fields (lesson 7) for anything used in equals and hashCode, or do not change those fields while the object is inside a hash-based collection.

getClass: o.getClass() returns a Class object describing the runtime class. o.getClass().getName() gives the full name like "java.lang.String", and getSimpleName() gives "String". It is used in equals, in logging, and in reflection, a more advanced feature that lets programs inspect classes at runtime. For a CSEStudent referenced by a Student variable, getClass() reports CSEStudent, the actual type.

clone and copying objects: Sometimes you need a copy of an object. Object has a protected method clone() that creates a field-by-field copy. To use it, the class must implement the marker interface Cloneable, otherwise clone throws CloneNotSupportedException, and it usually overrides clone as public: class Point implements Cloneable { int x, y; @Override public Point clone() { try { return (Point) super.clone(); } catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) { throw new AssertionError(); } } }.

Shallow copy versus deep copy: Object's clone makes a shallow copy: primitive fields are copied, but reference fields are copied as references, so the copy and the original share the same inner objects. If Team has a String[] players field, a shallow clone shares one array; changing a player in the copy changes the original too. A deep copy also copies the inner objects: copy.players = players.clone();. Exams love this distinction, so draw it: two outer boxes pointing to one inner box (shallow) versus two outer boxes each with its own inner box (deep).

Alternatives to clone: Many experienced Java programmers avoid clone because its rules are awkward. The usual alternatives are a copy constructor, Team(Team other), as in lesson 5, or a static factory method like Team.copyOf(other). Both make deep or shallow copying explicit and easy to read. For immutable objects you never need copies at all, since sharing is safe.

A worked HashSet trace: Suppose Student overrides equals on roll but not hashCode. Student a = new Student(101); Student b = new Student(101); Set<Student> set = new HashSet<>(); set.add(a); set.add(b); System.out.println(set.size());. Because a and b have different identity-based hash codes, they usually fall into different buckets, so the set never even calls equals between them, and the size is 2: a duplicate slipped in. After adding hashCode returning Objects.hash(roll), both land in the same bucket, equals returns true, the second add is rejected, and the size is 1.

Records, a modern shortcut: Since Java 16 you can declare a record, a compact immutable data class: record Point(int x, int y) { }. The compiler automatically generates private final fields, a constructor, getters named x() and y(), and correct equals, hashCode and toString based on all the fields. new Point(3, 5).equals(new Point(3, 5)) is true, and printing it shows Point[x=3, y=5]. Records are perfect for simple value objects, and they show exactly the methods this lesson told you to write by hand.

Real life example 1, a contact list app: class Contact { private final String name; private final String phone; ... toString returns name + " (" + phone + ")"; equals compares phone only; hashCode is Objects.hash(phone). } Now when the app imports contacts from two SIM cards into a HashSet<Contact>, duplicates with the same phone number appear only once, even if they were saved with slightly different names. And printing the set shows readable names and numbers instead of Contact@5e2de80c.

Real life example 2, an exam seat plan: class Seat { int row; int col; } with equals and hashCode on row and col lets a HashMap<Seat, Student> store who sits where. map.get(new Seat(3, 5)) finds the student, because a newly created Seat(3, 5) is equal to the stored key and has the same hash code. Without overriding both methods, the lookup would return null every time, since the new Seat is a different object.

Common mistakes: Overriding equals with a Student parameter instead of Object. Overriding equals but not hashCode. Comparing strings or wrapper fields with == inside equals. Including passwords in toString. Changing fields used in hashCode while the object is in a HashSet. Thinking clone makes a deep copy. Forgetting to implement Cloneable.

What exams ask: "What is the Object class? List its important methods", "Why should we override toString?", "Explain the contract between equals and hashCode", "What happens if you override equals but not hashCode?", "Differentiate between == and equals()", "What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy?" and "Write equals and hashCode for a given class".

Recap: Every class inherits from Object. Override toString to give readable output, and override equals and hashCode together, using the same fields, to define logical equality that works in collections. Follow the equals contract, take Object as the parameter, and use Objects.equals and Objects.hash. clone makes shallow copies and needs Cloneable; copy constructors are often clearer. Next we learn to organise many classes into packages.
key_points: Every Java class inherits from java.lang.Object.
Override toString to give readable output; never include secrets.
Object's equals is identity (==); override it to compare meaningful fields.
equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and false for null.
Declare equals(Object o) with @Override; equals(Student s) is an overload bug.
Equal objects must have equal hashCodes; override equals and hashCode together (Objects.hash).
Changing hashCode fields while in a HashSet makes the object unfindable.
clone needs Cloneable and makes a shallow copy; deep copies copy inner objects too.
lessons.tip: Whenever you write equals, write hashCode immediately after, using exactly the same fields. Treat them as one unit.
lessons.task: Write a Contact class with name and phone, override toString, equals (phone only) and hashCode. Add three contacts, two with the same phone, to a HashSet and print its size (it should be 2).

quiz.q: What does Object's default toString return?
options: Class name, @ and a hex hash code
quiz.explain: For example Student@1b6d3586.

quiz.q: Which rule is part of the equals contract?
options: Equal objects must have different hash codes
quiz.explain: That is symmetry; the others are wrong.

quiz.q: You override equals but not hashCode. What breaks?
quiz.explain: Equal objects may land in different buckets, so contains/get fail.

quiz.q: What kind of copy does Object.clone() make?
options: A copy of only static fields
quiz.explain: References inside are copied as references, so inner objects are shared.

quiz.q: Why is public boolean equals(Student s) a bug?
options: It overloads instead of overriding equals(Object)
quiz.explain: Collections call equals(Object), so they never use this method.

lessons.title: Packages
lessons.content:
Imagine a big government office building in Dhaka with no departments and no room numbers. Every file from every ministry is piled in one huge hall. Finding the passport file of one person would take days, and two files with the same name, say "Application.pdf", would get mixed up. Real offices solve this with floors, departments and labelled rooms. Java solves the same problem for code with packages. When a program grows to hundreds of classes, packages keep them organised, prevent name clashes and control who can see what.

What a package is: A package is a named group of related classes and interfaces, like a folder for code. Java's own library is organised this way: java.lang holds basic classes like String and Math, java.util holds collections like ArrayList and HashMap, java.io holds file input and output classes, and java.time holds dates and times. The full name of a class includes its package, so ArrayList's full name, called its fully qualified name, is java.util.ArrayList.

Why packages matter: Organisation, because related classes stay together and are easy to find. Name collision avoidance, because two classes can share a simple name if they are in different packages; Java itself has both java.util.Date and java.sql.Date. Access control, because default (package-private) and protected access depend on packages, as lesson 7 showed. And reuse, because a well designed package can be shipped as a library and used in many projects.

Declaring a package: Put a package statement as the very first line of the source file, before any import: package bd.edu.du.cse.library;. Every class in that file now belongs to that package. If you write no package statement, the class goes into the unnamed default package, which is fine for tiny exercises but should be avoided in real projects, because classes in the default package cannot be imported by classes in named packages.

Packages and folders: Java expects the folder structure to match the package name. A class Book in package bd.edu.du.cse.library should live in the file bd/edu/du/cse/library/Book.java, relative to the source root. The compiled Book.class goes into the matching folder of the output. The dots in the package name become folder separators. If the folders do not match, the compiler or the JVM will not find the class.

Naming conventions: Package names are all lowercase, with no spaces. To keep names unique worldwide, the convention is to start with your organisation's internet domain reversed. A company with the domain example.com uses com.example.something. A university project might use bd.ac.buet.cse.project or edu.du.cse.lab3. Inside, names usually follow the structure of the app: com.shop.model, com.shop.service, com.shop.ui.

Using classes from another package: There are three ways. Use the fully qualified name every time: java.util.Scanner sc = new java.util.Scanner(System.in);, which is long but always works. Import a single class at the top of the file: import java.util.Scanner;, after which you can write just Scanner. Or import every public class of a package with a wildcard: import java.util.*;. Imports go after the package statement and before the class declaration.

Single-type import versus wildcard import: import java.util.ArrayList; makes it clear exactly which classes are used, and most style guides prefer it. import java.util.*; is shorter but can hide where names come from and can cause ambiguity. Importing does not copy code or make the program bigger or slower; it only tells the compiler where to look up short names. Also note that a wildcard imports only the classes of that package, not its sub-packages: import java.util.*; does not import java.util.function.Function.

java.lang is automatic: You never need to import String, Math, System, Integer or Object, because every Java file automatically imports java.lang.*. Classes in the same package as your class are also visible without import. Everything else needs an import or a fully qualified name.

Handling name clashes: If you need both java.util.Date and java.sql.Date in one file, you cannot import both by their simple name. Import one, and write the other in full: import java.util.Date; ... java.sql.Date dbDate = ...;. If you import two wildcards that both contain a class called Date and then write Date, the compiler reports that the reference is ambiguous.

Static import: import static lets you use static members without the class name. import static java.lang.Math.PI; import static java.lang.Math.sqrt; then double r = sqrt(16) * PI;. It is handy for constants and in test code, but overusing it makes code confusing, because readers cannot tell which class sqrt comes from.

Packages and access control, revisited: Members with no access modifier are visible only inside the same package. Public classes and members are visible everywhere. Protected members are visible in the same package and in subclasses elsewhere. A class without public is visible only in its package. So when you split classes into packages, you must think about what each package exposes. A common design is to make only a few classes public, the package's front door, and keep helpers package-private.

A worked example of package access: package bd.shop.model; public class Product { String sku; public String name; protected double price; private int stock; }. From another class in bd.shop.model you can use sku, name and price, but not stock. From bd.shop.ui, an unrelated class can use only name. A subclass in bd.shop.ui, such as class DiscountProduct extends Product, can use name and also price through inheritance, but not sku or stock.

Sub-packages are separate packages: bd.shop and bd.shop.model look like parent and child, but to Java they are completely separate packages. A class in bd.shop gets no special access to package-private members of bd.shop.model, and vice versa. The dotted names are only for human organisation and folder layout.

Compiling and running packaged code from the command line: With source files under src, you can compile with javac -d out src/bd/shop/model/Product.java src/bd/shop/App.java, which writes class files into the out folder in the correct package structure. Run with java -cp out bd.shop.App, giving the fully qualified name of the class with main. The -cp option sets the classpath, the list of places the JVM searches for classes. IDEs such as IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse and NetBeans handle all of this automatically.

JAR files: A JAR (Java ARchive) file is a zip file that bundles compiled classes, organised by package, plus resources like images. Libraries are distributed as JARs: when you add a library to a project, you add its JAR to the classpath. A JAR can also be made runnable by naming the main class in its manifest, so a user can start it with java -jar app.jar. Build tools like Maven and Gradle download library JARs automatically.

Modules, a brief note: Java 9 added a module system on top of packages. A module groups packages and declares in a module-info.java file which packages it exports and which other modules it requires. Most second-year courses only mention modules, so it is enough to know they exist and that packages remain the main unit of organisation inside them.

A typical project layout: For a small library management app: bd.edu.lib.model holds Book, Member and Loan; bd.edu.lib.service holds LoanService, which contains the rules for borrowing; bd.edu.lib.storage holds FileStore, which saves data to files (lesson 20); bd.edu.lib.ui holds the console or GUI screens (lesson 24); and bd.edu.lib.App holds main. Each package has one clear job, and dependencies flow in one direction: ui uses service, service uses model and storage.

Step by step, creating and using your own package: Step 1, make a folder structure src/mylib/geometry. Step 2, write src/mylib/geometry/Circle.java starting with package mylib.geometry; and a public class Circle with a public constructor and a public area() method. Step 3, write src/app/Main.java starting with package app; then import mylib.geometry.Circle; and use new Circle(2).area() in main. Step 4, compile both with javac -d out and the two file paths. Step 5, run with java -cp out app.Main. Exam answers that list these steps, with the folder tree drawn, usually get full marks for "how to create a user-defined package".

Built-in packages worth knowing: java.lang: String, Math, Object, System, wrapper classes, Thread. java.util: collections (ArrayList, HashMap), Scanner, Random, Objects. java.io: File, FileReader, BufferedReader, PrintWriter, serialization. java.nio.file: modern file handling with Path and Files. java.time: LocalDate, LocalTime, Duration. java.net: networking such as URLs and sockets. java.sql: database access with JDBC. javax.swing and java.awt: classic GUI (lesson 24). Recognising the package from a class name helps you guess the right import quickly.

Package-info and documentation: A package can have a file called package-info.java that contains only a package declaration with a documentation comment above it. The javadoc tool uses it to describe the package as a whole on the generated web pages. In a large project, a one-paragraph description of each package's purpose helps new team members understand the layout quickly.

Designing package boundaries: A useful rule is that classes which change together should live together. If every new payment feature touches PaymentService, PaymentGateway and PaymentRecord, keep them in one package such as com.shop.payment, rather than scattering them across separate model, service and storage packages. Both layouts are common: by layer (model, service, ui) for small projects, and by feature (payment, delivery, catalogue) for larger ones.

Real life example 1, a mobile banking codebase: A bank's app might use packages like com.bank.auth for login and OTP, com.bank.transfer for sending money, com.bank.billpay for paying electricity and gas bills, and com.bank.common for shared utilities. Different teams can own different packages. Because a helper inside com.bank.auth is package-private, a developer in the billpay team cannot accidentally call an internal password-checking method; they must go through the public AuthService.

Real life example 2, a university lab assignment: Your teacher asks for a "Student Management System" with separate model, logic and main classes. Putting Student and Course in package lab.model, ResultCalculator in lab.logic and Main in lab, with proper imports, shows that you understand packages. Typical marks are lost for missing package lines, wrong folder structure, or forgetting public on classes that other packages need.

Common mistakes: Putting the package statement after imports. Folder names not matching the package. Forgetting public on a class used from another package. Expecting import java.util.* to import sub-packages. Thinking import makes the program bigger. Leaving everything in the default package. Running java with the file name instead of the fully qualified class name.

What exams ask: "What is a package? What are its advantages?", "Differentiate between built-in and user-defined packages", "How do you create and use a user-defined package? Show the steps", "What is the difference between import java.util.* and import java.util.Scanner?", "Which package is imported by default?" and the access modifier table across packages.

Recap: Packages group related classes, prevent name clashes and work with access modifiers to control visibility. Declare one with a package statement on the first line, match the folder structure, use lowercase reversed-domain names, and use classes from other packages through imports or fully qualified names. java.lang is imported automatically, wildcards do not include sub-packages, and sub-packages are separate packages. JAR files bundle packages for distribution. Next, we learn how Java handles things going wrong: exceptions.
key_points: A package groups related classes; the fully qualified name includes it (java.util.ArrayList).
Declare it with package on the first line; folders must match the package name.
Use lowercase, reversed-domain names like bd.ac.buet.cse.project.
Use other packages via fully qualified names, single-type imports or wildcard imports.
java.lang is imported automatically; wildcards do not import sub-packages.
Default (no modifier) access is limited to the same package; sub-packages are separate packages.
Resolve name clashes (java.util.Date vs java.sql.Date) with a fully qualified name.
JAR files bundle compiled packages; -cp sets where the JVM looks for classes.
lessons.tip: Before writing code for a project, sketch the packages (model, service, ui...) on paper. Deciding where a class lives forces you to decide what it is responsible for.
lessons.task: Create two packages, shop.model with a public Product class and shop.app with a Main class that imports and uses Product. Then remove public from Product and read the compiler error.

quiz.q: Which statement must come first in a Java source file that uses packages?
quiz.explain: The package statement must be the first statement.

quiz.q: Which package is imported automatically?
quiz.explain: java.lang (String, Math, System...) is always available.

quiz.q: Does import java.util.*; import java.util.function.Function?
quiz.explain: Wildcards import only the classes of that exact package.

quiz.q: A field with no access modifier is visible to:
quiz.explain: No modifier means package-private access.

quiz.q: How do you use java.util.Date and java.sql.Date in one file?
options: Import one and write the other with its fully qualified name
quiz.explain: Two classes with the same simple name cannot both be imported; qualify one.

lessons.title: Exception Handling
lessons.content:
You are sending 2,000 taka through a mobile banking app. Many things could go wrong: you might type the wrong PIN, your balance might be too low, the internet might drop in the middle, or the receiver's number might not exist. A good app does not simply crash in any of these cases. It shows a clear message, keeps your money safe and lets you try again. Handling such unexpected situations gracefully is what exception handling is about, and Java has one of the most structured systems for it.

What an exception is: An exception is an event that happens while a program runs and disrupts the normal flow of instructions. Dividing by zero, reading past the end of an array, opening a file that does not exist, or converting "abc" to a number all cause exceptions. In Java, an exception is represented by an object, created from an exception class, that carries information about what went wrong and where.

What happens without handling: int[] marks = new int[3]; marks[5] = 90; throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. If nothing catches it, the current method stops immediately, then its caller stops, and so on up to main. Finally the JVM prints a stack trace, a list of method calls showing where the exception happened, and the program terminates. Every line after the error is skipped. For a user, that is a crash.

The try-catch block: To handle an exception, put the risky code in a try block and the recovery code in a catch block. try { int result = total / count; System.out.println(result); } catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println("Cannot divide by zero"); }. If count is 0, the division throws an ArithmeticException, Java jumps straight to the matching catch block, prints the message, and then continues with the code after the whole try-catch. If no exception happens, the catch block is skipped.

The exception object: The catch parameter, e above, is the exception object. e.getMessage() returns a short description such as "/ by zero". e.toString() gives the class name and the message. e.printStackTrace() prints the full stack trace, which is very useful while debugging. Because exceptions are objects, they can carry extra fields and methods, as custom exceptions later in this lesson show.

Multiple catch blocks: One try can have several catch blocks for different exception types. try { int n = Integer.parseInt(text); int r = 100 / n; } catch (NumberFormatException e) { System.out.println("Not a number"); } catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println("Zero is not allowed"); }. Java checks the catch blocks from top to bottom and runs the first one whose type matches. At most one catch block runs for a given exception.

Order of catch blocks: Because the first match wins, more specific exception types must come before more general ones. If you put catch (Exception e) first and catch (ArithmeticException e) after it, the second can never run, and the compiler reports an error that the exception "has already been caught". Remember the rule as: children before parents.

Multi-catch: Since Java 7 you can catch several unrelated types in one block with a vertical bar: catch (NumberFormatException | ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println("Bad input: " + e.getMessage()); }. This avoids repeating the same handling code. The types in a multi-catch cannot be parent and child of each other.

The finally block: A finally block, placed after the catch blocks, runs no matter what: whether the try finished normally, an exception was caught, or an exception was not caught, and even if the try or catch contains a return statement. It is used for clean-up that must always happen, such as closing a file, releasing a lock or ending a database connection. The only usual ways to skip it are calling System.exit() or the JVM itself crashing.

A worked flow example: Consider try { System.out.println("A"); int x = 10 / 0; System.out.println("B"); } catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println("C"); } finally { System.out.println("D"); } System.out.println("E");. A prints first. The division throws, so B is skipped. The catch prints C. The finally prints D. Then the program continues and prints E. Output: A, C, D, E. If the division were 10 / 2, the output would be A, B, D, E.

The exception hierarchy: All exceptions and errors in Java descend from the class Throwable. It has two main children. Error represents serious problems in the JVM or environment that programs normally should not try to handle, such as OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError. Exception represents conditions a program might reasonably handle. Under Exception there is RuntimeException, the parent of exceptions caused by programming bugs, such as NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, ClassCastException, NumberFormatException and IllegalArgumentException.

Checked versus unchecked exceptions: Java divides exceptions into two groups. Unchecked exceptions are RuntimeException, Error and their subclasses; the compiler does not force you to handle them, because they usually mean a bug you should fix in code. Checked exceptions are all other subclasses of Exception, such as IOException, FileNotFoundException and SQLException; they represent problems outside your program's control, like a missing file or a broken network, and the compiler forces you to deal with them.

The catch-or-declare rule: For checked exceptions, every method must either catch them or declare them with throws in its header. new FileReader("marks.txt") can throw FileNotFoundException, a checked exception. If your method neither catches it nor says throws FileNotFoundException (or a parent like IOException), the code does not compile: "unreported exception FileNotFoundException; must be caught or declared to be thrown". This rule makes sure nobody forgets that files can be missing.

throw versus throws: These two keywords look alike but do different jobs. throw is a statement that actually throws an exception object: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");. throws appears in a method header and declares which checked exceptions the method may pass to its caller: void loadMarks(String file) throws IOException { ... }. Think of throw as the act and throws as the warning label.

Throwing your own exceptions: Methods should throw exceptions when they cannot do their job correctly. public void withdraw(double amt) { if (amt <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive"); if (amt > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient balance"); balance -= amt; }. This is better than silently returning or printing a message, because the caller decides how to react, for example by showing a dialog in an app or logging the problem on a server.

Custom exceptions: You can create your own exception classes for problems specific to your program. class InsufficientBalanceException extends Exception { private final double shortBy; InsufficientBalanceException(double shortBy) { super("Short by Tk " + shortBy); this.shortBy = shortBy; } double getShortBy() { return shortBy; } }. Extending Exception makes it checked; extending RuntimeException makes it unchecked. Then withdraw can declare throws InsufficientBalanceException and the caller can catch it specifically and read getShortBy().

Choosing checked or unchecked: Use a checked exception when the caller can reasonably recover and you want to force them to think about it, such as insufficient balance or a missing file. Use an unchecked exception for programming errors such as a null argument or an invalid index, which should be fixed in code rather than caught. Modern Java code uses unchecked exceptions more often, but exams expect you to know both and their compiler rules.

Propagation: When an exception is not caught in a method, it propagates to the caller, then to the caller's caller, until some method catches it or it reaches the top and ends the thread. If main calls processOrder(), which calls charge(), which throws, and only main has a try-catch, the exception travels up through charge and processOrder, skipping their remaining lines, and is handled in main. This lets you handle errors at the level that knows what to do about them.

try-with-resources: Resources like files and network connections must always be closed, even when errors occur. Before Java 7 that meant a finally block with its own try-catch. Java 7 added try-with-resources: try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("marks.txt"))) { System.out.println(br.readLine()); } catch (IOException e) { System.out.println("Could not read file"); }. Any object declared in the brackets must implement AutoCloseable, and Java automatically calls close() on it when the block ends, normally or by exception. Lesson 20 uses this constantly.

Exception chaining: Sometimes you catch a low-level exception and throw a higher-level one that makes more sense to your caller, while keeping the original as the cause: catch (IOException e) { throw new DataLoadException("Could not load student records", e); }. The cause is stored inside and appears in the stack trace as "Caused by", so no information is lost.

Good practice: Catch exceptions only where you can do something useful. Never write an empty catch block, catch (Exception e) { }, which silently hides bugs. Avoid catching Exception or Throwable broadly except at the very top of a program. Give exceptions clear messages. Do not use exceptions for normal control flow, such as ending a loop, because they are slower and harder to read than ordinary conditions.

Real life example 1, a fund transfer: public void transfer(Account from, Account to, double amt) throws InsufficientBalanceException { if (amt <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid amount"); from.withdraw(amt); to.deposit(amt); }. The app screen calls it inside try { service.transfer(a, b, 2000); showSuccess(); } catch (InsufficientBalanceException e) { showError("Not enough balance. Short by Tk " + e.getShortBy()); }. The user sees a friendly message, and no money is lost or created.

Real life example 2, reading a result file at a school: A program reads marks from results.csv. The file might be missing (FileNotFoundException), a line might contain "abs" instead of a number (NumberFormatException), or a line might have too few columns (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException). With try-with-resources around the reading and a try-catch around each line's parsing, the program skips bad lines, reports them with line numbers, and still produces results for every valid student instead of crashing on the first mistake.

Common mistakes: Catching a general exception before a specific one. Using throws when you meant throw. Swallowing exceptions with empty catch blocks. Forgetting that checked exceptions must be caught or declared. Thinking finally does not run when there is a return. Forgetting to close resources. Throwing Exception everywhere instead of a meaningful type.

What exams ask: "What is an exception? How is it different from an error?", "Differentiate between checked and unchecked exceptions with examples", "Explain try, catch, finally, throw and throws", "Draw the Java exception hierarchy", "How do you create a custom exception?", "What is try-with-resources?" and output questions tracing try-catch-finally flows.

Recap: Exceptions are objects that represent runtime problems. try holds risky code, catch handles specific types in order from specific to general, and finally always runs for clean-up. Throwable splits into Error and Exception, and RuntimeException marks unchecked exceptions; checked exceptions must be caught or declared with throws. throw raises an exception, custom exceptions carry domain information, exceptions propagate up the call stack, and try-with-resources closes resources automatically. Next, generics make our classes type safe and reusable.
key_points: An exception is an object representing a runtime problem; uncaught, it ends the program with a stack trace.
try holds risky code; catch handles matching types, specific before general.
finally always runs (even with return), except System.exit or a JVM crash.
Throwable -> Error and Exception; RuntimeException and its children are unchecked.
Checked exceptions (IOException...) must be caught or declared with throws.
throw raises an exception object; throws declares exceptions in a method header.
Custom exceptions extend Exception (checked) or RuntimeException (unchecked).
try-with-resources automatically closes AutoCloseable resources.
lessons.tip: When you trace exception code, use your finger: follow the try line by line, jump to the matching catch at the first exception, then always visit finally.
lessons.task: Write a program that reads two numbers as text, parses them and divides. Catch NumberFormatException and ArithmeticException separately, print a friendly message for each, and print 'Done' in finally.

quiz.q: Which block always runs, whether or not an exception occurs?
quiz.explain: finally is for clean-up and runs in all normal cases.

quiz.q: Which is a checked exception?
quiz.explain: IOException is not a RuntimeException, so the compiler checks it.

quiz.q: catch (Exception e) is placed before catch (ArithmeticException e). Result?
quiz.explain: The general catch already handles everything, so the specific one can never run.

quiz.q: What is the difference between throw and throws?
options: throw raises an exception; throws declares it in the method header
throws raises an exception; throw declares it
quiz.explain: throw is a statement; throws is part of a method signature.

quiz.q: To make a custom checked exception, you extend:
quiz.explain: Subclasses of Exception (but not RuntimeException) are checked.

lessons.title: Generics
lessons.content:
Think about the tiffin boxes your mother packs. The same steel tiffin carrier can hold rice one day, khichuri the next and noodles on Friday. The box is designed once, but what goes inside changes. Now imagine if every tiffin box had a label saying exactly what it holds, and the box refused to accept anything else. You would never open your "rice" box at school and find a wet towel. Generics in Java give you exactly this: a class or method designed once, that works with many types, while the compiler checks you only put in and take out the right type.

The problem before generics: Before Java 5, collections stored everything as Object. ArrayList list = new ArrayList(); list.add("Rahim"); list.add(42); String s = (String) list.get(1);. This compiles, because the list accepts any Object, but at runtime the cast fails with a ClassCastException, since element 1 is an Integer. You had to cast every time you took something out, and mistakes were found only when the program ran, often by users.

What generics are: Generics let you write classes, interfaces and methods with type parameters, placeholders for types that are filled in when the code is used. ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<String>(); means "a list of Strings". Now names.add(42) does not compile, and String s = names.get(0); needs no cast. Errors move from runtime to compile time, which is much cheaper to fix. This is called type safety.

The diamond operator: Since Java 7 you can omit the type on the right side and let the compiler infer it: ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();. The empty angle brackets <> are called the diamond operator. With the "program to an interface" habit from lesson 14, the common form is List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();.

Writing a generic class: class Box<T> { private T item; public void put(T item) { this.item = item; } public T get() { return item; } }. T is a type parameter, a name for "some type to be decided later". Box<String> b1 = new Box<>(); b1.put("Mango"); String fruit = b1.get();. Box<Integer> b2 = new Box<>(); b2.put(25); int n = b2.get();. One class, written once, safely holds any type. Trying b1.put(25) is a compile error because b1 holds Strings.

Naming type parameters: By convention, type parameters are single capital letters. T means Type, E means Element (used in collections), K and V mean Key and Value (used in maps), N means Number, and S, U, V are used for second, third and fourth types. These are only conventions, but following them makes your code instantly readable to other Java programmers.

Multiple type parameters: A class can have more than one type parameter. class Pair<K, V> { private final K key; private final V value; Pair(K key, V value) { this.key = key; this.value = value; } K getKey() { return key; } V getValue() { return value; } }. Pair<String, Integer> p = new Pair<>("Rahim", 101); gives a name and a roll number together. Pair<String, Double> could hold a product and its price.

Generic methods: A single method can be generic even inside a non-generic class. Declare the type parameter before the return type: static <T> void printAll(T[] items) { for (T x : items) System.out.println(x); }. You can call printAll(new String[]{"a", "b"}) or printAll(new Integer[]{1, 2, 3}), and the compiler infers T each time. Another example: static <T> T firstOrDefault(List<T> list, T def) { return list.isEmpty() ? def : list.get(0); }.

Bounded type parameters: Sometimes T cannot be just anything. To add up numbers, T must be some kind of Number. Write <T extends Number>: static <T extends Number> double sum(List<T> list) { double s = 0; for (T x : list) s += x.doubleValue(); return s; }. Now sum works for List<Integer> and List<Double>, and you can call Number's methods like doubleValue() on x, but sum(List<String>) is a compile error. Note that extends is used here for both classes and interfaces.

Bounds with interfaces, finding a maximum: static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(T[] arr) { T best = arr[0]; for (T x : arr) if (x.compareTo(best) > 0) best = x; return best; }. This works for any type that knows how to compare itself, such as Integer, String or your own Student class if it implements Comparable<Student> (lesson 19). You can also require several bounds at once with &, as in <T extends Number & Comparable<T>>, where a class bound must come first.

Generics and inheritance, a surprise: Integer is a subclass of Number, but List<Integer> is NOT a subtype of List<Number>. If it were, you could write List<Number> nums = intList; nums.add(3.5); and put a Double into a list of Integers, breaking type safety. So Java forbids it. Generic types are invariant: List<A> and List<B> are unrelated even if A and B are related. Arrays behave differently and are covariant, which is why arrays can throw ArrayStoreException at runtime.

Wildcards: To write methods that accept lists of related types, Java uses the wildcard ?. List<?> means "a list of some unknown type"; you can read elements as Object but cannot add anything except null. It is useful for methods like static void printSize(List<?> list) that do not care about the element type.

Upper-bounded wildcards: List<? extends Number> means "a list of Number or some subclass of Number". A method static double total(List<? extends Number> list) can accept List<Integer>, List<Double> or List<Number>, and can read each element as a Number. But it cannot add elements, because it does not know which exact subtype the list holds; adding a Double to what might be a List<Integer> would be unsafe.

Lower-bounded wildcards: List<? super Integer> means "a list of Integer or some superclass of Integer", such as List<Number> or List<Object>. A method static void addNumbers(List<? super Integer> list) { for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) list.add(i); } can safely add Integers into any of them. Reading from it gives only Object. A helpful memory rule is PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. If a parameter produces values you read, use extends; if it consumes values you put in, use super.

Type erasure: Generics exist only at compile time. After checking types, the compiler erases them: Box<String> and Box<Integer> both become plain Box in the bytecode, with T replaced by Object (or by its bound, such as Number), and the compiler inserts casts where needed. This kept new Java code compatible with old JVMs and libraries. But it has consequences you must know.

Restrictions caused by erasure: You cannot use primitives as type arguments, so List<int> is illegal; use List<Integer> and autoboxing (lesson 8). You cannot create an object of a type parameter with new T(), because the runtime does not know what T is. You cannot create a generic array with new T[10] directly. You cannot use instanceof with a parameterized type such as obj instanceof List<String>. And static fields cannot use the class's type parameter, because one static field is shared by Box<String> and Box<Integer> alike.

Raw types: Using a generic class without type arguments, such as ArrayList list = new ArrayList();, gives a raw type. It exists only for compatibility with pre-2004 code. The compiler warns about "unchecked" operations, and you lose all type safety. Never use raw types in new code; if you really do not care about the type, use List<?> instead.

Generic interfaces: Interfaces can be generic too. Comparable<T> declares int compareTo(T other). Comparator<T> declares int compare(T a, T b). A Repository<T> interface for a data layer might declare void save(T item); T findById(String id); List<T> findAll();. Then class StudentRepository implements Repository<Student> fills in T with Student, and its findById returns a Student with no casts.

A generic stack, worked example: class Stack<E> { private final ArrayList<E> items = new ArrayList<>(); void push(E x) { items.add(x); } E pop() { if (items.isEmpty()) throw new RuntimeException("Stack is empty"); return items.remove(items.size() - 1); } boolean isEmpty() { return items.isEmpty(); } }. Stack<String> undo = new Stack<>(); undo.push("typed A"); undo.push("typed B"); System.out.println(undo.pop()); prints "typed B". The same class gives Stack<Integer> for evaluating expressions or Stack<Page> for a browser's back button. Notice how we built it on top of another generic class, ArrayList<E>, passing our E along.

Generic methods with explicit and inferred types: Usually the compiler infers the type argument of a generic method from the arguments, but you can also write it explicitly: Util.<String>firstOrDefault(names, "none"). Inference also works from the target type: List<String> empty = Collections.emptyList(); knows that T is String because of the variable it is assigned to. If inference fails or picks something unexpected, giving the type explicitly is the fix.

Generics and static methods in utility classes: Java's own library is full of generic static methods. Collections.max(list) returns the largest element of any list whose elements are Comparable. Collections.sort(list) sorts it. Arrays.asList("a", "b") returns a List<String>. Optional<T> wraps a value that might be missing, as in Optional<Student> found = repo.findByRoll(101);, forcing callers to think about the "not found" case instead of getting a surprise null.

Real life example 1, an API response wrapper: Mobile apps that talk to servers often wrap every reply in a common shape. class ApiResponse<T> { boolean success; String message; T data; }. ApiResponse<User> carries a user profile after login, ApiResponse<List<Order>> carries a customer's Daraz-style order history, and ApiResponse<Balance> carries a wallet balance. The success and message handling is written once, and every screen gets its data already typed, without casts.

Real life example 2, a reusable cache for a school app: class Cache<K, V> { private final Map<K, V> map = new HashMap<>(); V get(K key) { return map.get(key); } void put(K key, V value) { map.put(key, value); } }. Cache<String, Student> caches students by roll, Cache<Integer, Result> caches results by exam id. The same tested class serves both, and putting a Result into the student cache is caught by the compiler before the app is ever installed on a phone.

Common mistakes: Writing List<int>. Expecting List<Integer> to be accepted where List<Number> is required. Trying to add to a List<? extends Number>. Writing new T() or new T[n]. Using raw types and ignoring unchecked warnings. Forgetting the <T> before the return type when declaring a generic method.

What exams ask: "What are generics? What are their advantages?", "Write a generic class Box<T> or Pair<K, V>", "Write a generic method to find the maximum element of an array", "What is a bounded type parameter?", "Explain wildcards: ?, ? extends T and ? super T", "What is type erasure?", and "Why can't primitive types be used as type arguments?".

Recap: Generics add type parameters to classes, interfaces and methods, giving reuse with compile-time type safety and no casts. Use the diamond operator, conventional names like T, E, K and V, and bounds like <T extends Number> or <T extends Comparable<T>> when you need certain methods. Generic types are invariant, so wildcards with extends (read) and super (write) make methods flexible. Type erasure removes generic types after compilation, which is why primitives, new T() and generic arrays are not allowed. Next, the Collections Framework puts generics to work.
key_points: Generics add type parameters (<T>) to classes, interfaces and methods for reuse with type safety.
Type errors move from runtime (ClassCastException) to compile time; no casts needed.
Diamond operator: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
Generic method: static <T> void printAll(T[] items).
Bounded type: <T extends Number> or <T extends Comparable<T>> allows calling those methods.
List<Integer> is not a List<Number> (invariance); use ? extends for reading, ? super for writing (PECS).
Type erasure removes generic types after compilation.
So no primitives (List<int>), no new T(), no new T[], no raw types in new code.
lessons.tip: When you see angle brackets, read them aloud: List<Student> is 'a list of Students'. It makes generic code feel like plain English.
lessons.task: Write a generic class Pair<K, V> with getters, and a generic method <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(T[] arr). Test max with an Integer array and a String array.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of generics?
quiz.explain: Type mistakes are caught by the compiler.

quiz.q: Which declaration is legal?
quiz.explain: Type arguments must be reference types; new T() and new T[] are not allowed.

quiz.q: Is List<Integer> a subtype of List<Number>?
quiz.explain: Otherwise you could add a Double into a List<Integer>.

quiz.q: Which wildcard lets a method safely ADD Integers to the list?
quiz.explain: Consumer Super: a list of Integer or a supertype can accept Integers.

quiz.q: What is type erasure?
options: The compiler removing generic type information after checking
quiz.explain: Box<String> and Box<Integer> become plain Box in bytecode.

lessons.title: The Collections Framework
lessons.content:
Think about the different ways a shop keeps things. The cashier keeps receipts in order, one after another, and duplicates are fine because two people can buy the same thing. The shop keeps a register of member phone numbers where each number appears only once. The delivery desk keeps a queue: first order in, first order out. And the price list maps each product name to its price. These are four different ways of keeping a group of things: a list, a set, a queue and a map. Java's Collections Framework gives you ready-made, tested classes for all of them.

What the Collections Framework is: It is a set of interfaces and classes in java.util for storing and processing groups of objects. The interfaces describe what kind of collection it is: List, Set, Queue, Deque and Map. The classes are implementations with different performance: ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, TreeSet, HashMap, TreeMap and others. There are also algorithms in the Collections utility class, such as sort, reverse, shuffle, max and min. Everything is generic (lesson 18), so a List<Student> holds only Students.

Why not just arrays: Arrays have a fixed size chosen at creation; collections grow and shrink automatically. Arrays have very few built-in operations; collections offer add, remove, contains, sort and many more. And collections come in different shapes, such as no-duplicates sets and key-value maps, that arrays cannot express. Arrays are still useful for fixed-size, primitive-heavy data, but for most groups of objects, collections are easier and safer.

The interface hierarchy: At the top is Iterable, which makes the enhanced for loop work. Collection extends it and declares basic methods such as add, remove, contains, size, isEmpty and clear. List, Set and Queue extend Collection. Deque extends Queue. Map is separate: it does not extend Collection, because it stores pairs, not single elements. Drawing this tree is a common exam question.

List, ordered and with duplicates: A List keeps elements in the order you add them, allows duplicates, and lets you access elements by index. List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); names.add("Rahim"); names.add("Fatima"); names.add("Rahim"); names.get(1) is "Fatima"; names.size() is 3; names.indexOf("Rahim") is 0; names.remove(0) removes the first Rahim; names.set(0, "Karim") replaces the element at index 0; names.contains("Fatima") is true.

ArrayList: ArrayList stores elements in an internal array that grows automatically when it gets full, by creating a bigger array and copying the elements. Getting or setting by index is very fast, constant time, O(1). Adding at the end is usually O(1). Inserting or removing in the middle is slower, O(n), because later elements must shift. ArrayList is the default choice for lists and the most used collection in Java.

LinkedList: LinkedList stores each element in a node that links to the next and previous nodes, a doubly linked list (covered in depth in Data Structures).
