quiz.q: Why should a long download not run inside actionPerformed?
options: It blocks the event dispatch thread and freezes the GUI
quiz.explain: Slow work belongs on a background thread.

quiz.q: What is an adapter class such as MouseAdapter for?
options: Providing empty listener methods so you override only the ones you need
quiz.explain: It saves writing empty bodies for unused interface methods.

lessons.title: Object Oriented Design: UML, SOLID and Design Patterns
lessons.content:
Knowing how to use a hammer, a saw and nails does not make you an architect. To build a good house, you need a plan: where the rooms go, how the plumbing connects, where the load-bearing walls stand. Over the last 24 lessons you collected OOP tools: classes, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces, exceptions, collections and more. This final lesson is about using them well: drawing designs with UML class diagrams, following the SOLID principles, and reusing proven solutions called design patterns. It ends with a recap of the whole course and what to learn next.

UML class diagrams: UML (Unified Modeling Language) is a standard visual language for describing software designs. The class diagram is the most used UML diagram in OOP courses. Each class is a box with three compartments: the class name at the top, attributes in the middle and operations (methods) at the bottom. Abstract class names are written in italics or marked {abstract}, and interfaces are marked with <<interface>> above the name.

Visibility and types in UML: Each member is prefixed with a visibility symbol: + for public, - for private, # for protected and ~ for package. Types are written after a colon. For example: - balance : double, + deposit(amount : double) : void, + getBalance() : double. Static members are underlined. So a class box for Account tells a reader at a glance what the class stores and offers, and what it hides.

Relationships in UML: A plain solid line is an association, optionally with an arrowhead for direction and multiplicities like 1, 0..1, * or 1..* at the ends (lesson 9). A hollow diamond at the whole's end marks aggregation; a filled diamond marks composition. A solid line with a hollow triangle pointing at the parent is inheritance (generalization). A dashed line with a hollow triangle pointing at the interface is realization, meaning a class implements an interface. A dashed arrow is a dependency. Exams often ask you to draw a small system with all of these.

A worked UML example: For a library: Library has a filled diamond to Book? No; books can move between branches, so it is a hollow diamond, aggregation, with multiplicity 1 on Library and * on Book. Book has a filled diamond to Page, composition. Member and Book are associated through Loan, with 1 Member to * Loans and 1 Book to * Loans over time. StudentMember and TeacherMember inherit from an abstract Member, drawn with hollow triangles. And Member realizes an interface Notifiable, drawn with a dashed line and hollow triangle. Practising one such diagram by hand prepares you for most design questions.

The SOLID principles: SOLID is a set of five design principles, popularized by Robert C. Martin, that help keep object oriented code easy to change. S is Single Responsibility, O is Open-Closed, L is Liskov Substitution, I is Interface Segregation and D is Dependency Inversion. Each one addresses a common way designs go wrong.

S, Single Responsibility Principle: A class should have one reason to change, meaning one job. Imagine a Report class that calculates results, formats them as text and saves them to a file. A change in the file format, the text layout or the GPA rules would all force changes to the same class. Better: ResultCalculator calculates, ReportFormatter formats, ReportSaver saves. Each class becomes smaller, easier to test and safer to change.

O, Open-Closed Principle: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. You should be able to add new behaviour without editing tested code. Lesson 12 showed this: a loop that calls shape.area() handles any new Shape subclass without changes, while a long if-else chain on shape types must be edited for every new shape. Polymorphism and interfaces are the main tools for following this principle.

L, Liskov Substitution Principle: Named after computer scientist Barbara Liskov, it says that objects of a subclass must be usable wherever the parent is expected, without breaking correct behaviour. The classic violation is Square extends Rectangle: code that sets a rectangle's width to 5 and height to 4 and expects area 20 gets 16 if the object is a Square that keeps its sides equal. If a child cannot honour the parent's promises, the inheritance is wrong, even if "a square is a rectangle" sounds true in maths.

I, Interface Segregation Principle: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. A huge interface Machine { print(); scan(); fax(); staple(); } forces a simple printer to implement fax and staple with empty or error-throwing bodies. Better: small interfaces Printer, Scanner and Fax, and a multifunction machine implements all three while a basic printer implements only Printer. Java's many small functional interfaces follow this idea.

D, Dependency Inversion Principle: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. An OrderService that creates new BkashGateway() inside itself is tied to bKash forever. Instead, OrderService should depend on a PaymentGateway interface (lesson 14) and receive the real gateway from outside, usually through its constructor: new OrderService(new BkashGateway()). This technique of passing dependencies in is called dependency injection, and it makes testing with a fake gateway easy.

Design patterns: A design pattern is a general, reusable solution to a problem that keeps appearing in software design, described in a way you can adapt to your own code. The famous 1994 book "Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software" by Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, known as the Gang of Four (GoF), catalogued 23 patterns in three groups: creational patterns (how objects are created), structural patterns (how classes and objects are combined) and behavioural patterns (how objects communicate). You have already met some of them: Template Method (lesson 13), Decorator (lesson 20) and Observer (lesson 24).

Singleton pattern (creational): Singleton ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global access point to it. class AppConfig { private static AppConfig instance; private AppConfig() { } public static AppConfig getInstance() { if (instance == null) instance = new AppConfig(); return instance; } }. The private constructor (lesson 5) stops other classes from using new, and the static method (lesson 6) returns the single object. This simple version is not thread-safe (lesson 21); a common fix is to create the instance eagerly, private static final AppConfig INSTANCE = new AppConfig();. Use Singleton sparingly, because it behaves like a global variable and makes testing harder.

Factory pattern (creational): A factory hides the details of which concrete class to create. interface Notification { void send(String msg); } with classes SmsNotification, EmailNotification and PushNotification. class NotificationFactory { static Notification create(String type) { switch (type) { case "sms": return new SmsNotification(); case "email": return new EmailNotification(); default: return new PushNotification(); } } }. The calling code writes Notification n = NotificationFactory.create(userPreference); n.send("Your order is on the way");, depending only on the interface. This simple form is often called a simple factory; the GoF Factory Method pattern lets subclasses decide which class to create.

Observer pattern (behavioural): Observer defines a one-to-many relationship: when one object, the subject, changes state, all its registered observers are notified automatically. interface PriceObserver { void priceChanged(String item, double price); } class Product { private List<PriceObserver> observers = new ArrayList<>(); void addObserver(PriceObserver o) { observers.add(o); } void setPrice(double p) { price = p; for (PriceObserver o : observers) o.priceChanged(name, p); } }. A wishlist screen, an email alert service and a price history logger can all observe the same product without the Product class knowing anything about them. Java's GUI listeners in lesson 24 are exactly this pattern.

Strategy pattern (behavioural): Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, each in its own class behind a common interface, so the algorithm can be chosen at runtime. interface DeliveryFee { double calculate(double km); } with classes NormalFee, ExpressFee and FreeFee (as in lesson 11, but now via composition instead of inheritance). class Checkout { private DeliveryFee fee; void setFee(DeliveryFee f) { fee = f; } double total(double items, double km) { return items + fee.calculate(km); } }. During an Eid campaign the app calls checkout.setFee(new FreeFee()); no Checkout code changes. With lambdas, a strategy can even be written inline: checkout.setFee(km -> 20 + 5 * km);.

Patterns are tools, not goals: Use a pattern when you face the problem it solves, not to make code look clever. A beginner who wraps every class in a factory and every value in a singleton creates more complexity than they remove. Knowing patterns gives you a shared vocabulary: telling a teammate "use a strategy for the fee rules" communicates a whole design in five words.

Course recap, part 1: We began with why OOP exists: keeping data and behaviour together and protecting data (lesson 1), then Java basics (lesson 2). We built classes and objects, references, the stack and the heap (lesson 3), methods and overloading (lesson 4), constructors and object lifetime (lesson 5), and this, static and final (lesson 6). Encapsulation and access modifiers protected our data (lesson 7), strings and wrappers showed immutability in action (lesson 8), and relationships like association, aggregation and composition connected objects (lesson 9).

Course recap, part 2: Inheritance (lesson 10), overriding (lesson 11) and polymorphism (lesson 12) gave us reuse and flexibility, while abstract classes (lesson 13) and interfaces (lesson 14) gave abstraction and contracts. The Object class taught toString, equals and hashCode (lesson 15), packages organised code (lesson 16), exceptions handled errors (lesson 17), generics added type safety (lesson 18) and collections stored groups of objects (lesson 19). File I/O saved data (lesson 20), threads ran tasks at once (lesson 21), C++ showed OOP with destructors, virtual functions, operator overloading and templates (lessons 22 and 23), and GUIs showed event-driven design (lesson 24).

Real life example, designing a small food delivery app: Using everything above: Customer, Restaurant, Rider and Order classes with private fields (encapsulation); Order composed of OrderItems (composition); a PaymentGateway interface with bKash, Nagad and card implementations chosen by a factory (polymorphism, Factory, Dependency Inversion); a DeliveryFee strategy for campaigns (Strategy, Open-Closed); order status updates pushed to the customer's screen and the rider's phone (Observer); orders saved to files or a database with exceptions handled (I/O, exceptions); and a thread pool for handling many orders at once (threads). That is OOP as it is used in real Bangladeshi startups.

Common mistakes: Drawing inheritance arrows the wrong way (they point to the parent). Mixing up aggregation and composition diamonds. Treating SOLID as strict laws instead of guidelines. Using Singleton everywhere. Forcing patterns into code that does not need them. Inheritance that violates Liskov, like Square extends Rectangle.

What exams ask: "Draw a UML class diagram for a given system with visibility and relationships", "Explain the SOLID principles with examples", "What is a design pattern? Classify the GoF patterns", "Implement the Singleton pattern. Is your version thread-safe?", "Explain the Observer pattern with a diagram" and "Differentiate between Strategy and Template Method" (Strategy uses composition and interchangeable objects; Template Method uses inheritance and overridden steps).

What to learn next: Data Structures will show how collections like ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap and TreeMap work inside, and Algorithms will analyse their speed. Software Engineering will use UML and design patterns on team projects. Database Systems will replace text files with proper storage. And if you want to build apps, Android with Kotlin or Flutter with Dart both use the same OOP ideas you now know. Keep building small projects, a library system, a result portal, a game, because design skill grows by designing.
key_points: UML class boxes show name, attributes and operations with + public, - private, # protected, ~ package.
UML lines: association, hollow diamond aggregation, filled diamond composition, hollow triangle inheritance, dashed triangle realization.
SOLID: Single responsibility, Open-closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion.
Liskov: a subclass must be usable wherever its parent is expected (Square extends Rectangle can break this).
Design patterns are reusable solutions; the GoF catalogued 23 in creational, structural and behavioural groups.
Singleton: private constructor + static access to one instance; beware thread safety and overuse.
Factory hides which concrete class is created; Observer notifies many listeners of changes.
Strategy swaps interchangeable algorithms through an interface using composition.
lessons.tip: Before coding any project, spend ten minutes drawing a UML class diagram on paper. Fixing a box and arrow costs nothing; fixing a built class hierarchy costs days.
lessons.task: Draw a UML class diagram for a food delivery app with Customer, Order, OrderItem, Restaurant, Rider and a PaymentGateway interface. Mark visibility, multiplicities and the right diamonds and triangles.

quiz.q: In UML, what does a filled black diamond mean?
quiz.explain: Filled diamond = composition; hollow diamond = aggregation.

quiz.q: Which SOLID principle says a class should have only one reason to change?
quiz.explain: S stands for Single Responsibility.

lessons.title: What Is a Data Structure?
lessons.content:
Imagine your mother's kitchen. Rice is in a big drum, spices are in a little rack with labelled jars, plates are stacked in a pile, and the onions hang in a net bag. Nobody planned this on paper, but every item lives in a shape that matches how it is used. You grab the top plate first. You scoop rice from the drum. You pick the cumin jar by its label. If someone threw everything into one giant sack, cooking a single meal would take an hour of digging. Computers have exactly the same problem, and the answer to that problem is called a data structure.

What it is: A data structure is a way of organising data in a computer's memory so that the things we want to do with that data become easy and fast. The data itself might be numbers, names, marks, phone contacts or roads on a map. The structure is the arrangement: a row of boxes, a chain of linked boxes, a pile, a line, a tree, a web. Same data, different arrangement, very different speed.

Here is a tiny example. Suppose you have the roll numbers of 60 students. If you keep them in a random jumble and someone asks 'Is roll 47 present?', you may have to look at all 60. If you keep them sorted in a row, you can open the middle, see if 47 is bigger or smaller, and throw away half the list each time. You will find the answer in about 6 looks instead of 60. Nothing about the data changed. Only the arrangement changed. That is the whole spirit of this course.

Data versus information: Data is raw facts, like 72, 85, 64. Information is data that has been processed so it means something, like 'Rahim's average mark is 73.7'. Data structures hold the data; algorithms (step-by-step procedures) turn it into information. The two always travel together. A famous book by Niklaus Wirth is literally called 'Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs', and that title is a good summary of what programmers do all day.

Why it matters: Facebook, Google, bKash and Daraz handle millions of requests every second. They can do that on ordinary hardware because their programmers chose structures that make the common operations cheap. A bad choice can turn a one-second job into a one-day job. Data structures are also the most asked topic in programming job interviews and in contests like ICPC, and later courses such as Algorithms, Database Systems, Operating Systems and Compiler Design all assume you know them well.

Abstract data type (ADT): Before choosing how to store something, we first describe what it should do. An abstract data type is a description of a kind of data and the operations allowed on it, without saying how it is built inside. For example, a 'Stack ADT' says: you can push an item, pop the top item, peek at the top, and check if it is empty. It says nothing about arrays or pointers. The data structure is the actual implementation, the concrete way we build that ADT in memory.

A good analogy for ADT versus implementation is a TV remote. The ADT is the list of buttons: volume up, volume down, next channel. The implementation is the circuit inside. You, the user, only care about the buttons. Two remotes from different companies can have completely different circuits and still offer the same buttons. In the same way, a stack can be built using an array or a linked list, and the person using it does not need to know which one.

Primitive versus non-primitive: Primitive data types are the basic building blocks a language gives you directly, like int, float, char and boolean. Non-primitive data structures are built from these, like arrays, lists, stacks, queues, trees and graphs. When people say 'data structures' in this course, they mostly mean the non-primitive ones.

Linear data structures: In a linear structure, the items sit one after another in a sequence, so each item (except the first and last) has exactly one item before it and one after it. Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues are linear. Think of people standing in a line at a bank counter, or train compartments joined end to end. You can walk through them from start to finish in one straight pass.

Non-linear data structures: In a non-linear structure, an item can be connected to many others, so there is no single straight order. Trees and graphs are non-linear. A family tree is a good picture: a grandfather has several children, each child has several children of their own. A map of Dhaka's roads is a graph: one junction like Farmgate connects to many roads going in many directions.

Static versus dynamic: A static data structure has a fixed size decided in advance. A plain array of 100 integers in C is static; it cannot grow to 101. A dynamic data structure can grow and shrink while the program runs. Linked lists, and the growable lists in Python or Java, are dynamic. Static structures are simple and fast; dynamic structures are flexible but need extra work to manage memory.

Homogeneous versus heterogeneous: An array in C holds items of only one type, all ints or all chars; that is homogeneous. A structure (struct) or a record can mix types, like a student record with a name (text), a roll (integer) and a CGPA (decimal). That is heterogeneous. Both ideas appear again and again when we build bigger structures.

The basic operations: Almost every data structure is judged by how well it supports a small set of operations. Traversal means visiting every item once, for example printing all marks. Searching means finding where an item is, or whether it exists. Insertion means adding a new item. Deletion means removing an item. Sorting means putting items in order. Merging means combining two collections into one. Updating means changing an item's value. When you meet a new structure, ask: how fast is each of these?

Here is the key trade-off. No structure is the best at everything. An array finds the 500th item instantly but is slow when you insert in the middle, because everything after must shift. A linked list inserts in the middle easily but must walk from the start to find the 500th item. A hash table finds items by key almost instantly but does not keep them in sorted order. Choosing a data structure means choosing which operations you want to be cheap.

How we measure 'fast': We do not measure speed in seconds, because seconds depend on the computer. Instead we count how the number of steps grows as the data grows, using Big O notation. Searching an unsorted list of n items takes about n steps, written O(n). Binary search on a sorted list takes about log n steps, written O(log n). The next lesson is all about this, so for now just remember that we care about growth, not exact time.

A quick tour of what is coming: We will start with arrays and strings, then dynamic arrays and pointers. Then come linked lists, stacks and queues, and recursion, which explains how stacks power function calls. After that we climb into trees: binary trees, binary search trees, balanced AVL trees, heaps and B-trees. Then hashing for super fast lookup, graphs for networks and maps, and finally searching and sorting, where all these ideas are used together.

Real life example 1, your phone's contact list: Think about what you do with contacts. You type 'Ra' and expect Rahim, Rakib and Rana to appear instantly. You scroll in alphabetical order. You add a new number now and then. A good design keeps names sorted so they can be shown in order, and uses a prefix-friendly structure (like a trie, which we will meet later) so typing a few letters filters the list quickly. If contacts were kept in the order you saved them, every search would have to check all of them one by one. With 2,000 contacts that is still fine, but with millions of records, like a telecom company's database, it would not be.

Real life example 2, a bus counter at Gabtoli: Passengers buying tickets stand in a line, first come first served; that is a queue. The tickets in the clerk's book are numbered seat by seat; that is an array, because you can jump to seat 23 directly. The route map on the wall, with towns connected by highways, is a graph. The clerk's tray of returned tickets, where the last one put down is the first one picked up, is a stack. One small bus counter already uses four different data structures, each chosen because it fits the job.

Choosing well, step by step: When you face a problem, first list the operations you need and how often. Second, think about the size of the data. Third, check whether order matters. Fourth, pick the structure that makes the most frequent operation cheapest. For a dictionary app, look-up by word is the main job, so a hash table or a trie fits. For an undo feature, the last action must be undone first, so a stack fits. For a printer that serves jobs in order, a queue fits.

Memory matters too: Speed is not the only cost. Some structures use extra memory. A linked list stores a pointer with every item, so a list of one million small integers can use two or more times the memory of an array. A hash table keeps some empty slots on purpose so that it stays fast. Good programmers balance time and space, and in phones or small devices, memory can be the bigger worry.

Common mistakes: Students often confuse an ADT with a data structure; remember, ADT is the 'what' and data structure is the 'how'. Many think linear means 'stored next to each other in memory', but a linked list is linear even though its nodes are scattered; linear is about the logical order, not the physical layout. Another mistake is thinking one structure is always best. Exams love to ask: define data structure, classify data structures with examples, difference between linear and non-linear, difference between static and dynamic, and list the basic operations.

A small exam-style question: 'Which structure would you use for the browser back button, and why?' The answer is a stack, because the most recently visited page should be the first one you go back to. Another: 'Is a tree linear or non-linear?' Non-linear, because one node can have several children. Practise giving a one-line reason every time; examiners give marks for the reason, not just the name.

Recap: A data structure is an organised way to store data so that operations on it are efficient. An ADT describes what operations exist; a data structure implements them. Structures can be primitive or non-primitive, linear or non-linear, static or dynamic. Every structure makes some operations cheap and others costly, and our job is to choose the one that fits the problem. In the next lesson we will learn the language for measuring 'cheap' and 'costly': complexity and Big O.
key_points: A data structure is a way to organise data in memory so operations on it are efficient.
An ADT describes what operations are allowed; a data structure is how they are built.
Linear structures (array, list, stack, queue) have one sequence; non-linear (tree, graph) branch out.
Static structures have fixed size; dynamic structures grow and shrink at run time.
Basic operations: traversal, search, insertion, deletion, sorting, merging, updating.
No structure is best at everything; choose based on which operations must be fast.
Algorithms + data structures = programs.
lessons.tip: For every new structure in this course, make a small table with rows for search, insert, delete and access, and fill in how fast each one is. That one table will save you in every exam.
lessons.task: Walk around your home or a shop and find one example each of an array, a stack, a queue, a tree and a graph. Write one line for each explaining why it fits that shape.

options: The operations allowed on the data, not how they are built
Only primitive types like int and char
quiz.explain: An ADT is the 'what': the operations and their behaviour. The data structure is the 'how'.

quiz.explain: Its size is fixed in advance, which is the definition of static.

lessons.title: Measuring Speed: Complexity and Big O
lessons.content:
Suppose two friends, Nadia and Tanvir, both write a program to find a name in a list. On Nadia's old laptop her program takes 2 seconds; on Tanvir's gaming PC his takes 1 second. Whose idea is better? You cannot tell, because the computers are different. Now give both programs a list a thousand times bigger. Nadia's finishes in 20 seconds, while Tanvir's takes 1,000 seconds. Suddenly the answer is obvious. Nadia's method grows slowly; Tanvir's grows fast. Algorithm analysis is the art of seeing that difference before you even run the code.

What it is: Algorithm analysis means predicting how much time and memory an algorithm needs as the input size grows. We call the input size n. For a list, n is the number of items. For a matrix, it may be the number of rows. Time complexity tells how the number of basic steps grows with n. Space complexity tells how much extra memory grows with n. We do not care about exact seconds; we care about the shape of the growth.

Why it matters: When data is small, almost any method is fast. But real systems are not small. Bangladesh's national ID database has more than a hundred million records. A method that checks every pair of records would need around 10^16 comparisons, which is hopeless. A method that sorts first and then compares neighbours would finish in reasonable time. Complexity analysis lets you reject the hopeless idea on paper. It is also the first question in every coding interview: 'What is the time complexity of your solution?'

Counting steps: We pretend each simple operation, such as an assignment, a comparison, an addition or an array access, costs one unit of time. Then we count. Look at this loop: sum = 0; for i = 1 to n: sum = sum + a[i]. The first line is 1 step. The loop body runs n times, and each time does a constant amount of work, say 3 steps. Total about 3n + 1. As n grows, the '+1' and even the '3' stop mattering for the shape of the growth. The work is proportional to n.

Nested loops: Now look at: for i = 1 to n: for j = 1 to n: print(i, j). The inner line runs n times for each of the n values of i, so n × n = n² times. If n is 10, that is 100 prints. If n is 1,000, it is a million. Whenever you see a loop inside a loop, both going up to n, expect n². A loop where j goes from i to n runs n + (n−1) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2 times, which is still about n²/2, so it is also in the n² family.

Halving loops: Now look at: i = n; while i > 1: i = i / 2. Each round cuts i in half. Starting from 1,024, it goes 512, 256, 128, ..., 1. That is just 10 rounds, because 2^10 = 1,024. In general, the number of rounds is about log₂ n. Logarithms grow incredibly slowly: log₂ of a million is about 20, and log₂ of a billion is about 30. Any time a problem is cut in half each step, think log n.

Big O notation: Big O gives an upper bound on growth. We say f(n) is O(g(n)) if, beyond some starting size n₀, f(n) is at most c × g(n) for some constant c. In plain words: f never grows faster than g, ignoring constant factors. For our sum loop, 3n + 1 ≤ 4n whenever n ≥ 1, so 3n + 1 is O(n). Rules of thumb: drop constant factors (5n becomes n), and keep only the fastest-growing term (n² + 100n + 7 becomes n²).

Big Omega and Big Theta: Big Omega, written Ω, is the lower bound: f(n) is Ω(g(n)) if f grows at least as fast as g, beyond some point. Big Theta, written Θ, means both at once: f(n) is Θ(g(n)) if it is both O(g(n)) and Ω(g(n)), so g describes the growth exactly up to constants. 3n + 1 is Θ(n). It is also O(n²), because n² is an upper bound too, but that bound is loose. In practice people often say 'Big O' while meaning the tight bound; in exams, use each symbol precisely.

The common growth classes, from fastest to slowest: O(1), constant time, like reading a[5] from an array. O(log n), logarithmic, like binary search. O(n), linear, like scanning a list. O(n log n), like good sorting algorithms such as merge sort. O(n²), quadratic, like simple sorts such as bubble sort, or checking every pair. O(n³), cubic, like naive matrix multiplication. O(2^n), exponential, like trying every subset of n items. O(n!), factorial, like trying every ordering of n cities.

Feel the numbers: Take n = 1,000. log₂ n is about 10. n log n is about 10,000. n² is 1,000,000. n³ is 1,000,000,000. 2^n is a number with more than 300 digits. If a computer does around a hundred million simple steps per second (a rough figure for estimates), the n² algorithm finishes in about a hundredth of a second, the n³ one in about 10 seconds, and the 2^n one would not finish before the Sun burns out. That is why complexity matters far more than buying a faster computer.

Best, worst and average case: The same algorithm can take different time on different inputs of the same size. Linear search for a value x in a list of n items: best case, x is the first item, 1 comparison, O(1). Worst case, x is last or missing, n comparisons, O(n). Average case, if x is equally likely to be anywhere in the list, about n/2 comparisons, which is still O(n). We usually report the worst case, because it is a guarantee: the algorithm will never be slower than that.

Space complexity: Memory counts too. An algorithm that reverses an array by swapping the first and last items, then the second and second-last, and so on, uses only a couple of extra variables: O(1) extra space, called in-place. An algorithm that copies the array backwards into a new array uses O(n) extra space. Recursive algorithms also use stack space for each pending call; a recursion that goes n levels deep uses O(n) space even if it creates no arrays. Often you can trade space for time, for example storing results to avoid recomputing them.

Rules for combining: Sequential blocks add: an O(n) loop followed by an O(n²) loop is O(n + n²) = O(n²); the bigger part wins. Nested blocks multiply: an O(n) loop containing an O(log n) step is O(n log n). An if-else costs the worse of its two branches. A function call costs whatever the function costs. With these four rules you can analyse most code you will meet in this course.

A worked example: Find whether a list has two equal numbers. Method A: compare every pair, for i in 0..n−1, for j in i+1..n−1, if a[i] == a[j] return true. That is about n²/2 comparisons, O(n²). Method B: sort the list first, O(n log n), then check neighbours in one pass, O(n). Total O(n log n). Method C: put each number in a hash set and check if it was already there, O(n) on average. Three correct answers, three very different costs. This kind of comparison is exactly what exams and interviews want.

Amortized analysis, a sneak peek: Sometimes one operation is occasionally expensive but cheap most of the time. Then we average the cost over a long sequence of operations. This is called amortized analysis, and we will use it in the dynamic array lesson, where adding an item is usually O(1) but sometimes needs an O(n) copy, yet averages out to O(1) per item.

Real life example 1, finding a name in the voter list: A polling centre in Cumilla has 3,000 voters printed in serial order. If a voter does not know their serial number, the officer scans page by page: linear search, O(n), up to 3,000 checks. If the list is printed alphabetically by name, the officer can open the middle, decide which half, and keep halving: about 12 checks, since 2^12 = 4,096. Same voters, same officer. The sorted printing turned O(n) into O(log n).

Real life example 2, the class handshake: On the first day of university, 50 students all want to shake hands with each other. The number of handshakes is 50 × 49 / 2 = 1,225. If 100 students do it, the number becomes 4,950, about four times as much. Doubling the people roughly quadrupled the work, which is the signature of O(n²). Compare that with everyone simply saying their name once to the class: 100 students, 100 introductions, O(n). Once you notice these patterns in real life, you will start seeing them in code too.

Common mistakes: Students often think O(2n) is different from O(n); it is not, constants are dropped. Some think O(log n) depends on the base of the logarithm; it does not, because log bases differ only by a constant factor. Many confuse 'worst case' with 'Big O'; they are separate ideas: worst case is which input, Big O is how we describe the bound. Another mistake is calling two separate loops O(n²); separate loops add, they do not multiply.

What exams ask: Define time and space complexity. Define Big O, Big Omega and Big Theta, often with the formal c and n₀ definition. Find the complexity of given code fragments, especially nested loops and halving loops. Arrange functions like n², n log n, 2^n, log n and n! in order of growth. Explain best, average and worst cases of linear search. Prove that something like 5n² + 3n + 2 is O(n²) by picking c = 10 and n₀ = 1.

Why we ignore constants: You might wonder why 100n and n are treated the same. The reason is that constants depend on details like the language, the compiler and the machine, while the growth shape depends only on the idea. A 100n algorithm will always beat an n² algorithm once n is bigger than 100, no matter how the constants look. For small inputs constants can matter, and real engineers do care about them, but the first question is always the growth class.

Recap: We measure algorithms by how their time and space grow with input size n, not by seconds. Big O is an upper bound, Big Omega a lower bound, and Big Theta a tight bound. Drop constants and lower-order terms. Loops in sequence add, nested loops multiply, and halving gives log n. Worst case is the usual guarantee. From now on, every structure in this course will come with its Big O cost, so keep this lesson close.

One more practice idea: Pick any piece of code you wrote in your first programming course, maybe a program that prints a multiplication table or finds the largest of n numbers. Next to each loop, write how many times it runs in terms of n. Then combine the counts using the add and multiply rules. Doing this for five or six old programs is the quickest way to make complexity feel natural rather than scary.
key_points: Complexity describes how time or memory grows with input size n, not seconds.
Big O is an upper bound, Big Omega a lower bound, Big Theta a tight bound.
Drop constant factors and lower-order terms: 3n² + 5n + 2 is O(n²).
Sequential code adds costs; nested loops multiply; halving loops give O(log n).
Order of growth: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2^n < n!.
Worst case gives a guarantee; best and average cases describe other inputs.
Space complexity counts extra memory, including recursion stack space.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see code, put your finger on each loop and ask two questions: how many times does it run, and is it inside another loop? That habit alone solves most complexity questions.
lessons.task: Write the numbers 10, 100 and 1,000 in a row. Under each, calculate log₂ n (roughly), n log n, n² and 2^n (just say 'huge' when it is too big). Look at how quickly each row explodes.

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of two nested loops that each run from 1 to n?
quiz.explain: The inner loop runs n times for each of n outer iterations: n × n.

quiz.q: A loop that halves i each time, starting from n, runs about how many times?
quiz.explain: Repeatedly halving n reaches 1 after about log₂ n steps.

quiz.q: Simplify 4n² + 10n + 7 in Big O.
quiz.explain: Drop constants and keep only the fastest-growing term.

quiz.q: Which notation describes a tight bound, both upper and lower?
quiz.explain: Θ means the function is both O(g) and Ω(g).

quiz.q: What is the worst-case time of linear search on n items?
quiz.explain: If the item is last or missing, all n items are checked.

lessons.title: Arrays: Boxes in a Row
lessons.content:
Picture the lockers in a school corridor. They are all the same size, standing shoulder to shoulder, and each has a number painted on it: 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. If the head teacher says 'Bring me what is in locker 37', you do not open lockers 0 to 36 first. You walk straight to 37, because you know exactly where it is. An array is that row of lockers inside the computer's memory, and it is the simplest and most used data structure of all.

What it is: An array is a collection of items of the same type stored in consecutive (side-by-side) memory locations, and each item is reached using an index. In C, int marks[5]; creates five integer boxes called marks[0] to marks[4]. Most languages, including C, C++, Java and Python, start counting from 0. So the first item is marks[0] and the last item of a size-5 array is marks[4], not marks[5].

Why it matters: Arrays are everywhere. Images are arrays of pixels. Sound is an array of samples. Your exam result sheet is an array of marks. Many other structures, such as stacks, queues, heaps and hash tables, are often built on top of arrays. If you understand arrays deeply, including how they sit in memory, half of this course becomes easier.

Declaring and initialising: In C you can write int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};. Now a[0] is 10 and a[4] is 50. If you write int a[5] = {1, 2}; the remaining items become 0. If you declare int a[5]; inside a function without initialising, the values are garbage, whatever bits were already in memory. In Python, a list like a = [10, 20, 30] behaves like an array for most purposes, though it can hold mixed types and can grow.

Why access is O(1): Because items sit next to each other and are all the same size, the computer can calculate the address of any item with one formula: address of a[i] = base address + i × size of one element. If an int array starts at address 1000 and each int takes 4 bytes, then a[0] is at 1000, a[1] at 1004, and a[7] at 1000 + 7 × 4 = 1028. One multiplication and one addition, no matter whether the array has 10 items or 10 million. That is why we say array access by index is O(1), constant time.

A worked address problem: Suppose an array A has indices from 5 to 20 (some textbooks allow lower bounds other than 0), its base address is 2000, and each element is 2 bytes. Where is A[12]? The formula with lower bound LB is: address = base + (i − LB) × size = 2000 + (12 − 5) × 2 = 2014. The number of elements is UB − LB + 1 = 20 − 5 + 1 = 16. Exams love this question, so practise it until it is automatic.

Traversal: Traversing means visiting each element once. for i = 0 to n−1: print(a[i]). It takes O(n) time because every element is touched once. Traversal is used to print, to add up totals, to count how many students got an A, or to find the largest value: max = a[0]; for i = 1 to n−1: if a[i] > max then max = a[i].

Insertion: Suppose an array has room for 10 items but currently holds 5: [12, 25, 31, 47, 58]. You want to insert 29 at index 2 to keep it sorted. You must first shift 58, 47 and 31 one place to the right, starting from the end so nothing is overwritten. Then put 29 in index 2. Result: [12, 25, 29, 31, 47, 58]. In the worst case, inserting at index 0, all n items move, so insertion is O(n). Inserting at the end, when there is room, is O(1).

Deletion: Deleting is the mirror image. To delete the item at index 1 from [12, 25, 29, 31, 47, 58], shift everything after it one place to the left: 29 moves to index 1, 31 to index 2, and so on. The size becomes 5. Worst case O(n) again. If order does not matter, there is a trick: copy the last item into the hole and reduce the size by one. That deletion is O(1), but the order changes.

Searching: In an unsorted array you must check items one by one, which is linear search, O(n). In a sorted array you can use binary search, O(log n), which we will study properly in the searching lesson. Keeping an array sorted makes searching fast but makes insertion slower, because you must shift to keep the order. That is a perfect example of the trade-offs we talked about in lesson one.

Two-dimensional arrays: A 2D array is a table with rows and columns, like a class routine with days as rows and periods as columns. In C: int m[3][4]; has 3 rows and 4 columns, 12 elements. m[1][2] means row 1, column 2. But memory is a single long line, not a grid. So the computer must decide how to lay the table out in that line. There are two ways: row-major and column-major.

Row-major order: Store the whole first row, then the whole second row, and so on. C, C++ and Python's NumPy (by default) use row-major. For an array with R rows and C columns, starting at base B, with element size w and indices starting at 0: address of m[i][j] = B + (i × C + j) × w. Example: m[3][4] of ints (4 bytes) at base 1000. m[1][2] is at 1000 + (1 × 4 + 2) × 4 = 1000 + 24 = 1024.

Column-major order: Store the whole first column, then the second column, and so on. Fortran and MATLAB use column-major. The formula becomes: address of m[i][j] = B + (j × R + i) × w. Same example, m[1][2] with R = 3: 1000 + (2 × 3 + 1) × 4 = 1000 + 28 = 1028. Notice the answer changed only because the layout changed. When an exam question gives you lower bounds other than 0, replace i with (i − LB_row) and j with (j − LB_col).

Why the layout matters for speed: Computers load memory in chunks into a fast cache. If you loop through a row-major array row by row, the next item is always right next door, so the cache helps a lot. If you loop column by column in a row-major language, you jump around memory and can run noticeably slower, even though the Big O is the same. This is a nice example of real performance that Big O does not show.

Multi-dimensional arrays: You can have 3D arrays too, like int cube[2][3][4], which you can picture as 2 tables, each 3 by 4. A colour image is often stored as height × width × 3, one value each for red, green and blue. The same idea of turning indices into one offset still applies; there are just more terms in the formula.

Advantages of arrays: O(1) access by index. Very little extra memory, because there are no pointers. Cache-friendly, because items are side by side. Simple to use and supported by every language. Disadvantages: fixed size in languages like C, so you must guess the size in advance, which wastes memory if you guess too big and fails if you guess too small. Insertion and deletion in the middle cost O(n) because of shifting. All elements must be the same type.

Real life example 1, a cricket scoreboard: In a T20 match, the runs scored in each over can be stored in an array runs[20]. runs[0] is the first over and runs[19] the last. To show the score after 10 overs, add runs[0] to runs[9], a traversal. To show the runs in the 15th over, read runs[14] instantly. The size is known in advance, 20 overs, so a fixed array is a perfect fit. The broadcast graphic that draws a bar for each over is just looping through this array.

Real life example 2, a cinema hall seat plan: A hall at Bashundhara City might have seats arranged in rows A to J and columns 1 to 20. A 2D array seat[10][20] of true/false values tells which seats are booked. When you tap seat F-7 in the booking app, the program converts F to row 5 and 7 to column 6 (because indexing starts at 0) and checks seat[5][6] in O(1). Showing the whole map is a traversal of all 200 seats, row by row.

Common mistakes: The most famous bug is the off-by-one error: writing for i = 0 to n instead of 0 to n−1, which reads one item past the end. In C this is not caught; it reads or overwrites whatever memory is next, causing strange bugs or crashes. Another mistake is forgetting to shift from the end during insertion, which overwrites values. In address questions, students often forget to subtract the lower bound or mix up the number of rows and columns in the formula.

What exams ask: Define an array and state its advantages and disadvantages. Calculate the address of an element in a 1D array with a given base, lower bound and element size. Calculate the address in a 2D array in row-major and column-major order. Write algorithms for insertion and deletion at a given position, and state their complexity. Find the number of elements given lower and upper bounds.

A quick self-test: An array B[−2..7] of 4-byte floats starts at address 500. How many elements does it have, and where is B[3]? Elements: 7 − (−2) + 1 = 10. Address of B[3] = 500 + (3 − (−2)) × 4 = 500 + 20 = 520. If you got both, you are ready for the exam version of this question.

Arrays in different languages: In C, the array name is really the address of the first element, and the language does not remember the array size for you, so you must pass the size to functions separately. In Java, every array knows its length (a.length) and the language checks every index, throwing an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException if you go past the end, which is safer. In Python, the list is really a dynamic array of references, so it can grow and hold mixed types, and negative indexes like a[-1] give the last item. The core idea of numbered, side-by-side boxes is the same everywhere.

Recap: An array stores same-type items in consecutive memory and reaches any item by index in O(1) using base + offset. Traversal and search are O(n), insertion and deletion in the middle are O(n) because of shifting. 2D arrays are laid out in row-major or column-major order, each with its own address formula. Arrays are fast and compact but fixed in size, which is the problem the next lessons on dynamic arrays and linked lists will solve.
key_points: An array stores same-type elements in consecutive memory locations, usually indexed from 0.
Address of a[i] = base + (i − lower bound) × element size, so access is O(1).
Insertion and deletion in the middle are O(n) because elements must shift.
Row-major stores rows one after another (C); column-major stores columns (Fortran, MATLAB).
Row-major 2D address: base + ((i − LBr) × columns + (j − LBc)) × size.
Arrays are compact and cache-friendly but have fixed size in languages like C.
Off-by-one errors are the most common array bug.
lessons.tip: For every address question, first write the formula with symbols, then substitute numbers. Most lost marks come from skipping the lower bound, not from bad arithmetic.
lessons.task: Draw a 3 × 4 grid on paper, fill it with numbers 1 to 12, and then write those numbers in one long line twice: once in row-major and once in column-major order. Use your base-1000, 4-byte formula to check where the number in row 2, column 1 lands in each layout.

quiz.q: An int array (4 bytes each) starts at address 1000. What is the address of a[6] (indices start at 0)?
Why is accessing a[i] in an array O(1)?
options: The computer searches from the start
The address is computed directly from the index
quiz.explain: Base address plus index times size gives the location in one calculation.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case time to insert an item at the beginning of an array of n items?
quiz.explain: All n existing items must shift one place to the right.

quiz.q: Which languages store 2D arrays in column-major order?
quiz.explain: Fortran and MATLAB store columns one after another; C and C++ use row-major.

quiz.q: How many elements does an array A[3..12] have?

lessons.title: Strings, Matrices and Sparse Matrices
lessons.content:
Think of a long necklace of beads, each bead with one letter painted on it: B, A, N, G, L, A, D, E, S, H. Read the beads left to right and you get a word. That necklace is a string. Now think of a teacher's mark register, a big grid with students down the side and subjects across the top. That grid is a matrix. Both are really arrays wearing a special costume, and in this lesson we learn the tricks that come with each costume.

What a string is: A string is a sequence of characters, such as "Dhaka" or "I love cricket". In C, a string is stored as an array of char, ending with a special invisible character '\0' (the null character) that marks where the string stops. So the word "CAT" needs 4 boxes: 'C', 'A', 'T', '\0'. In Java and Python, strings are objects that remember their own length, so there is no need for a terminating character, and they are immutable: you cannot change a letter in place; you create a new string instead.

Characters are numbers: Inside the computer every character is stored as a number. In ASCII, 'A' is 65, 'B' is 66, 'a' is 97 and '0' is 48. That is why in C you can write c − 'A' to turn 'D' into 3, or c + 32 to turn an uppercase ASCII letter into lowercase. Bangla letters live in Unicode, which has codes for nearly every script in the world, and they usually take more than one byte when stored as UTF-8. The first programming course covered encodings, so here we only need the idea that characters are small numbers in an array.

Length of a string: In C, strlen(s) walks from the start until it finds '\0', counting as it goes. That takes O(n) time for a string of n characters. A common slow pattern is writing for (i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++), which calls strlen on every loop round and turns an O(n) loop into O(n²). Store the length in a variable first. In Java and Python, length is stored with the string, so s.length() or len(s) is O(1).

Basic string operations: Concatenation joins two strings: "Dhaka" + " City" gives "Dhaka City"; it costs time proportional to the total length because characters are copied. Comparison checks letters one by one from the left until they differ; "apple" is less than "apricot" because at position 2, 'p' (112) is less than 'r' (114). Substring takes a slice, like characters 0 to 2 of "Bangladesh", giving "Ban". Reversal swaps the first and last characters, then the second and second-last, and so on, in O(n) time.

A worked example, palindrome check: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, like "madam" or "racecar". Use two indices: i at the start and j at the end. While i < j, if s[i] is not equal to s[j], it is not a palindrome; otherwise move i forward and j backward. For "madam": compare m-m, a-a, then i meets j at d, so it is a palindrome. That is O(n) time and O(1) extra space. The two-pointer trick will appear again and again in this course.

Pattern matching: A very common job is finding a pattern P inside a text T, like finding "cat" in "the cat sat". The naive (brute force) algorithm tries every starting position in T. At each position it compares P letter by letter. If all letters match, report the position; if a mismatch happens, slide P one step right and try again. For text length n and pattern length m, there are n − m + 1 starting positions and up to m comparisons each, so the worst case is O((n − m + 1) × m), roughly O(n × m).

Tracing the naive matcher: Text "AABAAB", pattern "AAB". Position 0: A=A, A=A, B=B, match at 0. Position 1: A=A, B vs A mismatch. Position 2: B vs A mismatch. Position 3: A=A, A=A, B=B, match at 3. So the pattern appears at positions 0 and 3. Faster algorithms such as KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) avoid re-checking letters and run in O(n + m); they are usually taught in the Algorithms course, so here we just know they exist.

Matrices as 2D arrays: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers with m rows and n columns, stored as a 2D array a[m][n]. You met the row-major and column-major layouts in the array lesson. Matrix operations are classic array exercises. Addition of two m × n matrices: c[i][j] = a[i][j] + b[i][j] for every i and j, which is O(m × n). Transpose turns rows into columns: t[j][i] = a[i][j], also O(m × n).

Matrix multiplication: To multiply A (m × n) by B (n × p), the result C is m × p, and each c[i][j] is the sum over k of a[i][k] × b[k][j]. The number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B. Three nested loops do it: for i, for j, for k. For square n × n matrices that is n × n × n = O(n³) multiplications. For 2 × 2 matrices A = [[1,2],[3,4]] and B = [[5,6],[7,8]], c[0][0] = 1×5 + 2×7 = 19 and c[0][1] = 1×6 + 2×8 = 22.

Special square matrices: Some matrices have a pattern that lets us save space. A diagonal matrix has non-zero values only on the main diagonal, so n values are enough instead of n². A lower triangular matrix has zeros above the diagonal; it has n(n+1)/2 possibly non-zero entries, which we can pack into a 1D array row by row. In row-major packing, element (i, j) with i ≥ j and indices from 0 lands at position i(i+1)/2 + j. An upper triangular matrix is the mirror image. A symmetric matrix, where a[i][j] = a[j][i], also needs only one triangle stored.

Sparse matrices: A sparse matrix is one where most entries are zero. Imagine a 1,000 × 1,000 matrix recording which of 1,000 students follow which of 1,000 Facebook pages, where each student follows only about 10 pages. That is 1,000,000 cells, but only about 10,000 are non-zero. Storing all the zeros wastes 99 percent of the memory. A dense matrix is the opposite, where most entries are non-zero.

Triplet (3-tuple) representation: Store only the non-zero entries as rows of (row, column, value). By convention, the first row stores (total rows, total columns, number of non-zeros). Example: a 4 × 5 matrix with 7 at (0,2), 3 at (1,4), 9 at (3,0). Triplet form: (4, 5, 3), (0, 2, 7), (1, 4, 3), (3, 0, 9). Four short rows instead of 20 cells. If the matrix has t non-zeros, triplet form uses 3(t + 1) numbers, which saves memory when t is small compared to rows × columns.

Is it worth it? Triplet form only saves space when non-zeros are few. A full 4 × 5 matrix has 20 cells. Triplet storage needs 3(t + 1) numbers, so it is smaller only if 3(t + 1) < 20, meaning t ≤ 5. As a rule of thumb, sparse storage pays off when fewer than about a third of the entries are non-zero. Exams sometimes ask exactly this calculation.

Linked representation of sparse matrices: Another approach stores each non-zero as a node in linked lists, one list per row (and sometimes one per column too, forming an orthogonal list). This makes inserting new non-zeros easier than in an array of triplets. We will learn linked lists in a few lessons; for now, just know that sparse matrices can be stored either as an array of triplets or as linked lists.

Transposing a sparse matrix: To transpose in triplet form, swap the row and column of each triplet: (0, 2, 7) becomes (2, 0, 7). But to keep the triplets sorted by row, the simple method scans the list once for each column, which costs O(columns × t). A smarter fast transpose first counts how many non-zeros are in each column, computes where each column's entries should start, and then places every triplet directly, which takes O(columns + t). This is a favourite exam question.

Real life example 1, mobile number validation: When you type a Bangladeshi mobile number into bKash, the app checks that it is a string of 11 digits starting with '01' and that the third digit is a valid operator code. That is a sequence of character checks on a string: s.length == 11, s[0] == '0', s[1] == '1', and every character between '0' and '9'. A wrong character at any position fails the check. Simple string operations on a char array protect millions of transactions from typos.

Real life example 2, road distances between districts: Suppose a transport app stores travel times between Bangladesh's 64 districts in a 64 × 64 matrix. Most district pairs are not directly connected by a single highway, so most entries are zero meaning 'no direct road'. Storing it as a sparse matrix of triplets (from, to, minutes) keeps only real road links. Later in the course you will see that this is basically a graph's adjacency list, which is the sparse-friendly way to store networks.

Common mistakes: In C, forgetting the extra box for '\0', so a 5-letter word in char s[5] overflows. Using == to compare C strings, which compares addresses, not letters; use strcmp. Calling strlen inside a loop condition. In matrix multiplication, mixing up the index order and writing a[i][j] × b[i][j], which is element-wise multiplication, not matrix multiplication. In triplet form, forgetting the header row with dimensions and count.

What exams ask: Represent a string in memory and explain the null terminator. Write an algorithm to reverse a string or check a palindrome. Trace the naive pattern matching algorithm and state its complexity. Write the algorithm for matrix multiplication and its complexity. Convert a given sparse matrix into triplet form, and find its transpose. Calculate the memory saved by sparse representation, and find the 1D index of an element in a packed lower triangular matrix.

A quick self-test: Convert the 3 × 3 matrix with 5 at (0,0), 8 at (1,2) and 2 at (2,1) into triplets. Answer: (3, 3, 3), (0, 0, 5), (1, 2, 8), (2, 1, 2). Now transpose it: (3, 3, 3), (0, 0, 5), (1, 2, 2), (2, 1, 8), sorted by row. If you got that, the sparse matrix exam question is yours.

Recap: Strings are arrays of characters; in C they end with '\0' and comparing or measuring them takes O(n). The naive pattern matcher is O(n × m). Matrices are 2D arrays; addition and transpose are O(mn), multiplication of n × n matrices is O(n³). Special matrices like diagonal and triangular ones can be packed into fewer cells, and sparse matrices are stored as triplets or linked lists to avoid wasting memory on zeros.
key_points: A string is an array of characters; C strings end with the null character '\0'.
Each character is stored as a number (ASCII/Unicode).
Naive pattern matching tries every position: worst case O(n × m).
Matrix addition and transpose are O(mn); n × n multiplication is O(n³).
Triangular and diagonal matrices can be packed into a 1D array to save space.
A sparse matrix stores only non-zeros, e.g. as (row, column, value) triplets.
Sparse storage saves memory only when non-zeros are few.
lessons.tip: For string questions, draw the boxes with indices under them, including the '\0' box for C. For sparse matrices, always write the header triplet first so you never forget it.
lessons.task: Write your full name in boxes on paper with indices under each letter. Then use two fingers as i and j to check whether it is a palindrome. Next, draw a 4 × 4 grid with only three non-zero numbers and write its triplet form.

quiz.q: How many bytes does the C string "CAT" need, counting the terminator?
quiz.explain: Three letters plus the '\0' character.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case time of naive pattern matching for text length n and pattern length m?
quiz.explain: Up to n − m + 1 positions, each with up to m comparisons.

quiz.q: Multiplying two n × n matrices with three nested loops takes:
quiz.explain: Each of n² result cells needs n multiplications.

quiz.q: In triplet representation, what does the first row usually store?
options: Total rows, total columns and number of non-zeros
quiz.explain: The header row records the matrix size and how many triplets follow.

quiz.q: Which matrix is called sparse?
quiz.explain: Sparse means most entries are zero, so storing them all wastes memory.

lessons.title: Dynamic Arrays and Amortized Analysis
lessons.content:
Imagine you are hosting a birthday party and you set up a table for 4 guests. A fifth friend arrives. You cannot stretch the table, so you move everyone to a bigger table for 8. It takes a few minutes of carrying plates, but now there is room for three more people with no fuss at all. When the ninth guest arrives, you move to a table for 16. You only move rarely, and most guests just sit down. That is exactly how a dynamic array works.

The problem: In the last lessons we saw that a plain C array has a fixed size. You must decide it before the program runs. But very often we do not know how much data will come: how many students will register, how many messages will arrive, how many items a shopper will put in a cart. Guess too small and you run out of room; guess too big and you waste memory. We want an array that can grow on demand but still gives O(1) access by index.

What a dynamic array is: A dynamic array (also called a growable array or resizable array) is an array that automatically gets bigger when it fills up. Python's list, Java's ArrayList and C++'s std::vector are all dynamic arrays. Inside, there is still an ordinary fixed-size array. The trick is in how it handles running out of space.

Size versus capacity: A dynamic array keeps track of two numbers. Size (or length) is how many items are actually stored. Capacity is how many items the internal array can hold before it needs to grow. For example, size 5 and capacity 8 means 5 boxes are used and 3 are free. When you append an item and size is less than capacity, you just put the item in box number size and increase size by one. That is O(1).

Growing: When size equals capacity and you append one more, the dynamic array must grow. Step 1: allocate a new, bigger array, usually double the old capacity. Step 2: copy every existing item into the new array. Step 3: free the old array. Step 4: put the new item in. Copying n items costs O(n), so this particular append is expensive. But because the capacity doubled, the next many appends will be cheap again.

A trace: Start with capacity 1. Append A: size 1, capacity 1. Append B: full, so grow to capacity 2, copy A (1 copy), add B. Append C: full, grow to 4, copy A and B (2 copies), add C. Append D: size 4, no copy. Append E: full, grow to 8, copy 4 items, add E. Appends F, G, H: no copies. Append I: grow to 16, copy 8 items. Count the copies for the first 9 appends: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15. Fifteen copies for nine appends, less than two copies per append on average.

Amortized analysis: The word 'amortized' comes from paying off a loan in instalments. Instead of asking 'what is the worst single operation?', we ask 'over a long sequence of operations, what is the average cost per operation in the worst case?'. This is not the same as average-case analysis, which depends on random inputs. Amortized cost is a guarantee for every sequence: no matter what order of appends happens, the total cost divided by the number of operations stays bounded.

Why doubling gives O(1) amortized: Suppose we do n appends starting from capacity 1. Copies happen when the capacity is 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on up to the largest power of two below n. The total copies are 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + (something less than n), and this geometric series adds up to less than 2n. Plus n writes for the items themselves. Total work is less than 3n, so the cost per append is less than 3, a constant. That is O(1) amortized time per append, even though one single append can cost O(n).

The banker's view: Another way to see it is the accounting method. Charge every append 3 coins. One coin pays for writing the item now. The other two coins are saved in the bank, attached to the item. When the array doubles from capacity k to 2k, the k/2 items added since the last doubling each saved 2 coins, which is k coins, exactly enough to pay for copying all k items. The bank never goes negative, so 3 coins per append is enough forever.

Why not grow by a fixed amount? Suppose instead we add 10 more boxes each time it fills. Then copies happen at sizes 10, 20, 30, 40, and so on. For n appends, the total copying is 10 + 20 + 30 + ... + n, which is about n²/20, so the total is O(n²) and each append is O(n) amortized. That is much worse. Growing by a constant factor, such as 2 or 1.5, is the key. Different libraries use different factors; the exact factor is an implementation detail, but it is always multiplicative.

Space cost: Doubling means that right after a growth, nearly half of the capacity is empty. So a dynamic array may use up to about twice the memory of the data it holds. This is a trade-off we accept for fast appends. Some libraries also let you reserve capacity in advance if you know roughly how many items will come, like C++'s v.reserve(1000), which avoids repeated copying entirely.

Shrinking: What happens when you delete items? If many items are removed, the array could shrink to save memory. A careless rule, 'halve the capacity when it becomes half full', causes trouble: if you are right at the boundary and alternately append and remove, you might double and halve over and over, each costing O(n). The standard fix is to halve only when the array becomes a quarter full. Then there is always a gap before the next resize, and both append and remove stay O(1) amortized.

Other operations: Access by index is still O(1), because inside it is a normal array. Updating a[i] is O(1). Removing the last item is O(1) (amortized if shrinking is used). Inserting or deleting in the middle is still O(n), because items must shift, just like a plain array. Searching an unsorted dynamic array is O(n). So a dynamic array fixes the fixed-size problem, but it does not fix the middle-insertion problem; that is what linked lists are for.

Pseudo-code for append: append(x): if size == capacity: newArr = allocate(2 × capacity); for i = 0 to size−1: newArr[i] = arr[i]; free(arr); arr = newArr; capacity = 2 × capacity. Then arr[size] = x; size = size + 1. In C you would use malloc or realloc for the allocation; we will see dynamic memory properly in the next lesson.

A hidden danger, stale references: Because growing moves all items to a new memory block, any pointer or reference you were holding to an old element may now point to freed memory. In C++, this is called iterator invalidation: after a vector grows, old pointers into it are no longer valid. Many tricky bugs come from keeping a pointer to v[0] and then calling push_back.

Real life example 1, a Daraz shopping cart: When you start shopping, the app does not know if you will add 2 items or 40. Your cart can be a dynamic array. Adding an item is a cheap append almost every time. Occasionally, when the cart's internal capacity fills, the app silently moves the items to a bigger array, which you never notice because it happens in microseconds. Viewing item number 3 is instant, because it is still an array with O(1) access.

Real life example 2, a class WhatsApp group's message list: In a chat screen, new messages always arrive at the end. A dynamic array is a natural fit: each new message is appended in O(1) amortized time, and scrolling to message 500 is a direct index jump. If a message is deleted from the middle, everything after it shifts, but deletions are rare compared to new messages, so the overall design is still efficient.

Dynamic array versus linked list, preview: A dynamic array gives O(1) access by index, uses less memory per item and is cache-friendly. A linked list, which we will study soon, gives O(1) insertion and deletion at a known position, never needs a big copy, but has O(n) access by index. Most real-world programmers reach for a dynamic array first, and only use linked lists when frequent middle insertions or deletions make it worth it.

Common mistakes: Thinking that a dynamic array append is always O(1); it is O(1) amortized, and a single append can be O(n). Confusing amortized with average case; amortized holds for every sequence, average case depends on input probability. Thinking growing by +10 or +100 is good enough; it gives O(n) amortized append. Forgetting that capacity and size are different, for example printing capacity when asked for the number of items.

What exams ask: Explain how a dynamic array grows and why it doubles. Prove that n appends with doubling cost O(n) total, so O(1) amortized. Compare doubling with growing by a constant. Explain the difference between amortized and average-case analysis. Trace capacity and copy counts for a sequence of appends. Explain why shrinking at a quarter, not a half, avoids thrashing.

Try it yourself: In Python, the function sys.getsizeof(lst) reports the memory used by the list object. If you append items one at a time and print the size after each, you will see it jump up in steps instead of growing by one slot each time. The exact steps depend on the Python version, but the stepped pattern is the dynamic array growing its capacity in advance.

Using realloc in C: C has a library function, realloc(ptr, newSize), that asks the memory manager to resize a block. Sometimes there is free space right after the block and it can simply extend it without copying; otherwise it allocates a new block, copies the old contents and frees the old one, just like our manual steps. Either way you must use the pointer that realloc returns, because the block may have moved. If realloc fails it returns NULL and leaves the old block untouched, so careful code stores the result in a temporary pointer first.

Building a stack or queue on top: Because appending and removing at the end are O(1) amortized, a dynamic array is a natural home for a stack: push is append, pop is remove-last. Python programmers use a list as a stack all the time. Queues are trickier, because removing from the front shifts everything; we will solve that with a circular buffer in the queue lesson.

Recap: A dynamic array is a fixed array plus a growing rule. It tracks size and capacity; when full, it allocates a bigger array (usually double), copies everything, and continues. One append can cost O(n), but over any sequence of n appends the total is O(n), so each append is O(1) amortized. Growth must be by a constant factor, not a constant amount. Access stays O(1), and middle insertion stays O(n).
key_points: A dynamic array (Python list, Java ArrayList, C++ vector) grows automatically when full.
Size is the number of items; capacity is the room in the internal array.
When full, allocate a bigger array (often double), copy all items, then add the new one.
Doubling makes append O(1) amortized, even though one append can cost O(n).
Amortized analysis averages cost over a worst-case sequence, unlike average-case analysis.
Growing by a fixed amount gives O(n) amortized append; always grow by a factor.
Shrink only when a quarter full to avoid repeated resizing.
lessons.tip: When you see the word 'amortized', think 'total cost of n operations divided by n'. Write the total as a sum, then add it up; most proofs are just a geometric series.
lessons.task: On paper, simulate 17 appends to a dynamic array starting with capacity 1 and doubling. Make columns for size, capacity and copies made. Add up the copies and divide by 17.

quiz.q: When a full dynamic array of size n grows by doubling, how much does that single append cost?
quiz.explain: All n existing items are copied into the new array.

quiz.q: What is the amortized cost of append in a dynamic array that doubles?
quiz.explain: Total copies over n appends are less than 2n, so the per-append cost is constant.

quiz.q: If a dynamic array grows by adding 10 boxes each time, n appends cost:
quiz.explain: Copies of 10 + 20 + 30 + ... + n add up to about n²/20.

quiz.q: Which statement about amortized analysis is true?
options: It measures only the best case
It bounds the average cost per operation over any sequence
quiz.explain: Amortized cost is a worst-case guarantee spread over a sequence, not a probability statement.

quiz.q: Why shrink a dynamic array only when it is one quarter full?
options: To avoid repeated grow-shrink cycles near the boundary
Because memory cannot be freed otherwise
quiz.explain: Leaving a gap between grow and shrink points prevents thrashing.

lessons.title: Pointers, Structures and Dynamic Memory
lessons.content:
Imagine your friend lives in a flat in Mirpur. You do not carry the whole flat around with you; you carry a slip of paper with the address: House 12, Road 5, Section 10. With that slip, anyone can find the flat. If your friend moves, you just write a new address on the slip. In programming, that slip of paper is called a pointer, and it is the key that unlocks linked lists, trees and graphs, the structures that make up most of this course.

Memory and addresses: The computer's main memory is like a very long street of numbered houses, each house holding one byte. Every variable you create lives at some address. If you write int x = 42; in C, the computer picks, say, address 5000 to store x (an int usually takes 4 bytes, so it uses 5000 to 5003). The name x is for you; the computer only cares about the address 5000.

What a pointer is: A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. In C: int x = 42; int *p = &x;. The & operator means 'address of', so p now holds 5000. The * in the declaration says p is a pointer to an int. To reach the value through the pointer, we use * again: *p gives 42. This is called dereferencing. If we write *p = 50;, then x becomes 50, because p points to x.

A tiny trace: int a = 10, b = 20; int *p = &a; *p = *p + 5; p = &b; *p = *p * 2;. Step by step: p points to a, so a becomes 15. Then p is moved to point at b, and b becomes 40. At the end a = 15 and b = 40. Notice that changing where p points did not change a or b; only writing through *p did.

The NULL pointer: Sometimes a pointer should point to nothing yet. We give it the special value NULL (in C) or nullptr (in C++), or null in Java. Dereferencing a NULL pointer is an error; in C it usually crashes the program with a segmentation fault. In linked structures, NULL is used to mark the end of a list or a missing child in a tree, so you will check 'if (p != NULL)' a lot.

Pointers and arrays: In C, an array name behaves like a pointer to its first element. If int a[5] starts at 1000, then a is 1000, and a + 1 is 1004, not 1001, because pointer arithmetic moves in units of the element size. So *(a + 2) is the same as a[2]. This is exactly the address formula from the array lesson, now written with pointers. It also explains why C does not check array bounds: a[7] is just *(a + 7), whatever is there.

Structures: Real data usually has several fields. A student has a name, a roll and a CGPA. In C we group them with a struct: struct Student { char name[30]; int roll; float cgpa; };. Then struct Student s; s.roll = 7;. If we have a pointer to a struct, struct Student *ps = &s;, we access fields with the arrow operator: ps->roll, which is a short way to write (*ps).roll. You will write the arrow operator hundreds of times in this course.

The self-referential structure: Here is the magic idea. A struct can contain a pointer to another struct of the same type: struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; };. Each node holds one value and the address of the next node. This is called a self-referential structure, and it is the building block of linked lists. A tree node is the same idea with two pointers: struct TreeNode { int data; struct TreeNode *left, *right; };.

Static versus dynamic memory: Variables declared normally inside a function live on the stack (a memory area managed automatically); they are created when the function starts and destroyed when it returns. Their size must be known at compile time. Dynamic memory lives in a separate area called the heap, where you can request memory while the program is running, in whatever amount you need, and it stays until you release it. (This 'heap' memory area is not the same as the heap data structure we will study later; they just share a name.)

malloc and free in C: To get memory from the heap, call malloc(number of bytes). It returns a pointer to the new block, or NULL if no memory is available. Example: struct Node *n = (struct Node*) malloc(sizeof(struct Node));. The sizeof operator tells the exact size needed. When you are done with the memory, call free(n);. calloc(count, size) is similar but also fills the block with zeros, and realloc changes the size of a block, as we saw with dynamic arrays.

new and delete in C++, and garbage collection: In C++ you write Node *n = new Node; and later delete n;. For arrays: int *arr = new int[100]; and delete[] arr;. In Java and Python you create objects with new or just by calling a constructor, and you never free them yourself. A garbage collector runs in the background, finds objects that no variable can reach any more, and frees them automatically. That is convenient, but the ideas of references and nodes are exactly the same.

Creating a node, step by step: To make a node with value 25: n = malloc(sizeof(struct Node)); check if n == NULL (out of memory); n->data = 25; n->next = NULL;. Now n points to a tiny box on the heap with 25 inside and an empty 'next' slot. To link a second node m with value 40 after it: n->next = m;. Now following n->next from n leads you to m. Two boxes, scattered anywhere in memory, joined by an address. That is a linked list of length two.

Memory leaks: If you allocate memory and lose every pointer to it without calling free, that memory can never be used again until the program ends. That is a memory leak. Example: n = malloc(...); n = malloc(...);. The first block is now unreachable. A program that leaks a little memory on every request, like a server, can slowly eat all the RAM and crash after hours or days. In C, every malloc should have a matching free.

Dangling pointers: The opposite problem is using memory after freeing it. free(n); then n->data = 5;. The pointer n still holds the old address, but that memory may now belong to something else. This is called a dangling pointer, and it causes some of the hardest bugs to find. A good habit is to set n = NULL; right after free(n);, so an accidental use will crash immediately instead of silently corrupting data.

Passing pointers to functions: In C, function arguments are copied. If a function receives int x and changes it, the caller's variable does not change. If it receives int *p and writes *p = 7, the caller's variable does change, because the function knows its address. This is how C functions modify arrays and linked lists.
