What exams ask: Define an m-way search tree and a B-tree of order m, with its properties. Insert a sequence of keys into a B-tree of order 3, 4 or 5, drawing each split. Explain deletion with borrowing and merging. Compare B-trees and B+ trees. Explain why B-trees are used in databases and file systems. Define a trie, draw one for a set of words, and give the complexity of search and insertion.

A drawing habit for B-tree inserts: Write each node as a box with its keys separated by bars, like [20 | 40]. When a node overflows, draw it once with the extra key, circle the median, and draw the two halves below with the median moving up. Showing the overflow and the split separately earns step marks and makes errors obvious.

Recap: Multiway trees store many keys per node to stay short, which matters when every node visit is a slow disk read. A B-tree of order m keeps nodes between half full and full, keeps all leaves at the same depth, and grows by splitting at the root, giving O(log_m n) operations. B+ trees keep data only in linked leaves, making them ideal for database indexes and range queries. Tries store strings character by character, giving O(L) search and fast prefix queries such as autocomplete.
key_points: Multiway trees hold many keys per node, keeping height small for disk-based data.
B-tree of order m: at most m children and m − 1 keys per node; internal nodes at least ⌈m/2⌉ children; all leaves at one depth.
Insertion goes into a leaf; overflow splits the node and pushes the median up; the tree grows at the root.
B-tree operations take O(log_m n) node visits.
B+ trees store data only in leaves and link leaves for fast range queries; used in database indexes.
A trie stores strings by characters; search and insert take O(L) for a word of length L.
Tries power prefix search and autocomplete but can waste memory without compression.
lessons.tip: In B-tree problems, write the maximum and minimum number of keys per node for your order before you begin. With those two numbers in front of you, you will never split too early or too late.
lessons.task: Insert 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 75 into a B-tree of order 3 on paper, drawing every split. Then draw a trie for the words to, tea, ten, in and inn, marking the end-of-word nodes.

quiz.q: In a B-tree of order 5, what is the maximum number of keys in a node?
quiz.explain: Order m allows at most m − 1 keys per node.

quiz.q: When a B-tree node overflows during insertion, what happens?
options: It splits and the median key moves up to the parent
The tree is rebuilt from scratch
A rotation is performed as in AVL trees
quiz.explain: Splitting and pushing up the median keeps all leaves at the same depth.

quiz.q: Why are B-trees preferred for databases stored on disk?
options: They keep the height small so fewer slow disk reads are needed
quiz.explain: Fat nodes match disk blocks and make the tree very short.

quiz.q: What is a key feature of a B+ tree?
options: Data is stored only in the root
Leaves are never at the same level
All data is in the leaves, which are linked for range scans
quiz.explain: Internal nodes route; linked leaves give fast sequential access.

quiz.q: Searching for a word of length L in a trie takes:
quiz.explain: You follow one edge per character, regardless of how many words are stored.

lessons.title: Hashing and Hash Tables
lessons.content:
Picture the cloakroom at a wedding hall. You hand over your bag and receive a token with a number, say 47. Later you give back the token, and the attendant walks straight to hook 47. Nobody searches the whole room, and nobody keeps the bags sorted. The number on the token tells exactly where your bag is. A hash table works the same way: a small calculation on the key tells us which slot to look in, so finding things takes about the same time whether there are ten items or ten million.

What it is: A hash table stores key-value pairs in an array of slots (also called buckets). A hash function takes a key, like a phone number, a name or a student ID, and turns it into an array index. To insert, compute the index and store the pair there. To search, compute the same index and look there. When things go well, insert, search and delete all take O(1) time on average, which beats the O(log n) of balanced trees.

Why it matters: Hash tables are probably the most used data structure in practical programming. Python's dict and set, Java's HashMap and HashSet, C++'s unordered_map and JavaScript objects are all hash tables underneath. They power database lookups, caches, compilers' symbol tables (mapping variable names to information), spell checkers, counting word frequencies, and detecting duplicates. Interviewers love them because many O(n²) problems become O(n) with a hash table.

The ideal and the problem: If keys were small integers, say roll numbers from 1 to 100, we could use a direct-address table: an array of size 101 where key k lives in slot k. That is perfect O(1). But real keys come from huge ranges: an 11-digit mobile number has 10^11 possible values, and we might only store a few thousand. We cannot make an array that big. So we use a smaller table of size m and a hash function that squeezes the huge key space into indices 0 to m − 1.

Hash functions, division method: The simplest is h(k) = k mod m. With m = 10, the key 1234 goes to slot 4. But m = 10 is a poor choice, because the slot then depends only on the last digit, and real data often has patterns in its last digits. A common recommendation is to choose m as a prime number not too close to a power of 2. With m = 7, the key 50 goes to 50 mod 7 = 1, and 700 goes to 0.

Other hash function methods: The multiplication method computes h(k) = ⌊m × (k × A mod 1)⌋ for a constant A between 0 and 1 (a value near 0.618 is often suggested); 'mod 1' means keeping only the fractional part. Here m can be any size. The mid-square method squares the key and takes digits from the middle: 3205² = 10272025, and the middle two digits give 72. The folding method splits the key into parts and adds them: 123456789 becomes 123 + 456 + 789 = 1368, then take it mod m. Exams often ask you to name and apply these methods.

Hashing strings: For a string key like a name, we must first turn the characters into a number. A popular approach treats the string as digits in some base: for 'cat', compute ((c × 31 + a) × 31 + t) using character codes, then take the result mod m. Simply adding the character codes is a weak hash, because 'abc' and 'cba' would collide. A good hash function should be fast to compute and should spread keys evenly over the table, so that every slot is about equally likely.

Collisions: Since many keys map into few slots, two different keys will sometimes get the same index. That is a collision. With m = 7, the keys 50 and 85 both hash to 1. Collisions are unavoidable when there are more possible keys than slots (the pigeonhole principle), and they happen surprisingly early: in a room of only 23 people, the chance that two share a birthday is already over 50 percent. So every hash table needs a collision resolution strategy. There are two main families: separate chaining and open addressing.

Separate chaining: Each slot holds a linked list (a chain) of all the pairs that hash there. Insert adds to the chain (at the front for O(1)). Search computes the slot and scans its chain. Delete removes the node from the chain. Example with m = 7 and keys 50, 700, 76, 85, 92, 73, 101: slot 0 holds 700; slot 1 holds 50, 85, 92; slot 3 holds 73, 101; slot 6 holds 76; other slots are empty. Chaining is simple, deletion is easy, and the table never 'fills up', but each node costs a pointer and chains may be scattered in memory.

Load factor: The load factor α = n / m is the average number of keys per slot. With chaining, an unsuccessful search scans a whole chain, about α nodes on average, and a successful one scans about half a chain plus one, so the expected time is O(1 + α), assuming the hash function spreads keys evenly. If we keep α below a constant, for example by growing the table, operations stay O(1) on average. In the worst case, if every key lands in the same slot, the table degrades to a single linked list and search is O(n).

Open addressing: Here all pairs live directly in the array, with no chains. When the home slot is taken, we probe other slots in a fixed sequence until we find an empty one. Searching follows the same sequence until it finds the key or hits an empty slot (which proves the key is absent). The table can never hold more than m items, so α must stay below 1, and in practice it is kept well below that, often around 0.5 to 0.75.

Linear probing: Try h(k), then h(k) + 1, h(k) + 2, and so on, wrapping around mod m. Insert 50, 700, 76, 85, 92, 73, 101 into a table of size 7. 50 to slot 1; 700 to slot 0; 76 to slot 6; 85 hashes to 1 (taken), so slot 2; 92 hashes to 1, slots 1 and 2 taken, so slot 3; 73 hashes to 3 (taken), so slot 4; 101 hashes to 3, slots 3 and 4 taken, so slot 5. Final table: 700, 50, 85, 92, 73, 101, 76. Linear probing is simple and cache-friendly, but suffers from primary clustering: occupied slots bunch together into long runs, and any key landing in a run must walk to its end, making the run even longer.

Quadratic probing: Try h(k), h(k) + 1², h(k) + 2², h(k) + 3², ... mod m. The jumps grow, so keys escape clusters faster. With m = 7, after 50 in slot 1 and 85 in slot 2 (1 + 1), the key 92 tries slot 1, then 2, then 1 + 4 = 5, landing in slot 5. Quadratic probing avoids primary clustering, but keys with the same home slot still follow the same sequence, called secondary clustering. It also may fail to find an empty slot even when some exist, unless the table size and load factor are chosen carefully (for example, a prime m and α at most one half guarantee an empty slot is found).

Double hashing: Use a second hash function to choose the step size: probe h1(k), h1(k) + h2(k), h1(k) + 2 × h2(k), ... mod m. Different keys with the same home slot now get different step sizes, which removes both kinds of clustering. h2(k) must never be 0; a common choice is h2(k) = R − (k mod R) for a prime R smaller than m. Example with m = 7 and R = 5: for 92, h1 = 1 and h2 = 5 − (92 mod 5) = 5 − 2 = 3, so the probes are 1, 4, 0 (7 mod 7), and so on.

Deleting with open addressing: You cannot simply empty a slot, because that would break probe sequences: a later search would stop at the empty slot and wrongly report that a key further along is absent. Instead, mark the slot with a special 'deleted' marker, often called a tombstone. Searches skip over tombstones; insertions may reuse them. If many tombstones pile up, the table is rebuilt.

Rehashing: When the load factor gets too high, performance drops, so the table is resized, typically to about double the size (often the next prime), and every key is reinserted using the new m, because each key's slot depends on m. Rehashing costs O(n), but as with dynamic arrays it happens rarely enough that insertion stays O(1) amortized. Java's HashMap, for example, by default resizes when its load factor passes 0.75.

Hash tables versus balanced trees: Hash tables give O(1) average lookups, but their worst case is O(n), they keep no order, and range queries like 'all keys between 100 and 200' are slow. Balanced BSTs give guaranteed O(log n) and keep keys sorted, supporting min, max, successor and range queries. Choose a hash table for pure lookups by exact key; choose a balanced tree when order matters.

Real life example 1, bKash checking a mobile number: When you send money, the system must check in an instant whether the receiver's number has an account. Keeping all registered numbers in a hash table means each check is one hash computation and a quick look in one slot, regardless of how many tens of millions of accounts exist. A sorted list would need about 25 comparisons per check, and an unsorted list could need millions.

Real life example 2, counting votes or words: Suppose a newspaper wants to know which words appear most often in a year of articles. Scan each word and use a hash table mapping word to count: if the word is present, add one; otherwise insert it with count 1. With n words in total, the whole job is O(n) on average. The same pattern counts votes per candidate, sales per product on Daraz, or visits per page on a website.

Real life example 3, a library's cache of book covers: A library app shows book cover images, which are slow to download. It keeps recently loaded covers in a hash table keyed by ISBN. Before downloading, it checks the table: if the cover is there (a cache hit), it shows it instantly. Combined with a doubly linked list for least-recently-used eviction, as we saw in lesson 8, this is the classic LRU cache.

Common mistakes: Choosing a table size like 10 or 100 with the division method, so only the last digits matter. Forgetting to wrap around with mod m during probing. Emptying a slot on deletion in open addressing instead of using a tombstone. Saying hash table search is always O(1); it is O(1) on average with a good hash function, and O(n) in the worst case. Forgetting to rehash every key when the table grows.

What exams ask: Define hashing, hash function, collision and load factor. Describe hash function methods: division, multiplication, mid-square and folding. Insert a list of keys into a table of a given size using linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing and chaining, and draw the final table. Explain primary and secondary clustering. Explain why deletion needs special care in open addressing. Explain rehashing. Compare chaining with open addressing.

Recap: A hash table turns a key into an array index with a hash function, giving average O(1) insert, search and delete. Collisions are unavoidable and are handled by separate chaining (lists in each slot) or open addressing (linear, quadratic or double-hash probing). The load factor α = n/m controls performance; keep it low by rehashing into a bigger table. Hash tables are unbeatable for exact-key lookups but keep no order, so balanced trees remain the choice when sorted order or range queries are needed.
key_points: A hash function maps a key to an array index; average insert, search and delete are O(1).
Division method h(k) = k mod m works best with m a prime not close to a power of 2.
Collisions are unavoidable; resolve them by chaining or open addressing.
Chaining: a linked list per slot; expected time O(1 + α), where α = n/m.
Open addressing probes: linear (primary clustering), quadratic (secondary clustering), double hashing.
Open addressing deletes with tombstones; rehash into a bigger table when α gets high.
Hash tables keep no order; worst case O(n); use balanced trees for sorted or range queries.
lessons.tip: For hashing questions, draw the table as a numbered column of empty boxes first, then insert keys one at a time, writing the probe sequence next to each key (for example 92: 1 → 2 → 3). Examiners want to see the probes, not just the final table.
lessons.task: Take a table of size 11. Insert the keys 22, 1, 13, 11, 24, 33, 18, 42, 31 using h(k) = k mod 11 and linear probing, writing each probe sequence. Then redo it with chaining and compare the longest probe sequence with the longest chain.

quiz.q: With h(k) = k mod 7, which slot does the key 50 go to?
quiz.explain: 50 = 7 × 7 + 1, so the remainder is 1.

quiz.q: What is the load factor of a hash table with 30 keys and 60 slots?
Primary clustering is a problem mainly of which method?
quiz.explain: Consecutive occupied runs grow and attract more keys.

quiz.q: Why does open addressing use a 'deleted' marker instead of emptying a slot?
options: So that searches do not stop early at a gap in a probe sequence
quiz.explain: An empty slot would end a search too soon and hide keys further along.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case search time in a hash table with n keys?
quiz.explain: If all keys collide into one chain or run, every key may be checked.

lessons.title: Graphs: Terminology and Representation
lessons.content:
Look at a map of Bangladesh's highways. Dhaka connects to Cumilla, Cumilla to Chattogram, Dhaka to Mymensingh, Mymensingh to Sylhet, and so on. There is no single top city, no parent and child, and you can often travel in loops. Or look at your Facebook friends: you are friends with Rina, Rina with Arif, Arif with you, a triangle. Trees cannot describe such webs. For that we need the most general structure in this course: the graph.

What a graph is: A graph G = (V, E) is a set of vertices V (also called nodes) and a set of edges E, where each edge connects two vertices. Cities and roads, people and friendships, web pages and links, computers and cables, courses and prerequisites are all graphs. We usually write n = |V| for the number of vertices and m = |E| (or e) for the number of edges.

Why graphs matter: Many of the hardest and most useful problems in computing are graph problems. Google Maps finds shortest paths in a road graph. Facebook suggests 'people you may know' using friends of friends. Search engines rank pages using the link graph. Compilers order tasks using dependency graphs. Network engineers route packets through graphs of routers. Even a tree is just a special graph: connected, with no cycles.

Undirected and directed graphs: In an undirected graph, an edge {u, v} has no direction; if Dhaka connects to Cumilla, Cumilla connects to Dhaka. Facebook friendship is undirected. In a directed graph (digraph), each edge (u, v) goes from u to v, drawn as an arrow. Following someone on Instagram or X is directed: you can follow a celebrity without them following you. One-way streets in Old Dhaka make the road map partly directed.

Weighted graphs: Edges can carry numbers, called weights or costs: the distance in kilometres, the travel time in minutes, the price of a ticket or the bandwidth of a cable. A weighted graph of districts might say Dhaka to Cumilla is 100 km and Cumilla to Chattogram is 150 km. Unweighted graphs treat every edge as equal. Shortest path problems, which you will meet in the Algorithms course, depend on weights.

Basic vocabulary: Two vertices are adjacent if an edge joins them; such vertices are neighbours. An edge is incident on its two endpoints. A self-loop is an edge from a vertex to itself. Multiple edges between the same pair make a multigraph. A simple graph has no self-loops and no multiple edges; most textbook problems assume simple graphs unless they say otherwise.

Degree: In an undirected graph, the degree of a vertex is the number of edges touching it. In a directed graph, each vertex has an in-degree (arrows coming in) and an out-degree (arrows going out). A famous fact, the handshaking lemma: in any undirected graph, the sum of all degrees equals 2m, because every edge adds one to the degree of each of its two ends. Consequence: the number of vertices with odd degree is always even.

An example graph: Let the vertices be A, B, C, D, E with edges A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D and D–E. Degrees: A 2, B 2, C 2, D 3, E 1. Sum 10 = 2 × 5 edges, as the lemma promises. E is a vertex of degree 1, sometimes called a pendant vertex. If there were also a vertex F with no edges, it would be an isolated vertex with degree 0.

Paths and cycles: A path is a sequence of vertices where each consecutive pair is joined by an edge, like A, B, D, E. Its length is the number of edges, here 3. A simple path repeats no vertex. A cycle is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex with at least one edge and no other repeated vertices, like A, B, D, C, A in our example. A graph with no cycles is acyclic. A directed graph with no directed cycles is called a DAG (directed acyclic graph), which is very important for scheduling tasks with prerequisites.

Connectivity: An undirected graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of vertices. If not, it splits into connected components, maximal pieces that are internally connected. A friendship graph of a school might have one big component plus a few small groups. For directed graphs, strongly connected means every vertex can reach every other following arrow directions. A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph, and it always has exactly n − 1 edges.

Special graphs: A complete graph Kₙ has an edge between every pair of vertices, so it has n(n − 1)/2 edges; K₅ has 10. A bipartite graph's vertices split into two groups with edges only between the groups, like students and the clubs they join. A graph is sparse if m is much smaller than n², like road networks, where each junction has a handful of roads, and dense if m is close to n². This distinction decides which representation to use.

Subgraphs and spanning trees: A subgraph uses a subset of the vertices and edges. A spanning tree of a connected graph is a subgraph that includes every vertex, is a tree, and so has exactly n − 1 edges. A road authority wanting to connect all districts with the least total road length is looking for a minimum spanning tree, solved by algorithms like Kruskal's and Prim's, which you will study in the Algorithms course.

Representation 1, adjacency matrix: Use an n × n array M where M[i][j] = 1 if there is an edge from i to j, and 0 otherwise (or the weight, with a special value such as 0 or infinity for 'no edge'). For our example with A to E as 0 to 4: row A is [0, 1, 1, 0, 0]; row B is [1, 0, 0, 1, 0]; row C is [1, 0, 0, 1, 0]; row D is [0, 1, 1, 0, 1]; row E is [0, 0, 0, 1, 0]. For an undirected graph the matrix is symmetric: M[i][j] = M[j][i]. For a directed graph it need not be.

Adjacency matrix costs: Space is O(n²), whatever the number of edges. Checking whether an edge (i, j) exists is O(1): just read M[i][j]. Listing all neighbours of a vertex is O(n), because you scan a whole row. Adding or removing an edge is O(1). The sum of a row gives the degree (or out-degree), and the sum of a column gives the in-degree. A matrix is ideal for dense graphs or when you need fast edge checks, but wasteful for sparse graphs: a road network with 100,000 junctions would need 10^10 cells, almost all zero.

Representation 2, adjacency list: Keep an array of n lists. List i holds the neighbours of vertex i (with weights if any). For our example: A: B, C. B: A, D. C: A, D. D: B, C, E. E: D. In an undirected graph each edge appears twice, once in each endpoint's list, so the total size of all lists is 2m; in a directed graph it is m. The lists can be linked lists, dynamic arrays, or even hash sets.

Adjacency list costs: Space is O(n + m), which is excellent for sparse graphs. Listing the neighbours of v takes O(degree of v), which is exactly what traversal algorithms need. Checking whether a specific edge (u, v) exists takes O(degree of u) by scanning u's list, slower than the matrix's O(1), unless the lists are hash sets. Most real-world graphs are sparse, so adjacency lists are the default choice, and BFS and DFS run in O(n + m) with them.

Other representations: An edge list simply stores all edges as pairs (u, v) or triples (u, v, weight); it is compact and convenient for algorithms like Kruskal's, which sort edges by weight. An incidence matrix has n rows and m columns, with a mark where vertex i touches edge j; it appears in some textbooks and exam questions, but is rarely used in programs because it is large. Graphs in object-oriented code are often stored as vertex objects that hold lists of edge objects.

Choosing a representation: Ask how many edges there are and what you will do most. Dense graph, frequent 'is there an edge between u and v?' questions: adjacency matrix. Sparse graph, algorithms that walk from each vertex to its neighbours (BFS, DFS, shortest paths): adjacency list. Need to process edges sorted by weight: edge list. Memory tight and the graph huge: adjacency list or a compressed form.

Real life example 1, Dhaka's road network: Every junction (Farmgate, Shahbag, Kawran Bazar) is a vertex, and every road segment is an edge weighted by length or current travel time. One-way roads are directed edges; two-way roads are pairs of directed edges or undirected edges. With tens of thousands of junctions and only a few roads at each, the graph is very sparse, so navigation apps store it as adjacency lists. Rerouting around a traffic jam on Mirpur Road means changing a few edge weights and running a shortest path search again.

Real life example 2, a university course prerequisite chart: At a university, 'Data Structures' requires 'Structured Programming', 'Algorithms' requires 'Data Structures' and 'Discrete Mathematics', and so on. Each course is a vertex and each prerequisite is a directed edge from the required course to the course that needs it. This must be a DAG; a cycle would mean a course indirectly requires itself, and no student could ever take it. Planning a valid semester order is a topological sort of this DAG, coming up in the next lesson.

Real life example 3, a social network: In Facebook's friendship graph, vertices are people and undirected edges are friendships. Your degree is your number of friends. 'People you may know' suggestions often come from vertices at distance two, friends of your friends, who are not yet your friends. With billions of people but only hundreds of friends each, the graph is enormously sparse, so it is stored as adjacency lists spread across many servers.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that each undirected edge appears twice in adjacency lists. Using a non-symmetric matrix for an undirected graph. Mixing up in-degree and out-degree. Saying adjacency lists give O(1) edge checks. Calling a graph a tree when it has a cycle or is disconnected. Writing K₅ has 20 edges; the formula is n(n − 1)/2, so 10.

What exams ask: Define graph, directed and undirected graphs, weighted graphs, degree, path, cycle, connected graph, component, complete graph and DAG. State and use the handshaking lemma. Draw the adjacency matrix and adjacency list of a given graph, for both directed and undirected cases. Compare the space and time costs of the two representations. Identify sparse and dense graphs and choose a representation.

Recap: A graph is a set of vertices and edges, possibly directed and weighted, and it models any network. Learn the vocabulary: adjacency, degree (in and out), path, cycle, connected component, complete, bipartite, DAG and spanning tree. The sum of degrees is 2m. Adjacency matrices use O(n²) space with O(1) edge checks; adjacency lists use O(n + m) space and list neighbours in O(degree), which suits the sparse graphs of the real world. Next, we explore graphs systematically with BFS and DFS.
key_points: A graph G = (V, E) is a set of vertices and edges; edges may be directed and weighted.
Degree counts edges at a vertex; directed graphs have in-degree and out-degree.
Handshaking lemma: the sum of degrees equals 2 × number of edges.
A DAG is a directed graph with no directed cycle; a tree is a connected acyclic graph with n − 1 edges.
A complete graph Kₙ has n(n − 1)/2 edges.
Adjacency matrix: O(n²) space, O(1) edge check, O(n) to list neighbours.
Adjacency list: O(n + m) space, O(degree) to list neighbours; best for sparse graphs.
lessons.tip: For representation questions, draw the graph, then label vertices with numbers 0 to n − 1 in a fixed order and write that mapping at the top. Matrix and list answers become mechanical and easy to check.
lessons.task: Draw a graph of 6 friends and who among them are friends with each other. Write its adjacency matrix and adjacency list. Check that the sum of the degrees is twice the number of edges.

quiz.q: An undirected graph has 7 edges. What is the sum of the degrees of all vertices?
quiz.explain: Each edge adds 1 to the degree of both endpoints: 2 × 7.

quiz.q: How much space does an adjacency matrix need for a graph with n vertices?
quiz.explain: It has an n × n grid of cells regardless of the number of edges.

quiz.q: How many edges does the complete graph K₆ have?
Which representation is usually best for a large sparse graph like a road network?
options: A single array of vertices only
quiz.explain: It uses O(n + m) space and lists neighbours quickly.

quiz.q: Following accounts on Instagram, where following is not mutual, is best modelled as a:
quiz.explain: Each follow is a one-way relationship from follower to followed.

lessons.title: Graph Traversal: BFS, DFS and Topological Sort
lessons.content:
Imagine news of a cricket victory spreading through your neighbourhood. First your own family hears it. Then each of them tells their nearest neighbours. Then those neighbours tell theirs. The news spreads in rings, nearest people first. Now imagine instead a curious child exploring an old house: she walks down one corridor as far as it goes, opens the last door, and only when she hits a dead end does she come back and try the next corridor. Those two styles of exploring, ring by ring and deep first, are breadth-first search and depth-first search, the two fundamental ways to traverse a graph.

What traversal means for graphs: A graph traversal visits every vertex reachable from a starting vertex, each exactly once. Unlike trees, graphs can have cycles and several paths to the same vertex, so we must remember which vertices we have already visited, usually with a boolean array visited[]. Without it, a traversal could go round a cycle forever. Traversals are the building blocks of almost every graph algorithm.

Our example graph: We reuse the graph from the last lesson: vertices A, B, C, D, E, edges A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D and D–E, stored as adjacency lists in alphabetical order. A: B, C. B: A, D. C: A, D. D: B, C, E. E: D. Draw it now; every trace below uses it.

Breadth-first search (BFS): BFS explores the graph in layers: first the start vertex, then all vertices at distance 1, then all at distance 2, and so on. It uses a queue. Mark the start as visited and enqueue it. While the queue is not empty: dequeue a vertex u and process it; for each neighbour v of u, if v is not visited, mark it visited and enqueue it. Marking when enqueuing, not when dequeuing, prevents the same vertex from being added twice.

BFS trace from A: Queue [A], visited {A}. Dequeue A: neighbours B and C are new, so mark and enqueue them; queue [B, C]. Dequeue B: A is visited, D is new; queue [C, D]. Dequeue C: A and D are visited; queue [D]. Dequeue D: B and C visited, E is new; queue [E]. Dequeue E: D visited; queue empty. Visit order: A, B, C, D, E. The edges used to discover new vertices (A–B, A–C, B–D, D–E) form a BFS tree.

BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs: If we also record dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 whenever u discovers v, BFS computes the minimum number of edges from the start to every vertex. From A: A 0, B 1, C 1, D 2, E 3. If we also store parent[v] = u, we can rebuild the actual shortest path by following parents backwards: E's parent is D, D's is B, B's is A, so a shortest path is A, B, D, E. This works only when all edges count equally; with different weights you need Dijkstra's algorithm, studied in the Algorithms course.

Depth-first search (DFS): DFS goes as deep as possible along one path before backtracking. It is naturally recursive: dfs(u): mark u visited; process u; for each neighbour v of u: if v is not visited, dfs(v). The recursion uses the call stack; an iterative version uses an explicit stack, exactly like the maze-solving idea from the stack lesson.

DFS trace from A: dfs(A): visit A; first neighbour B is new, so dfs(B): visit B; its neighbours are A (visited) and D (new), so dfs(D): visit D; its neighbours are B (visited), C (new), so dfs(C): visit C; its neighbours A and D are visited, so return to D; D's next neighbour E is new, so dfs(E): visit E; return all the way back. Visit order: A, B, D, C, E. Different from BFS: DFS went A, B, D before ever looking at C, A's second neighbour.

Complexity: With adjacency lists, both BFS and DFS visit each vertex once and examine each adjacency list once. The total work is O(n + m): n for the vertices and the sum of all list lengths, which is 2m for undirected graphs (m for directed). With an adjacency matrix, finding the neighbours of each vertex takes O(n), so the total becomes O(n²). Space is O(n) for the visited array plus the queue or stack.

Connected components: To find all connected components of an undirected graph, loop over all vertices; whenever you find an unvisited one, start a BFS or DFS from it, and label every vertex it reaches with a new component number. The number of times you start a new search is the number of components. The whole process is still O(n + m). This answers questions like 'how many separate friend groups are there?' or 'is the road network connected after this bridge collapses?'.

Cycle detection in undirected graphs: During DFS, if you meet a neighbour that is already visited and is not the vertex you just came from (your parent in the DFS tree), you have found a cycle. In our trace, when DFS was at C (reached from D), it saw neighbour A, already visited and not C's parent, so there is a cycle: A, B, D, C, A. A connected undirected graph with no cycles is a tree, so this test also checks whether a graph is a tree.

Cycle detection in directed graphs: For directed graphs, the rule is different, because reaching an already visited vertex might just be a cross link, not a cycle. Use three states: white (not visited), grey (currently on the recursion stack) and black (finished). If DFS meets a grey vertex, it has found a back edge into its own current path, which means a directed cycle. If it meets a black vertex, there is no cycle through that edge. This is how build tools and spreadsheet programs detect circular dependencies.

Topological sort: In a DAG, a topological order is a listing of all vertices such that for every edge u → v, u comes before v. It answers 'in what order can I do these tasks so that every prerequisite comes first?'. Only DAGs have one; if there is a cycle, no valid order exists. There can be several valid orders for the same DAG.

Kahn's algorithm (BFS-style): Compute the in-degree of every vertex. Put all vertices with in-degree 0 into a queue. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex u, append it to the output, and for each edge u → v, decrease v's in-degree by one; if it becomes 0, enqueue v. If the output contains all vertices, it is a topological order; if some vertices are never output, the graph has a cycle. Time O(n + m).

Topological sort example: Courses: P (Programming), M (Discrete Maths), D (Data Structures), A (Algorithms), B (Databases), with prerequisites P → D, D → A, M → A, D → B. In-degrees: P 0, M 0, D 1, A 2, B 1. Queue [P, M]. Take P: output P; D's in-degree drops to 0, enqueue D. Take M: output M; A drops to 1. Take D: output D; A drops to 0 and B to 0, enqueue both. Take A, then B. Order: P, M, D, A, B. Every prerequisite comes before the course that needs it.

DFS-based topological sort: Another method runs DFS on the DAG and records each vertex when it finishes (after all its descendants are done). Listing vertices in reverse finishing order gives a topological order. Intuitively, a vertex finishes only after everything that depends on it has finished, so reversing puts it before them. Both methods are O(n + m); Kahn's is easier to trace by hand, and the DFS version is short to code.

BFS versus DFS, when to use which: Use BFS for shortest paths in unweighted graphs, for finding everything within k steps (friends of friends), and for level-by-level processing. Use DFS for cycle detection, topological sorting, finding connected components, solving mazes and puzzles with backtracking, and as the basis for more advanced algorithms such as finding strongly connected components. BFS's queue can grow wide; DFS's stack can grow deep.

Two-colouring with BFS: A graph is bipartite if its vertices can be coloured with two colours so that every edge joins different colours. Run BFS, giving the start colour 0 and each newly discovered vertex the opposite colour of its parent. If an edge ever joins two vertices of the same colour, the graph is not bipartite. Our example graph is bipartite (A and D are colour 0, B, C and E colour 1); a triangle never is, because any cycle of odd length breaks two-colouring.

Real life example 1, Facebook's 'people you may know': Start a BFS from you in the friendship graph. Distance 1 vertices are your friends; distance 2 vertices are friends of friends. A simple suggestion list is everyone at distance exactly 2, ranked by how many mutual friends (distance-1 neighbours) you share. BFS stops after two layers, so even in a graph of billions of people the work is limited to your neighbourhood.

Real life example 2, spreading a flood warning: The disaster management office needs to send a cyclone warning through a network of union offices, each able to call only the offices it is directly connected to. A BFS from the district headquarters tells how many relay steps each union needs and which offices are unreachable (separate components) and need a different channel, such as radio. The BFS tree is the actual calling plan.

Real life example 3, a university semester planner: The course prerequisite DAG from the last lesson is fed into Kahn's algorithm. All courses with no prerequisites go into the first semester's candidate list. After 'taking' them, their dependants' in-degrees drop, and new courses become available for the next semester. The same idea schedules tasks in build systems like Gradle, which a Flutter developer sees every time an Android app is compiled.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the visited array, causing infinite loops on cycles. In BFS, marking vertices visited only when dequeued, which can enqueue the same vertex several times. Using the undirected cycle rule (visited and not parent) on a directed graph. Trying to topologically sort a graph with a cycle. Assuming BFS gives shortest paths in weighted graphs. Ignoring disconnected vertices; a single BFS or DFS from one start reaches only its own component.

What exams ask: Write BFS and DFS algorithms and state their complexity for adjacency lists and matrices. Trace BFS and DFS on a given graph from a given vertex, showing the queue or stack and the visit order. Draw the BFS or DFS tree. Find connected components. Detect a cycle. Find a topological order of a DAG with Kahn's algorithm or DFS. Compare BFS and DFS and give applications of each.

Recap: Graph traversal needs a visited array to cope with cycles. BFS uses a queue, explores in layers and finds shortest paths by edge count. DFS uses recursion or a stack, goes deep first and backtracks. Both run in O(n + m) with adjacency lists. DFS detects cycles (visited non-parent in undirected graphs, grey vertices in directed ones), and both underpin connected components and bipartite checks. Topological sort orders a DAG so every edge points forward, using Kahn's in-degree method or reversed DFS finishing times.
key_points: Graph traversals use a visited array so cycles do not cause infinite loops.
BFS uses a queue, explores level by level, and gives shortest paths by edge count in unweighted graphs.
DFS uses recursion or a stack, goes deep first, then backtracks.
BFS and DFS take O(n + m) with adjacency lists, O(n²) with an adjacency matrix.
Undirected cycle: DFS meets a visited vertex that is not its parent; directed cycle: DFS meets a grey (in-progress) vertex.
Topological sort orders a DAG so every edge u → v has u before v; Kahn's algorithm uses in-degrees.
Repeated BFS/DFS from unvisited vertices finds all connected components.
lessons.tip: When tracing BFS or DFS, keep three columns on paper: current vertex, queue (or stack) contents, and visited set. Process neighbours strictly in the order given in the adjacency list; most wrong answers come from picking neighbours in a different order.
lessons.task: Draw a graph of 7 places you visit in a week (home, school, mosque, market, a friend's house...) with edges where you travel directly between them. Run BFS and DFS from home on paper and write both visit orders.

quiz.q: Which data structure does BFS use?
quiz.explain: BFS processes vertices in the order they are discovered: FIFO.

quiz.q: For our example graph (A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D, D–E, alphabetical lists), what is the DFS order from A?
quiz.explain: A, then B, then D, then C (D's first unvisited neighbour), back to D, then E.

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of BFS with adjacency lists?
quiz.explain: Each vertex and each adjacency list entry is handled once.

quiz.q: Which graphs have a topological order?
quiz.explain: A cycle makes it impossible to put every vertex before its successors.

quiz.q: In Kahn's algorithm, which vertices are put into the queue first?
quiz.explain: Vertices with no incoming edges have no prerequisites and can come first.

lessons.title: Searching: Linear and Binary Search
lessons.content:
Your mother asks you to find the electricity bill from March in a drawer full of papers. If the papers are thrown in randomly, you have no choice but to pick them up one by one until you find it. But if your father keeps them in a file sorted by month, you can open the file near the middle, see 'June', flip back, see 'February', flip forward a little, and there is March. The first method is linear search; the second is binary search. They are the two most basic searching techniques, and the difference between them is enormous on large data.

What searching is: Searching means finding whether a target value (the key) exists in a collection, and if so, where. A successful search returns its position (or the record); an unsuccessful search reports 'not found', often by returning −1. Searching is the most frequent operation in computing: checking a username at login, finding a product in an online shop, looking up a word in a dictionary. Hash tables and trees from earlier lessons are also searching tools; this lesson focuses on searching in arrays.

Linear (sequential) search: Start at the first element and compare each element with the key until you find it or reach the end. linearSearch(a, n, key): for i = 0 to n − 1: if a[i] == key return i; return −1. It works on any array, sorted or not, and on linked lists too. It needs no preparation and no extra memory.

Linear search analysis: Best case: the key is the first element, 1 comparison, O(1). Worst case: the key is last or absent, n comparisons, O(n). Average case for a successful search, if every position is equally likely: (1 + 2 + ... + n) / n = (n + 1) / 2 comparisons, still O(n). For 1,000 items that is about 500 comparisons on average and 1,000 in the worst case.

Sentinel linear search: Each loop round of linear search actually makes two checks: 'is i < n?' and 'is a[i] == key?'. A small trick removes the first one. Save the last element, place the key itself at the end of the array as a sentinel, and loop while a[i] != key, without checking the bound, because the loop is guaranteed to stop at the sentinel. Afterwards, restore the last element and check whether you stopped before the end or the original last element was the key. The complexity is still O(n), but each step does less work.

Improving linear search for repeated lookups: If some items are searched much more often than others, move-to-front (move a found item to the start) or transposition (swap a found item with the one before it) makes popular items quicker to reach next time. These are self-organising lists. They help in practice, for example in a phone's recent-call list, but the worst case remains O(n).

Binary search, the idea: Binary search works only on a sorted array. Compare the key with the middle element. If equal, done. If the key is smaller, it can only be in the left half; if larger, only in the right half. Throw away the other half and repeat on the remaining half. Each comparison halves the search range, which is the same halving idea as the number-guessing game and the binary search tree.

Binary search, iterative code: low = 0, high = n − 1. While low <= high: mid = low + (high − low) / 2; if a[mid] == key return mid; else if a[mid] < key, low = mid + 1; else high = mid − 1. When the loop ends without finding the key, return −1. Notice the + 1 and − 1: mid itself has already been checked, so it must be excluded, otherwise the loop can get stuck.

Trace, successful search: Array [3, 8, 15, 21, 27, 34, 42, 56, 63, 77], key 42. low 0, high 9, mid 4: a[4] = 27 < 42, so low = 5. low 5, high 9, mid 7: a[7] = 56 > 42, so high = 6. low 5, high 6, mid 5: a[5] = 34 < 42, so low = 6. low 6, high 6, mid 6: a[6] = 42, found at index 6 after 4 comparisons. Linear search would have needed 7.

Trace, unsuccessful search: Same array, key 10. low 0, high 9, mid 4: 27 > 10, high = 3. low 0, high 3, mid 1: 8 < 10, low = 2. low 2, high 3, mid 2: 15 > 10, high = 1. Now low (2) > high (1), so the loop stops: not found. Interestingly, low = 2 is exactly the index where 10 would be inserted to keep the array sorted, which is useful for insertion and 'lower bound' queries.

Binary search analysis: After k comparisons the range has about n / 2^k elements, and the search ends when the range is empty, so the number of comparisons in the worst case is ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1. For n = 10 that is 4; for n = 1,000 it is 10; for n = 1,000,000 it is 20; for a billion, about 30. Best case O(1) (the middle element is the key), worst and average O(log n). Space O(1) for the iterative version.

Recursive binary search: binarySearch(a, low, high, key): if low > high return −1; mid = low + (high − low) / 2; if a[mid] == key return mid; if key < a[mid] return binarySearch(a, low, mid − 1, key); else return binarySearch(a, mid + 1, high, key). It is the same algorithm, written as a recursion on a smaller range. It uses O(log n) stack space; since the recursive call is the last action, it is tail recursive and easy to turn into the loop above.

The famous overflow bug: Many programs once computed mid = (low + high) / 2. If low and high are both large, their sum can exceed the largest value an int can hold, producing a negative number and a crash. This bug sat unnoticed for years in widely used libraries, including Java's, until it was reported in 2006. Writing mid = low + (high − low) / 2 gives the same value without overflow. Exams and interviewers like to ask about it.

Variants: first and last occurrence: With duplicates, plain binary search returns any matching index. To find the first occurrence, when a[mid] == key, record mid and continue searching the left half (high = mid − 1); to find the last, continue in the right half. The count of a key in a sorted array is last − first + 1, found in O(log n). Lower bound (first element ≥ key) and upper bound (first element > key) are standard library functions in C++, and Python's bisect module does the same.

Binary search beyond arrays: The same halving idea works whenever a yes/no question flips once over a range. For example, the smallest speed at which a delivery rider can finish all deliveries in 8 hours can be found by binary searching over possible speeds. Finding a square root to a given precision, or the first bad software version among 100 releases (as tools like git bisect do), are other examples. Any monotonic condition can be binary searched.

Other searching methods: Jump search checks every √n-th element to find the right block, then searches linearly inside it: O(√n), useful when jumping backwards is expensive. Interpolation search guesses the position from the key's value, like opening a dictionary near the back for a word starting with 'w'; on uniformly distributed sorted data its average is O(log log n), but its worst case is O(n). Exponential search doubles the range (1, 2, 4, 8, ...) until it passes the key, then binary searches, useful for unbounded or very long lists.

Linear versus binary, when to use which: Binary search needs a sorted array with O(1) random access. If the data is unsorted and searched only once, sorting first (O(n log n)) costs more than a single linear search (O(n)). If the data is searched many times, sorting once and then binary searching wins quickly. Binary search does not work well on linked lists, because reaching the middle is O(n). For frequent inserts plus searches, a balanced BST or hash table is better than a sorted array.

Real life example 1, finding your result on the board website: When SSC results are published, millions of students search by roll number. The results are kept sorted (or indexed) by roll number, so the server can find any roll with about 20 to 25 comparisons using binary search or a tree index, rather than scanning millions of records. That is a big part of why result sites can answer quickly even on result day.

Real life example 2, the dictionary and the phone book: Looking up 'nostalgia' in a printed dictionary, you open somewhere in the middle, see 'mango', flip right, see 'peacock', flip left, and narrow down. You are doing binary search, slightly improved by interpolation, since you open near 'n' rather than at the exact middle. The old printed telephone directories worked the same way, sorted by name.

Real life example 3, finding the bug that broke the app: A Flutter team notices that version 50 of their app crashes, but version 1 was fine. Testing every version would take 50 builds. Binary search over versions: test 25 (fine), then 38 (crashes), then 31 (fine), and so on. About 6 tests (since 2^6 = 64) pinpoint the first bad version. Git's bisect command automates exactly this.

Common mistakes: Using binary search on an unsorted array. Writing while (low < high) instead of while (low <= high), which skips the last remaining element. Setting low = mid or high = mid instead of mid ± 1, causing infinite loops. Computing mid with possible overflow. Returning a wrong index after the loop. Forgetting that linear search works on unsorted data and linked lists, while binary search does not.

What exams ask: Write algorithms for linear and binary search (iterative and recursive). Trace binary search on a given array for a present and an absent key, showing low, high and mid at each step. State the best, average and worst case complexity of both. Find the maximum number of comparisons for a given n. Compare linear and binary search. Explain the sentinel technique, or find the first occurrence of a key.

Recap: Linear search checks elements one by one, works on any data, and costs O(n). Binary search needs sorted data with random access and halves the range each step, costing O(log n) with at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons. Write mid as low + (high − low)/2, update with mid ± 1 and loop while low <= high. Variants find first or last occurrences and insertion points, and the halving idea solves many problems beyond arrays. Next, we learn how to sort, so that binary search has sorted data to work on.
key_points: Linear search checks each element in turn: O(n) worst and average, works on unsorted data.
Binary search needs a sorted array and halves the range each step: O(log n).
Binary search makes at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons (20 for a million items).
Use mid = low + (high − low) / 2 to avoid integer overflow.
Loop while low <= high and move low = mid + 1 or high = mid − 1.
Variants find the first/last occurrence and the insertion point (lower/upper bound).
Sorting once pays off when data is searched many times.
lessons.tip: For every binary search trace, make a table with columns low, high, mid, a[mid] and decision. Stop only when you find the key or low becomes greater than high, and write that condition explicitly.
lessons.task: Write 16 numbers in sorted order on a page. Ask a friend to pick one secretly. Find it using only 'higher or lower' answers and count your guesses. Repeat three times; you should never need more than 5.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case number of comparisons for binary search on 1,000 sorted items?
Which condition must hold for binary search to work?
options: The array must have no duplicates
The array size must be a power of two
The array must be stored in a linked list
quiz.explain: Discarding half the range relies on the order of elements.

quiz.q: Why is mid = low + (high − low) / 2 preferred over (low + high) / 2?
options: It avoids integer overflow when low and high are large
quiz.explain: low + high may exceed the int range; the difference never does.

quiz.q: What is the average-case complexity of linear search?
quiz.explain: About (n + 1)/2 comparisons for a successful search, which is O(n).

quiz.q: Searching [3, 8, 15, 21, 27, 34, 42, 56, 63, 77] for 42, what is the first mid index checked?

lessons.title: Simple Sorting: Bubble, Selection and Insertion
lessons.content:
Think about how you sort a hand of cards in a game of call break. Most people pick up the cards one at a time and slide each new card into the right place among the cards already held. Others spread all thirteen cards out, find the smallest, put it at the left, then find the next smallest, and so on. Both methods work, and both are easy to understand. They are, in fact, insertion sort and selection sort, two of the three simple sorting algorithms every computer science student learns first.

What sorting is: Sorting means arranging items in order, usually ascending (smallest first) or descending, by some key: numbers by value, names alphabetically, students by GPA, transactions by date. Sorting matters because sorted data makes so many other tasks easy: binary search, finding duplicates (they become neighbours), finding the median, merging lists and presenting results to people. Many algorithms start with 'first, sort the data'.

Words to know: An in-place sort uses only O(1) extra memory beyond the array itself. A stable sort keeps items with equal keys in their original relative order; if Rahim and Karim both have GPA 3.75 and Rahim came first in the input, a stable sort keeps Rahim first. An adaptive sort runs faster on input that is already nearly sorted. A comparison sort decides order only by comparing pairs of keys. All three algorithms in this lesson are comparison sorts with O(n²) worst-case time.

Bubble sort, the idea: Walk through the array comparing each pair of neighbours, and swap them if they are in the wrong order. After the first pass, the largest element has 'bubbled up' to the last position, like a big air bubble rising in water. The second pass does the same on the first n − 1 elements, placing the second largest, and so on. After n − 1 passes, the array is sorted.

Bubble sort trace: Sort [5, 2, 9, 1, 6]. Pass 1: 5 and 2 swap, giving [2, 5, 9, 1, 6]; 5 and 9 stay; 9 and 1 swap, [2, 5, 1, 9, 6]; 9 and 6 swap, [2, 5, 1, 6, 9]. Now 9 is in place. Pass 2: 2 and 5 stay; 5 and 1 swap, [2, 1, 5, 6, 9]; 5 and 6 stay. Pass 3: 2 and 1 swap, [1, 2, 5, 6, 9]; 2 and 5 stay. Pass 4: 1 and 2 stay, and no swaps happened at all, so we can stop.

Bubble sort code and the early-exit flag: for pass = 0 to n − 2: swapped = false; for j = 0 to n − 2 − pass: if a[j] > a[j + 1]: swap them; swapped = true. If swapped is still false after a pass, break. Without the flag, bubble sort always does n(n − 1)/2 comparisons. With the flag, a sorted array needs only one pass of n − 1 comparisons, so the best case becomes O(n).

Bubble sort analysis: Worst case (reverse sorted): n(n − 1)/2 comparisons and the same number of swaps, O(n²). Average O(n²). Best case with the flag: O(n). It is in place and stable, because it swaps only neighbours that are strictly out of order, so equal items never jump over each other. It is easy to write and explain, but in practice it is usually the slowest of the three because it does many swaps.

Selection sort, the idea: Divide the array into a sorted part on the left (initially empty) and an unsorted part on the right. Repeatedly find the minimum of the unsorted part and swap it into the first position of the unsorted part, which then joins the sorted part. for i = 0 to n − 2: minIndex = i; for j = i + 1 to n − 1: if a[j] < a[minIndex], minIndex = j; swap a[i] and a[minIndex].

Selection sort trace: Sort [5, 2, 9, 1, 6]. i = 0: the minimum of the whole array is 1 at index 3; swap with index 0, giving [1, 2, 9, 5, 6]. i = 1: the minimum of [2, 9, 5, 6] is 2, already in place. i = 2: the minimum of [9, 5, 6] is 5 at index 3; swap, giving [1, 2, 5, 9, 6]. i = 3: the minimum of [9, 6] is 6; swap, giving [1, 2, 5, 6, 9]. Done after n − 1 = 4 rounds.

Selection sort analysis: It always does n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, whatever the input, so best, average and worst are all O(n²); it is not adaptive. But it does at most n − 1 swaps, the fewest of the simple sorts, which helps when writing to memory is expensive, such as on flash storage. It is in place. The usual array version is not stable: sorting [4a, 4b, 1] swaps 1 with 4a, giving [1, 4b, 4a], so the two 4s have changed order.

Insertion sort, the idea: Like sorting cards in your hand. Keep the left part sorted. Take the next element (the key), and shift every larger element in the sorted part one place to the right until you find the spot where the key belongs; drop it there. for i = 1 to n − 1: key = a[i]; j = i − 1; while j >= 0 and a[j] > key: a[j + 1] = a[j]; j = j − 1; then a[j + 1] = key.

Insertion sort trace: Sort [5, 2, 9, 1, 6]. i = 1, key 2: 5 > 2, shift 5 right; insert 2 at index 0: [2, 5, 9, 1, 6]. i = 2, key 9: 5 is not greater, nothing moves. i = 3, key 1: shift 9, 5 and 2 right; insert 1 at index 0: [1, 2, 5, 9, 6]. i = 4, key 6: shift 9; 5 is not greater; insert 6: [1, 2, 5, 6, 9]. Total shifts: 1 + 0 + 3 + 1 = 5.

Insertion sort analysis: Worst case (reverse sorted): every key shifts past all previous elements, about n²/2 shifts, O(n²). Best case (already sorted): each key is compared once and never moves, so O(n). In general, the number of shifts equals the number of inversions in the array, pairs that are out of order; [5, 2, 9, 1, 6] has exactly 5 inversions, (5,2), (5,1), (2,1), (9,1) and (9,6), matching our 5 shifts. Insertion sort is in place, stable (because of the strict > in the loop), adaptive and online: it can sort items as they arrive one by one.

Why insertion sort matters in practice: For small arrays, say fewer than about 10 to 50 elements, insertion sort is often faster than the clever O(n log n) algorithms, because its loop is tiny and it moves data with very little overhead. That is why library sorts commonly switch to insertion sort for small pieces, for example inside quick sort or merge sort implementations, and Python's built-in sort (Timsort) uses insertion sort on short runs.

Comparing the three: Bubble: best O(n) with flag, worst O(n²), up to O(n²) swaps, stable, in place. Selection: always O(n²) comparisons, at most n − 1 swaps, not stable, in place. Insertion: best O(n), worst O(n²), shifts equal to inversions, stable, in place, adaptive, online. In practice, insertion sort is usually the best of the three, selection sort is useful when swaps are expensive, and bubble sort is mostly a teaching tool.

Shell sort, a quick look: Insertion sort is slow on random data because each element moves only one step at a time. Shell sort, invented by Donald Shell in 1959, first does insertion sort on elements far apart (for example, every 5th element), then on closer elements (every 3rd), and finally a normal insertion sort with gap 1. The early passes move items long distances cheaply, so the final pass has little work to do. Its exact running time depends on the gap sequence chosen; with good sequences it is far faster than O(n²) in practice.

Sorting records by a key: Real programs rarely sort bare numbers. They sort records, such as students with name, roll and GPA, by one field, the key. The algorithms are identical; only the comparison changes: compare a[j].gpa instead of a[j]. Stability becomes important here: to sort students by GPA and, within equal GPAs, by roll number, you can first sort by roll and then do a stable sort by GPA. A stable sort keeps the roll order inside each GPA group.

Real life example 1, arranging the class for a photo: The photographer at a school in Rajshahi wants students lined up by height. He walks along the line swapping any neighbours who are in the wrong order, again and again, until no swaps are needed: bubble sort. If instead he picks the shortest child from the crowd and places them first, then the next shortest, that is selection sort, which needs the fewest moves of children, useful if each move is slow and fussy.

Real life example 2, a shopkeeper's receipts: A grocery shop owner keeps today's receipts in a sorted pile by time. When a customer comes back with an old receipt to add, he slides it into the right place in the pile, moving later receipts aside: insertion sort, online, one item at a time. Because the pile is almost sorted all day, each insertion is quick, which is exactly where insertion sort shines.

Real life example 3, ranking a quiz competition: A school quiz has 30 teams with scores. The organiser needs a ranking by score, and for teams with equal scores, the team that finished earlier must stay ahead. The finishing order is the input order, so a stable sort like insertion sort or bubble sort keeps tied teams in finishing order automatically, while selection sort might swap them unfairly.

Common mistakes: In bubble sort, running the inner loop to n − 1 every pass instead of n − 1 − pass (wasteful, though still correct) or to n (out of bounds). In selection sort, swapping inside the inner loop instead of once per pass. In insertion sort, using >= instead of >, which makes it unstable, or forgetting the j >= 0 check. Claiming selection sort has a best case of O(n). Forgetting that the bubble sort best case of O(n) needs the swapped flag.

What exams ask: Write algorithms for bubble, selection and insertion sort. Trace each on a given array, showing the array after every pass. Count comparisons and swaps. State best, average and worst complexities and explain why. Define stable, in-place and adaptive sorting and classify each algorithm. Explain why insertion sort is good for nearly sorted data and small arrays. Show with an example why selection sort is not stable.

Recap: Bubble sort swaps neighbours and bubbles the largest to the end each pass; with an early-exit flag its best case is O(n). Selection sort repeatedly selects the minimum, always O(n²) comparisons but only n − 1 swaps, and is not stable. Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by shifting larger elements, costs O(n + inversions), is stable, adaptive and online, and is the practical winner for small or nearly sorted data. All three are in place and O(n²) in the worst case; next we break the n² barrier with merge sort and quick sort.
key_points: Bubble sort swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs; the largest bubbles to the end each pass.
With a 'swapped' flag, bubble sort's best case is O(n); worst and average are O(n²).
Selection sort always makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons but at most n − 1 swaps; not stable.
Insertion sort shifts larger elements to insert each key; best O(n), worst O(n²).
Insertion sort's work equals the number of inversions; it is stable, adaptive and online.
Stable sorts keep equal keys in their original order; in-place sorts use O(1) extra memory.
Libraries use insertion sort for small pieces because it is fast on small or nearly sorted data.
lessons.tip: When tracing a sort, write the full array on a new line after every pass and draw a vertical bar between the sorted and unsorted parts. Examiners check the intermediate lines, and the bar keeps you from re-sorting the finished part.
lessons.task: Write the ages of 6 family members on paper slips. Sort them three times, once with each algorithm, counting comparisons and swaps (or shifts) each time. Which method needed the fewest moves of slips?

quiz.q: After the first pass of bubble sort on [4, 1, 3, 2], what is the array?
quiz.explain: Swaps: 4–1, 4–3, 4–2, so 4 bubbles to the end.

quiz.q: Which algorithm makes at most n − 1 swaps?
quiz.explain: It swaps once per pass to place the minimum.

quiz.q: What is the best-case time of insertion sort?
quiz.explain: On sorted input, each key is compared once and never shifted.

quiz.q: Which of these simple sorts is NOT stable in its usual array form?
quiz.explain: A long-distance swap can jump an item past an equal one.

quiz.q: How many inversions does [3, 1, 2] have?
quiz.explain: The out-of-order pairs are (3, 1) and (3, 2).

lessons.title: Fast Sorting and Course Wrap-Up
lessons.content:
Suppose the education board has to sort the exam scripts of a million students by roll number. With insertion sort, about n²/4 shifts on random data means roughly 250 billion moves; even at a hundred million moves per second, that is over 40 minutes, and it gets four times worse every time the data doubles. With merge sort or quick sort, it takes about n log₂ n ≈ 20 million steps, a fraction of a second. The difference is not a faster computer; it is a smarter idea called divide and conquer. This final lesson covers the fast sorts and then pulls the whole course together.

Divide and conquer: Split a problem into smaller subproblems of the same kind, solve them recursively, and combine their answers. If splitting and combining are cheap, the whole thing is fast. Binary search used a simple form (keep one half). Merge sort and quick sort split an array into parts, sort the parts recursively, and then either merge them (merge sort) or arrange things so no merging is needed (quick sort).

Merge sort, the idea: If the array has 0 or 1 elements, it is already sorted. Otherwise split it into two halves, sort each half recursively, and merge the two sorted halves into one sorted array. mergeSort(a, l, r): if l >= r return; m = (l + r) / 2; mergeSort(a, l, m); mergeSort(a, m + 1, r); merge(a, l, m, r). All the real work happens in the merge step.

The merge step: Given two sorted lists, repeatedly compare their front elements and move the smaller one to the output. When one list runs out, copy the rest of the other. Merge [3, 27, 38, 43] and [9, 10, 82]: 3 vs 9, take 3; 27 vs 9, take 9; 27 vs 10, take 10; 27 vs 82, take 27; 38 vs 82, take 38; 43 vs 82, take 43; the left list is empty, copy 82. Result [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82]. Merging lists of total length n takes O(n) time and needs a temporary array of size n.

Merge sort trace: Sort [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]. Split into [38, 27, 43, 3] and [9, 82, 10]. The left splits into [38, 27] and [43, 3], which become [27, 38] and [3, 43], then merge to [3, 27, 38, 43]. The right splits into [9, 82] and [10]; [9, 82] stays as it is, and merging with [10] gives [9, 10, 82]. Finally merge the two halves as above: [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82].

Merge sort analysis: The recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn: two half-size sorts plus a linear merge. The recursion tree has about log₂ n levels, and each level does O(n) total merging work, so T(n) = O(n log n). This holds in the best, average and worst case alike: merge sort is not fooled by bad input. It is stable if the merge takes from the left list when two elements are equal. Its weakness is the O(n) extra memory for merging. On linked lists, merging only relinks nodes, so merge sort is the natural choice there.

Quick sort, the idea: Pick an element called the pivot. Partition the array so that every element smaller than the pivot is on its left and every larger element is on its right; the pivot is then in its final sorted position. Recursively sort the left part and the right part. No merging is needed, because after partitioning, everything on the left is already smaller than everything on the right. Quick sort was invented by Tony Hoare around 1960.

Lomuto partition: A simple partition scheme uses the last element as the pivot. Keep an index i marking the end of the 'small' region, starting at l − 1. For j from l to r − 1: if a[j] <= pivot, increase i and swap a[i] with a[j]. Finally swap a[i + 1] with the pivot at a[r]; the pivot now sits at index i + 1. Another classic scheme, Hoare's partition, moves two pointers inwards from both ends and usually does fewer swaps; textbooks use either.

Partition trace: [7, 2, 1, 8, 6, 3, 5, 4], pivot 4, i = −1. j = 0: 7 > 4, skip. j = 1: 2 <= 4, i = 0, swap a[0] and a[1]: [2, 7, 1, 8, 6, 3, 5, 4]. j = 2: 1 <= 4, i = 1, swap: [2, 1, 7, 8, 6, 3, 5, 4]. j = 3 and 4: 8 and 6 are bigger, skip. j = 5: 3 <= 4, i = 2, swap a[2] and a[5]: [2, 1, 3, 8, 6, 7, 5, 4]. j = 6: 5 > 4, skip. Finally swap a[3] with the pivot: [2, 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 5, 8]. The pivot 4 is at index 3, its final place; now sort [2, 1, 3] and [6, 7, 5, 8] recursively.

Quick sort analysis: Partitioning n elements is O(n). If the pivot splits the array roughly in half each time, the recurrence is again T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn = O(n log n), and the average case over random inputs is also O(n log n). But if the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, for example choosing the last element on an already sorted array, each partition removes only one element: T(n) = T(n − 1) + cn = O(n²). Quick sort is in place apart from the recursion stack (O(log n) on average), and it is not stable.

Avoiding the worst case: Choose the pivot randomly, or use the median of the first, middle and last elements (median-of-three). With a random pivot, the expected time is O(n log n) for every input. Practical libraries go further: C++'s std::sort is typically introsort, which starts with quick sort, switches to heap sort if the recursion gets too deep (guaranteeing O(n log n)), and uses insertion sort on small pieces. Quick sort is often the fastest in practice because its inner loop is simple and cache-friendly.

The n log n barrier: Can a comparison sort beat O(n log n)? No. Any algorithm that sorts only by comparing pairs must, in the worst case, make at least about log₂(n!) comparisons, because there are n! possible orderings and each comparison has two outcomes, like a yes/no decision tree. log₂(n!) grows like n log₂ n. So merge sort and heap sort are asymptotically optimal comparison sorts. To go faster, an algorithm must use something other than comparisons, such as the digits of the keys.

Counting sort: If keys are integers in a small range 0 to k, count how many times each value appears in an array count[0..k], then compute running totals to find where each value's block starts, and place each element into an output array. For marks out of 100 for 50,000 students, k = 100, and the sort is O(n + k), linear. Counting sort can be made stable by placing elements from the end of the input backwards. It needs O(n + k) extra space, so it is only practical when k is not huge.

Radix sort: Sort numbers digit by digit, starting from the least significant digit, using a stable sort (often counting sort) for each digit. Example [170, 45, 75, 90, 802, 24, 2, 66]. By ones digit: 170, 90, 802, 2, 24, 45, 75, 66. By tens: 802, 2, 24, 45, 66, 170, 75, 90. By hundreds: 2, 24, 45, 66, 75, 90, 170, 802. Sorted. With d digits and base b, the cost is O(d × (n + b)). Stability at each step is essential: it keeps the order produced by earlier digits.

Comparison table: Bubble, selection, insertion: O(n²) worst, in place; insertion is stable and O(n) on sorted data. Merge sort: O(n log n) always, stable, O(n) extra space. Quick sort: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst, in place, not stable, often fastest in practice. Heap sort: O(n log n) always, in place, not stable. Counting sort: O(n + k), stable, small integer keys only. Radix sort: O(d(n + b)), stable, fixed-length keys. Python's built-in sort, Timsort, is a stable hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort; Java uses Timsort for objects and a dual-pivot quick sort for primitive arrays.

Choosing a sort: For small arrays or nearly sorted data, insertion sort. For a guaranteed O(n log n) with stability, merge sort (or Timsort). For general in-memory sorting where speed matters and stability does not, quick sort with a good pivot or introsort. When memory is tight and you need a guarantee, heap sort. For small integer keys like marks or ages, counting sort; for fixed-length numbers or strings like phone numbers, radix sort. For data too large for memory, external merge sort, which sorts chunks and merges them from disk.

Course wrap-up, the toolbox: Look back at what you can now do. Arrays give O(1) indexing; dynamic arrays grow with O(1) amortized appends. Linked lists give O(1) insertion and deletion at known positions. Stacks (LIFO) handle undo, brackets, expressions and recursion; queues (FIFO) handle fairness, buffering and BFS. Trees organise hierarchies; BSTs and balanced trees like AVL keep keys sorted with O(log n) operations; heaps serve priority queues; B-trees and tries serve disks and strings. Hash tables give O(1) average lookups. Graphs model networks, explored by BFS and DFS.

Course wrap-up, the method: Every time you meet a problem, ask: what operations do I need, how often, and on how much data? Do I need order, or just membership? Is the data fixed or changing? Then pick the structure whose costs fit, and measure with Big O, remembering the hidden constants, memory, cache behaviour and worst cases. This way of thinking, more than any single algorithm, is what employers and contest judges look for.

Real life example 1, sorting Daraz search results: When you search 'headphones' and choose 'price: low to high', the server sorts thousands of matching products by price. Engineers usually use a stable library sort, so that products with the same price keep their relevance order from before. For the top results only, they might use a heap to pick the cheapest 40 without sorting everything.

Real life example 2, preparing an SSC merit list: The board sorts over a million results by GPA (descending), and within equal GPAs by total marks, then by roll. Using a stable sort three times, from the least important key to the most important (roll, then marks, then GPA), produces the right order, the same principle as radix sort. Since GPA takes only a few distinct values, a counting-sort-style grouping by GPA is extremely fast.

Real life example 3, your contacts app, end to end: Contacts are stored in a database indexed by a B-tree; the app loads them into a dynamic array and sorts them by name with Timsort; typing a prefix walks a trie; the recent calls list is a deque capped at a fixed size; favourites are a hash set for O(1) 'is this a favourite?' checks; and syncing with the cloud uses a queue of pending changes. One everyday app quietly uses almost every structure from this course.

Common mistakes: Saying quick sort is always O(n log n); its worst case is O(n²). Saying merge sort is in place; standard array merge sort needs O(n) extra space. Forgetting that the partition places the pivot in its final position. Using counting sort when the key range k is enormous. Running radix sort with an unstable per-digit sort. Writing the merge step so that it is not stable by taking from the right list on ties.

What exams ask: Explain divide and conquer. Write and trace merge sort and quick sort (with a given partition scheme) on an array, showing every split, merge or partition. Derive their recurrences and complexities, including quick sort's worst case and when it happens. Compare all sorting algorithms in a table (time, space, stability, in place). Explain the Ω(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorting. Trace counting sort or radix sort. Choose a suitable sort for a described situation.

Recap: Merge sort splits, sorts halves and merges in O(n log n) always, stably, with O(n) extra space. Quick sort partitions around a pivot, is O(n log n) on average and usually fastest in practice, but O(n²) in the worst case unless the pivot is chosen well. No comparison sort can beat Ω(n log n), but counting and radix sort can by using the keys themselves. With these sorts and every structure before them, you have the full Data Structures toolbox. Next comes the Algorithms course, where you will use these tools for shortest paths, spanning trees, dynamic programming and more.
key_points: Divide and conquer: split, solve recursively, combine.
Merge sort is O(n log n) in every case and stable, but needs O(n) extra memory.
Quick sort partitions around a pivot: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst, in place, not stable.
Random or median-of-three pivots avoid quick sort's worst case in practice.
Comparison sorts need Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.
Counting sort (O(n + k)) and radix sort (O(d(n + b))) beat n log n using key values.
Choose structures and algorithms by the operations, data size and guarantees you need.
lessons.tip: For merge sort, draw the splitting tree downward and the merging tree upward on the same page. For quick sort, underline the pivot and box its final position after each partition. Pictures make both traces quick and easy to check.
lessons.task: Write 8 random two-digit numbers on cards. Sort them once with merge sort (split into piles and merge pairs of piles) and once with quick sort (pick the last card as pivot and partition). Count the comparisons in each and compare with insertion sort on the same cards.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort?
quiz.explain: It always splits in half and merges in linear time: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn.

quiz.q: When does quick sort with the last element as pivot hit its O(n²) worst case?
options: When n is a power of two
quiz.explain: Each partition then removes only the pivot, giving n − 1 levels.

quiz.q: Which sort is stable and guarantees O(n log n) but needs O(n) extra space?
quiz.explain: Merging into a temporary array costs O(n) memory.

quiz.q: Why can counting sort run faster than O(n log n)?
options: It uses the key values directly instead of comparisons
quiz.explain: The n log n lower bound applies only to comparison sorts.

quiz.q: After Lomuto partition of [7, 2, 1, 8, 6, 3, 5, 4] with pivot 4, where is the pivot?
quiz.explain: Three elements (2, 1, 3) are smaller, so 4 lands at index 3.
